how: Throw one six-sided die three times (or three dice in order); the three numbers name one of 216 lines of Homer.

entries.greek: ἄνδρʼ ἀπαμύνασθαι, ὅτε τις πρότερος χαλεπήνῃ.
entries.english: to defend yourself, when someone else starts the quarrel.
entries.reading:
Night on the plain of Troy, a wagon heavy with treasure, and an old man driving it toward the tent of the one who killed his son. Out of the dark steps a young stranger who looks him over and says, kindly enough, that neither Priam nor his herald is fit to fend off a man who picks a fight. It is a hard thing to hear. It is also true. And the stranger is Hermes in disguise, who in the next breath promises to guard the old king rather than harm him.

This line comes to you when you are bracing for a quarrel you did not begin. Someone has pushed, or you fear they will, and you are measuring your strength against theirs and finding it thin. The oracle does not flatter you: there may be a contest here you cannot win by force. But notice the order of things. Defence is honourable when the other hand moves first; it is not your task to strike before you are struck, nor to prove your strength in advance.

Go on with your errand. Keep your purpose clear and your hands open. Help often arrives disguised as a stranger on the road, and the one who notices your weakness may be the one sent to cover it.
entries.context: In Iliad 24, as Priam drives by night to Achilles' camp to ransom Hector's body, Hermes meets him disguised as a young Myrmidon. He remarks that neither the old king nor his aged herald is young enough to fight off a man who starts a quarrel, then promises to protect him rather than harm him.

aspects.love: If a partner or friend has started a quarrel, you may answer it, but answer the words that were said, not the ones you fear are coming. Defend what is true about you calmly, and refuse to be drawn into a battle larger than the one in front of you.
aspects.work: A colleague or rival may be testing you. You need not attack first or match their noise. Keep a clear record, state your position once and plainly, and look around: someone with more standing than you may be willing to walk beside you, if you let them see the road you are on.
aspects.home: In a family, old grievances flare quickly, and it can be hard to tell who struck first. Before you defend yourself, find out whether anyone has actually raised a hand. If they have, speak; if not, let the night pass quietly and arrive at morning with your dignity whole.
aspects.health: You may feel less able to fend things off than you once were: tired, older, more easily knocked. That is not shame; it is information. Let others help carry the load, and save your strength for what truly comes against you, rather than for every shadow at the roadside.
aspects.journeys: You are travelling through unfamiliar ground carrying something precious. Go carefully and do not provoke. If a stranger offers guidance, weigh it with open eyes; the old king accepted an escort in the dark, and it brought him safely to the very place he feared most.

entries.message: You are allowed to defend yourself. You are not required to do it alone.
entries.reflect: Where are you preparing for a fight that no one has yet begun?

entries.greek: θαρσῶν νῦν Διόμηδες ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι μάχεσθαι·
entries.english: Take courage now, Diomedes, and fight against the Trojans.
entries.reading:
An arrow has gone through Diomedes' shoulder, and the blood is welling up through his corslet. A friend has drawn the shaft out, and Diomedes prays, not for rescue, but for the chance to strike back. Athena comes and stands close beside him. Take courage now, she says. She has put into his chest the fearless spirit of his father, and she has taken the mist from his eyes so that he can see which shapes on the field are gods and which are men.

There are two gifts here, and you need both. The first is nerve. You have taken a hit, perhaps a recent one, and part of you has decided to sit the rest of this out. The line says the opposite: now, while the wound is fresh, is when the courage is given. It does not come from nowhere. It comes from what you inherited, the steadiness of people who went before you and stood their ground.

The second gift is sight. Much of your fear comes from not knowing what you face, mistaking ordinary people for giants. Look again, clearly. Then step back into the fight that is yours, and only that one.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, Diomedes has been wounded by an arrow from Pandarus and prays to Athena. She answers him in person, telling him to fight the Trojans with confidence, for she has put his father Tydeus' fearless spirit in his breast and lifted the mist from his eyes so that he can tell gods from men.

aspects.love: A hurt in love has made you cautious, and caution has hardened into hiding. The line asks you to step forward again: to say the honest thing, to ask for the meeting, to show your face. You carry more courage from those who loved you first than you remember.
aspects.work: A setback at work has drawn blood, and you have been quietly retreating. Go back in now, while the matter is still live. Look carefully at the people you are up against: most are ordinary, open to persuasion, and not the immovable powers your worry has made them.
aspects.home: Think of the parent, grandparent or elder whose steadiness you most admired. Some of that spirit lives in you. In a family difficulty now, act as they would have acted: plainly, bravely, without waiting for someone else to go first.
aspects.health: After an injury or a hard season, the body often heals faster than confidence does. Return to ordinary strength gradually but deliberately. Ask for help, as Diomedes did, and then take the step that the help makes possible, rather than waiting until every trace of the wound is gone.
aspects.journeys: A decision has been waiting while you nursed an old wound. The mist is lifting; you can see the shape of the choice more clearly than before. Do not ask for a sign larger than that. Make the move you already know is yours.

entries.message: You have been wounded, not finished. Pray, then stand up: the courage you need is already in your blood.
entries.reflect: What would you attempt if you could see clearly which of your fears are gods and which are only men?

entries.greek: ἦ ῥά νύ τοι μεγάλων δώρων ἐπεμαίετο θυμὸς
entries.english: Truly, your heart was set on great gifts,
entries.reading:
Dolon went out in the dark wearing a wolf's grey skin, a bow on his shoulder, to spy on the Greek ships. His price was the finest horses in the world, the immortal team of Achilles, and Hector had sworn to give them. Caught between Odysseus and Diomedes, his teeth chattering, he blurts out the bargain. Odysseus smiles. Truly, he says, your heart was set on great gifts: horses that no mortal man but Achilles can master or drive.

The smile is the warning. This line is drawn when you are reaching for something dazzling, perhaps promised by someone with no power to give it, perhaps a prize you could not handle if it were placed in your hands. The danger is not in wanting much. It is in wanting so fiercely that you stop counting the risk: the darkness of the road, the two men lying in wait beside it.

Ask yourself plainly who is offering this, what it will cost to reach, and whether you could live with it once it was yours. If the answers are good, go with your eyes open. If they are not, there is no shame in turning back before the night closes round you.
entries.context: In Iliad 10, Odysseus and Diomedes capture the Trojan scout Dolon, who confesses that Hector promised him Achilles' horses and chariot for spying on the Greek ships. Odysseus smiles and says that his heart was set on great gifts indeed, horses that no mortal but Achilles can master; Dolon is soon killed after telling them what they want to know.

aspects.love: You may be drawn to someone partly for what they seem to promise: status, rescue, a different life. Look at the person, not the prize. A love chosen for its glitter asks you to drive horses you cannot master, and the reins will burn your hands.
aspects.work: An offer, a promotion or a venture looks magnificent, and someone is swearing it will be yours. Check who truly controls the reward, and what you are being asked to risk to earn it. Write down the cost before you go out into the dark for it.
aspects.home: Families sometimes push one member toward a great prize, a grand house, a famous school, an inheritance, without asking whether it suits them. If the ambition at home is someone else's, gently say so before it carries you into ground you never chose.
aspects.health: Beware the dazzling goal: the dramatic change, the punishing regime promised to transform you. Choose something you can actually sustain. The horses that serve a person for a lifetime are the ones they can feed, harness and drive on every ordinary day.
aspects.journeys: A big move tempts you with what waits at the far end. Look hard at the road between. Who sent you, and will they still be there when you arrive? Go if the way is sound, but do not let the size of the reward blind you to the dark.

entries.message: Ask what the prize will cost and whether you could even hold it. Some rewards are promised precisely because they can never be delivered.
entries.reflect: If you won the prize you are reaching for, could you actually hold its reins?

entries.greek: νίκην καὶ μέγα κῦδος, ἀτὰρ Δαναοῖσί γε πῆμα·
entries.english: victory and great glory, but ruin for the Greeks.
entries.reading:
Three times Zeus thunders from the peaks of Ida, and Hector hears in it exactly what he wants. I know, he shouts to his men, that the son of Cronus has granted me victory and great glory, and ruin for the Greeks. He boasts that his horses will leap the ditch and that he will set the ships on fire. For a while, he is right. The day is his.

When this card comes, something is shifting in your favour. You may have been pinned down a long time, and now the sky is speaking on your side. Move with it; hesitation in such an hour wastes the gods' good will. But hear the whole line. Your glory and another's ruin arrive in the same breath. Someone will lose what you win, and how you treat them will be remembered longer than the win itself.

And keep a little of your judgement back from the thunder. Hector read one day's sign as the shape of the whole war, and pushed too far. Take what is given today. Do not mistake it for everything, and do not boast of tomorrow's fire.
entries.context: In Iliad 8, Zeus thunders three times from Mount Ida as a sign to the Trojans. Hector calls to his men that he knows the son of Cronus has granted him victory and great glory, and ruin for the Greeks, and he boasts that he will leap their ditch and burn their ships.

aspects.love: A difficult season in a relationship may be ending in your favour: an argument settled, a heart turning toward you. Receive it gracefully. Winning a point is not the same as winning a person, and a partner who feels defeated will not rest easily beside you.
aspects.work: Momentum is with you: a deal, a contest, a role that looked out of reach. Press while the advantage lasts. But be generous to those who lost to you, and resist announcing grand plans; promise only what today's ground can actually hold.
aspects.home: A family decision may go your way. Before you celebrate, look at the one who wanted something else. A kind word to them now keeps the household whole, and the house you have to live in afterwards is worth more than the glory of being right.
aspects.health: A good sign arrives: better results, returning strength, a week of feeling well. Let it encourage you, and keep up the habits that brought it. Do not take one bright day as permission to leap every ditch at once and undo what is mending.
aspects.journeys: The signs favour a bold move, and you can feel the wind at your back. Go. Simply keep the ships of others in mind as you pass: a change that lifts you may unsettle people close to you, and they deserve care in your victory.

entries.message: The tide has turned your way. Take it, but remember that every victory falls on someone, and that a favourable sign is a season, not a promise for ever.
entries.reflect: Who stands on the other side of the victory you are hoping for, and what do you owe them?

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ οὐ πείσονται Τρῶες καὶ Δαρδανίωνες
entries.english: But the Trojans and the Dardanians will not believe it,
entries.reading:
A thunderbolt has struck the ground in front of Diomedes' horses, and they cower back under the chariot. Nestor, who knows when a god is against them, tells him to turn and go. Diomedes is in agony, not from fear of death but from fear of a sentence: Hector will stand among the Trojans and say that the son of Tydeus ran from him. Nestor's answer is this line. Let him say it. The Trojans and the Dardanians will not believe it, nor the women whose husbands you have laid in the dust.

You may be facing a retreat that feels like disgrace: stepping back from a fight, leaving a role, letting someone else have the last word. What hurts most is not the loss itself but the story that will be told about it. The oracle asks you to remember who actually holds your reputation. It is not the loudest voice. It is everyone who has watched what you do, season after season.

So do the wise thing, even if it looks like flight. Turn the horses when the sky is against you. Those who know your record will read the retreat correctly, and those who don't were never going to be convinced.
entries.context: In Iliad 8, Zeus' thunderbolt halts Diomedes' attack and Nestor urges him to turn the chariot and flee. Diomedes is anguished that Hector will boast that he ran away; Nestor replies that even if Hector calls him a coward, the Trojans and Dardanians will not believe it, nor will the widows of the men he has killed.

aspects.love: Someone may be telling a version of you that is unkind: a former partner, a rival, a gossip. Do not exhaust yourself correcting it. The people who love you have seen your daily faithfulness, and a few words from a bitter tongue will not undo years of evidence.
aspects.work: You may need to withdraw from a project, a dispute or a position, and you fear it will look like weakness. Do it anyway if it is right. Colleagues and clients judge by the long record of your work, not by one man's boast on one afternoon.
aspects.home: A relative may criticise a choice you made, loudly and often. Answer once, calmly, and then let your life answer for you. Those who share your table know your character, and in time even the critic will find the story wearing thin.
aspects.health: Stepping back to recover can feel like losing face, especially if you are known as the strong one. Rest is not cowardice. Let the people around you see you take care of yourself, and trust that the regard you have built over years will not vanish in a week.
aspects.journeys: Turning back from a plan, or changing course, may draw comment. Make the decision on its merits. A wise retreat when the signs are against you is a warrior's skill, and anyone whose good opinion matters will understand why you turned the horses.

entries.message: Your name does not live in your enemy's mouth. It lives in what you have actually done, and those who saw it will not forget.
entries.reflect: Whose opinion of you are you guarding most fiercely, and have they ever really known you?

entries.greek: εἰ δʼ ἄγε τοι κεφαλῇ κατανεύσομαι ὄφρα πεποίθῃς·
entries.english: Come, I will nod my head to you, so that you may trust me.
entries.reading:
Thetis has risen from the sea at dawn and climbed to the highest peak of Olympus, where Zeus sits apart from the other gods. She kneels, takes his knees with one hand and his chin with the other, and asks for her son's honour. For a long time he says nothing. He knows Hera will be furious. Then he speaks: Come, I will nod my head to you, so that you may trust me. He bends his dark brows, his immortal hair falls forward, and great Olympus shakes.

This line is about the moment a promise is truly given. You may be waiting on someone's word, or you may be the one asked to give it. Notice what makes Zeus's nod worth having. It is not easy for him. It will cost him a quarrel at home. And once given, it is never taken back; his whole standing rests on that.

If you are seeking assurance, look for that kind: not quick yeses, but a pledge given with its cost in view. If you are making one, nod slowly, and only to what you will carry through. A single kept promise shakes more mountains than a hundred easy ones.
entries.context: In Iliad 1, Thetis clasps Zeus' knees on Olympus and begs him to give the Trojans the upper hand until the Greeks honour her son Achilles. Zeus, uneasy about Hera's anger, agrees and says he will nod his head so that she may trust him, for his nod is the greatest pledge among the gods and is never revoked.

aspects.love: A commitment is on the table, spoken or not. Whether you are asking for it or giving it, let it be real: said once, clearly, with its cost understood. A partner who hesitates before promising may well be the one whose word will hold.
aspects.work: An agreement is near. Make sure the essential undertaking is clearly stated, in words both sides understand. And be careful what you nod to yourself; your reliability is your most valuable asset, and a pledge you cannot keep will cost more than a deal you decline.
aspects.home: Someone in your family needs to know they can count on you. Tell them plainly what you will do, and then do it, even when it becomes inconvenient. Children especially learn trust from promises that are kept when keeping them is hard.
aspects.health: Make one promise to your body and keep it: a walk each morning, an earlier night, a meal eaten sitting down. Small and unbreakable is better than grand and abandoned. Let your own word to yourself become something you can trust.
aspects.journeys: A big decision waits on your yes. Do not give it lightly or under pressure. Sit with it until you can nod knowing what it will cost and what it will bring. Then commit fully, without the backward glances that unsettle a firm choice.

entries.message: A real promise costs the one who makes it. Look for the pledge given in spite of difficulty, and give your own the same weight.
entries.reflect: What promise are you being asked to make, and are you ready to let it cost you something?

entries.greek: οὐκ ἐάᾳ Κρονίδης ἐπαμυνέμεν Ἀργείοισιν.
entries.english: The son of Cronus will not allow you to help the Greeks.
entries.reading:
The chariot is already moving. Hera has yoked the horses, Athena has put on her father's armour, and the gates of heaven, kept by the Hours, have groaned open of their own accord. They are going to save the Greeks, whom they love, against the express command of Zeus. From the ridges of Ida he sees them, and sends golden-winged Iris to meet them at the gates. The son of Cronus will not allow it, she says. Go on, and he will lame your horses and shatter your chariot. They turn back.

This is a hard card for those who love fiercely. Someone you care for is struggling, and you are ready, armed and harnessed, to rush in. The line says the way is closed. Perhaps the matter is not yours to fix; perhaps your help would make it worse; perhaps a larger order of things must play out before rescue is possible.

Turning back is not the same as abandoning. Hera and Athena did not stop caring for the Greeks; they waited, and their time came. Keep your love ready and your horses fed. Respect the closed gate today. It will not be closed for ever.
entries.context: In Iliad 8, Hera and Athena drive out from Olympus to help the Greeks against Zeus' command. Zeus sends Iris, who stops them at the gates and tells them that the son of Cronus will not allow them to aid the Argives, and repeats his threat to lame their horses and strike them with the thunderbolt. They turn back.

aspects.love: You want to rescue someone you love from a mess of their own: a bad choice, a hard family, a downward stretch. You may not be allowed in yet. Stay near, keep your words kind, and let them know the chariot is ready when they open the gate.
aspects.work: A decision has come from above you, and it blocks the help you wanted to give a colleague, a client or a team. Argue once if you must, then accept it with grace. Defying it openly may cost you the very standing you will need later.
aspects.home: A grown child or a sibling is making a choice you would never make. Your instinct is to intervene. For now, the line says, you cannot. Love them from the threshold, and keep the household a place they can return to without having to admit you were right.
aspects.health: Sometimes the body or sound medical advice closes a gate: no running, no lifting, not yet. Turn the horses round without resentment. Accepting a limit now is how you keep the strength to ride out later, when the way opens again.
aspects.journeys: A plan to go somewhere and help, to move, or to take something on is being stopped by circumstances outside your control. Do not force the gates. Unharness for now, rest your horses, and watch for the day when the same road opens freely.

entries.message: Not every rescue is yours to make. When a greater power has closed the gate, turning back is not betrayal; it is wisdom.
entries.reflect: Whose struggle are you trying to carry that may not be yours to end?

entries.greek: σοὶ δʼ ἐγὼ οὐχ ἅλιος σκοπὸς ἔσσομαι οὐδʼ ἀπὸ δόξης·
entries.english: I will be no useless scout for you, nor fall short of your hopes.
entries.reading:
I will not fail you. It is one of the oldest promises in the world, and Dolon makes it to Hector by the Trojan watch-fires. He is rich, swift on his feet, not much to look at, and he wants the immortal horses of Achilles as his reward. Swear it, he says, and I will go to the Greek ships and bring back everything they plan. Hector swears. Dolon pulls on a wolfskin and sets off into the dark, and never comes back.

This line comes as a mirror. You may be on the point of making a large promise, eager to prove your worth to someone whose good opinion you crave. The words come easily, because you want what lies on the far side of them. But a promise made to win a reward has a way of outrunning the one who makes it. Dolon had the speed, not the cunning, and he ran straight into the two most dangerous men in the Greek camp.

Before you say I won't let you down, ask what you are truly able to deliver, and say that instead. A smaller promise, faithfully kept, will carry you further than a grand one that leads you into the dark.
entries.context: In Iliad 10, at a night council of the Trojans, Dolon offers to spy on the Greek ships if Hector swears to give him Achilles' horses and chariot. He promises Hector he will be no useless scout and will not disappoint his hopes. On the way he is caught and killed by Odysseus and Diomedes.

aspects.love: In the rush of new feeling you may offer more than you can give: always, for ever, never again. Speak from what you know of yourself. A partner is better served by modest, true words than by vows made to win a heart and then quietly abandoned.
aspects.work: You may be tempted to volunteer for the hardest assignment to win a big reward. Check whether you have the skill, not just the will. Promise a clear and achievable result, and ask for the support you will need before you head out alone.
aspects.home: At home it is easy to promise to fix everything: the money, the move, the quarrel. Choose one thing you can actually do this month and do it well. Family trust is built on kept promises, not on brave speeches beside the fire.
aspects.health: Grand resolutions about the body are often Dolon's promises: sincere, eager and quickly broken. Set a goal you are certain you can keep, and let success grow from there. Proving yourself to others is a poor reason to overreach your strength.
aspects.journeys: Before you commit to a venture, a voyage or a change, look honestly at your preparation. Enthusiasm is not a map. Find out what lies between you and the goal, and who might be waiting along the road, before you swear to anyone that you will return in triumph.

entries.message: Promise what you can do, not what you hope to do. A boast made to win a prize is a debt the dark road may call in.
entries.reflect: What are you promising in order to be valued, and could you keep it?

entries.greek: ἔγρεο Τυδέος υἱέ· τί πάννυχον ὕπνον ἀωτεῖς;
entries.english: Wake up, son of Tydeus! Why do you sleep the whole night through?
entries.reading:
It is the middle of the night, and the Trojan fires are burning on the plain so close that the Greeks can almost hear the horses champing. Diomedes is asleep outside his hut, his head on a rolled hide, his comrades' spears driven upright into the ground around him. Old Nestor comes through the dark and stirs him awake with his foot. Wake up, son of Tydeus. Why do you sleep the whole night through? The Trojans are camped almost at the ships.

Something in your life has moved closer than you realise, and you have been resting as if it were still far off. It may be a matter you have been putting off, a relationship drifting, a deadline, a problem quietly settling in beside your door. The oracle does not scold you for being tired; Diomedes had earned his sleep. It simply tells you that this is not the hour for it.

Notice too who wakes you. It is the oldest man in the camp, without ceremony, using his foot. Wisdom often arrives that way: blunt, a little rude, from someone who has seen this before. Do not resent the nudge. Get up, take your spear from the ground, and go and look at the fires.
entries.context: In Iliad 10, in the night after the Trojans have camped on the plain beside the Greek ships, old Nestor goes round waking the leaders. He stirs the sleeping Diomedes with his foot, asking why he sleeps all night when the Trojans are encamped so close to the ships.

aspects.love: A relationship may need your attention more urgently than you think. Small silences, unshared plans, a growing distance: these are fires on the plain. Wake up to them now, while a conversation can still turn things, rather than discovering in daylight how close they have come.
aspects.work: There is a matter at work you have been leaving for later: an overdue report, a competitor's move, an unanswered warning. Later is now. If an older colleague has been nudging you about it, listen, however clumsy their manner, and act tonight rather than tomorrow.
aspects.home: Something at home has been creeping nearer: a leaking roof, an unpaid bill, a child who has gone quiet. It is time to rise and look. A little alertness tonight may spare the whole household a great deal of trouble when morning comes.
aspects.health: Your body may have been sending signals you keep sleeping through. Do not ignore them any longer; take them to someone qualified to advise you. Being woken is uncomfortable, but it is far better than being caught by surprise.
aspects.journeys: A decision you thought was far off is suddenly near. The time for drifting is over. Gather what you need, consult those with experience, and be ready to move; the chance, or the danger, will not wait until you have finished your rest.

entries.message: The danger is camped close, and you are still asleep. Get up; this is a night for watching.
entries.reflect: What have you been sleeping through that is now camped close to your ships?

entries.greek: παύσειε κλαυθμοῖο γόοιό τε δακρυόεντος.
entries.english: that she should cease from her weeping and tearful lament.
entries.reading:
Penelope has learned two things in one day: that her son has sailed away in secret, and that the suitors mean to ambush him on his way home. She has not eaten. She lies in her upper room like a lion ringed by hunters, turning the danger over until sleep finally takes her. Then Athena makes a phantom in the likeness of her sister Iphthime, who lives far away, and sends it slipping in past the door-bolt to stand above her head. It comes for one purpose: that she should cease from her weeping and tearful lament. Your son will come home, it tells her. He has a guardian.

This card is drawn by people who have been carrying fear alone in the dark. You may have gone over the worst so many times that it feels like a duty, as if stopping would mean you no longer cared. The line gently refuses that. Grief and worry have their time, but you are allowed to rest from them.

Watch for comfort in the form of a familiar voice: a sister, an old friend, a dream, a word that reaches you just when you need it. Let it in. Then sleep, and meet tomorrow with a little more strength.
entries.context: In Odyssey 4, Penelope has learned that Telemachus has sailed secretly and that the suitors plan to ambush him; she lies sleepless and fasting. Athena makes a phantom in the form of her sister Iphthime and sends it to her room, so that Penelope might cease from her weeping, and the phantom assures her that her son will come home.

aspects.love: If you are anxious about someone you love who is far away or in difficulty, you cannot ride out to guard them yourself. Reach for the people who share your love for them, and let their company quiet the worst of the fear while you wait for news.
aspects.work: Worry about work may be following you to bed. Write down what troubles you, decide what can be done tomorrow, and then put it down. A mind that is allowed to rest will meet the problem more wisely than one that has wept through the night.
aspects.home: Someone in the household may be grieving or afraid and hiding it. Be the sister at the bedside: sit with them, speak simply, remind them they are not alone. Your presence may do more than any advice you could give.
aspects.health: Sleeplessness and not eating, as Penelope found, make every fear larger. Look after the simple things first: food, rest, a quiet room. If the sorrow will not lift, seek someone trained to help carry it; comfort is meant to be shared.
aspects.journeys: You may be waiting for someone to come back, or for word about a decision far out of your hands. The line offers reassurance, not a timetable. Let yourself be comforted, keep the house in order, and wait with a steadier heart.

entries.message: Comfort is being sent to you, though it may come in a shape you do not expect. You are allowed to stop weeping for a while.
entries.reflect: What would you have to believe in order to let yourself stop weeping tonight?

entries.greek: οὐκ οἶδʼ· οὐ γάρ πώ τις ἑὸν γόνον αὐτὸς ἀνέγνω.
entries.english: I do not know: for no one has ever known for sure who his own father is.
entries.reading:
A tall stranger sits at Telemachus' table, a guest he has welcomed while the suitors carouse around them. Are you really his son, the stranger asks; you have his head and his fine eyes. The young man's answer is sharp with sorrow. My mother says I am. I do not know, for no one has ever known for sure who his own father is. And he wishes he were the son of some luckier man who had grown old among his own possessions.

The bitterness in that reply belongs to someone who has never been shown who he is. Telemachus has grown up in a house full of strangers, with a father he cannot remember. You may know that feeling: uncertain of your inheritance, of whether you truly belong to the family, the trade or the place you were born into, or of what you are made of.

The oracle does not settle the doubt with a fact. Notice instead what happens next in the poem. The stranger, who is Athena, sends Telemachus to sea to seek news of his father, and in the seeking he becomes recognisably Odysseus' son. Identity is not only received; it is proved in action. Set out, and let your deeds answer the question.
entries.context: In Odyssey 1, Athena, disguised as the stranger Mentes, asks Telemachus whether he is truly Odysseus' son. He replies, in a bitter mood, that his mother says so but that he himself does not know, for no one has ever known for sure his own parentage, and wishes he were the son of some luckier man.

aspects.love: You may doubt whether you are truly loved, or whether you belong in the circle you have joined. Assurances alone will not settle it. Show up, act generously, and let belonging grow from what you give and share, rather than from proof you can never quite obtain.
aspects.work: You may feel like an impostor in your role, unsure you have the right pedigree for it. No one is ever fully certain. Take up the work as though it were yours by right, and let your conduct over the coming months answer what words cannot.
aspects.home: Questions of family can run deep: unknown parentage, a distant parent, a sense of being the odd one out. They deserve gentleness and, where possible, honest conversation. Whatever the facts turn out to be, you can decide which of the family's ways you will carry forward.
aspects.health: Doubt about your inheritance can reach the body too: will you suffer what your parents suffered? What you inherit is not the whole of your fate. Learn what you can, look after what is yours to look after, and do not let worry about the past rob you of strength for the present.
aspects.journeys: A change of place or path may be how you discover who you are. Telemachus found his father's courage by setting sail. If you are uncertain of your roots, consider a venture that tests you; it may answer the question better than staying home and wondering.

entries.message: Some questions about where you come from cannot be settled by proof. You become who you are by what you do next.
entries.reflect: If no one could tell you where you came from, what would you choose to prove about yourself?

entries.greek: εἶμι μέν, οὐδʼ ἅλιον ἔπος ἔσσεται ὅττί κεν εἴπῃ.
entries.english: I will go, and the word will not be spoken in vain, whatever it says.
entries.reading:
Thetis is in her cave beneath the sea, with the sea-nymphs gathered round her, mourning a son who is not yet dead but soon will be. Iris arrives: Zeus summons you. Thetis does not want to go. She is ashamed to sit among the immortals with grief so raw. Yet she says it: I will go, and whatever he says, the word will not be spoken in vain. She takes a dark veil, the blackest garment she owns, and rises through the water toward Olympus.

You may have been called to something at a moment when you would rather hide: a meeting, a family gathering, a hard conversation, a return to the world after loss. The temptation is to wait until you feel fit to be seen. The oracle says go now, veiled if you must.

There is a reason in Thetis' words. She trusts that what is said will matter, though she does not yet know what it will be. In fact it is the word that will end the dishonouring of Hector and bring Priam to Achilles' tent. Your answering may set something healing in motion that you cannot yet see. Answer the summons. Your sorrow can come with you.
entries.context: In Iliad 24, Iris finds Thetis in her sea cave mourning the coming death of Achilles and tells her that Zeus summons her. Thetis says she is ashamed to mingle with the gods in her grief, but she will go, for whatever he says will not be said in vain. Zeus then sends her to tell Achilles to give back Hector's body.

aspects.love: If someone you love has asked to see you, and you feel too low or too ashamed to be good company, go anyway. They asked for you, not for a polished version of you. What passes between you may matter more than either of you knows.
aspects.work: A summons at work, perhaps an uncomfortable meeting or an invitation to return, comes when your confidence is low. Attend. Listen properly to what is said; it may bring a resolution or a role you could never have reached by staying away.
aspects.home: A family occasion may be hard to face: a gathering after a death, a reunion after a rift. You do not need to perform happiness. Wear your dark veil, in whatever form that takes, and let your presence be enough.
aspects.health: When you are low, the instinct is to withdraw from people, appointments, the world. Keep at least one door open. Answer the call to see someone, and let them see you as you are; healing often begins with simply turning up.
aspects.journeys: A change is calling you before you feel ready. You will not wake one morning feeling fit for it; grief and doubt can travel alongside you. Rise from the deep cave and go to hear what is offered. It will not be said in vain.

entries.message: You do not have to be ready, or cheerful, to answer the call. Go as you are; what you will hear there matters.
entries.reflect: What call are you avoiding because you do not feel presentable in your grief?

entries.greek: ἔσσεται ἢ ἠὼς ἢ δείλη ἢ μέσον ἦμαρ
entries.english: It will be at dawn, or in the evening, or at midday.
entries.reading:
Some answers arrive as a date and a place. This one arrives as a shrug of the sky: dawn, or evening, or midday. Achilles spoke these words on a riverbank to a young man pleading for more time, and he spoke them about himself as much as about his enemy. The greatest of the Greeks did not know his hour either, only that it was certain.

Drawn for your question, this line loosens your grip on the clock. Something you are waiting for is on its way, but you have been treating its timing as a test you must pass, checking each morning whether today is the day. The oracle asks you to put that watch down. Whether it comes early or late is not a verdict on your worth.

What is yours is the meantime. Dawn asks for beginnings, midday for steady work, evening for gratitude and rest. Live each of them fully, and whenever the hour arrives it will find you already living the life you were waiting to begin.
entries.context: In Iliad 21, the Trojan prince Lycaon begs Achilles for his life by the river Scamander. Achilles refuses, reminding him that Patroclus has died and that he too must die: a dawn, an evening or a midday will come when someone takes his life in battle. He then kills Lycaon.

aspects.love: You cannot schedule another person's heart. If you are waiting for a word, a return or a yes, let it come in its own light and its own season, and meanwhile be someone worth arriving to.
aspects.work: The result is not late; it is simply not yours to time. Keep your hands on the work in front of you, the morning task and the midday task, and stop scanning the horizon for a sail. Work done well in the meantime is what the hour will find.
aspects.home: Every household has its seasons of arrival and leaving, birth and loss, and none of them keeps to our timetable. Tell the people under your roof what they mean to you now, at whatever hour of the day you are in, rather than saving it for an occasion.
aspects.health: Your body keeps its own clock, and healing rarely follows the calendar we hope for. Rest at evening as faithfully as you strive at noon; both are part of getting well. Measure your progress by seasons, not by single mornings.
aspects.journeys: A departure is coming, whether you set the date or it is set for you. Pack lightly in your mind now, so that dawn, noon or dusk, you can step out when the moment comes.

entries.message: What is coming will come. Your task is not to choose the hour, but to be ready at any of them.
entries.reflect: If you knew it was certain to come, how would you spend the waiting?

entries.greek: ἴσχεο, μηδʼ ἔθελʼ οἶος ἐριζέμεναι βασιλεῦσιν·
entries.english: Hold back, and do not try to quarrel alone with kings.
entries.reading:
Thersites is the ugliest man who came to Troy, bandy-legged, round-shouldered, with a shrill voice and a gift for insult. In the assembly he screams at Agamemnon what many were thinking: that the king is greedy, that the army should leave him to his loot and sail home. Odysseus rises, stands over him, and gives the rebuke of this line. Hold back. Do not try to quarrel alone with kings. Then he strikes him across the back with the golden sceptre, and the soldiers, who half agreed with Thersites a moment ago, laugh.

It is not a kind scene, and the oracle does not ask you to admire it. It asks you to learn from it. You may be on the edge of speaking out against someone with far more power than you, convinced, perhaps rightly, that they are wrong. The danger lies in the word alone. A lone voice, however correct, is easily mocked and quickly silenced, and the crowd that nodded along will laugh when the sceptre falls.

Hold back for now. That is not surrender. Gather those who see what you see, choose your moment and your words with care, and when you speak, speak in a way that cannot be laughed away.
entries.context: In Iliad 2, Thersites rails at Agamemnon before the assembled army and urges the Greeks to sail home. Odysseus stands over him and rebukes him harshly, telling him to hold back and not try to quarrel alone with kings, then strikes him with the sceptre while the soldiers laugh.

aspects.love: In a quarrel with a strong-willed partner or friend, you may be right and still lose if you shout. Lower your voice. Choose a calm hour, and say the one thing that matters most, rather than every grievance at once in front of an audience.
aspects.work: You may be tempted to challenge a manager or a powerful client openly. Before you do, find out who else shares your concern, and whether there is a proper channel for it. A complaint carried by several careful voices is heard; one angry voice is dismissed.
aspects.home: In many families there is one person everyone defers to. Standing up to them alone at the dinner table rarely changes anything. Talk to a sibling or another relative first, and look for a way to raise the matter that leaves everyone some dignity.
aspects.health: Raging alone against a condition or a system can drain you. You are not wrong to want better care or clearer answers, but you need allies: a friend at appointments, others who share your situation, a trusted adviser. Spend your strength where it counts.
aspects.journeys: A big decision may set you against powerful interests: an institution, a landlord, the expectations of your elders. Do not walk out to meet them alone and unprepared. Take counsel, find allies, and move when you have firm ground beneath you.

entries.message: Being right is not enough when you stand alone against power. Hold your tongue today, and find the others who see what you see.
entries.reflect: Who else sees what you see, and have you asked them to stand with you?

entries.greek: ἀντίον εἶμʼ αὐτῶν· τρεῖν μʼ οὐκ ἐᾷ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη.
entries.english: I will go to meet them: Pallas Athena does not let me be afraid.
entries.reading:
Two men come thundering across the plain in a single chariot: Aeneas, son of a goddess, and Pandarus, the archer whose arrow has already drawn Diomedes' blood. Sthenelus, beside him, begs his friend to fall back. Diomedes looks at him darkly. Do not talk to me of flight. He will not even mount the chariot. I will go to meet them as I am, on foot, he says. Pallas Athena does not let me be afraid.

Here the courage is not a sudden gift but a settled thing. It belongs to someone who knows what he serves. You may be at a point where well-meaning people are advising you to retreat, to play safe, to let this pass. Their counsel comes from love, and it is not foolish. But you know, somewhere deeper than argument, that this is the moment to go forward, and to go plainly, without the advantages you might have wished for.

Fear is not banished by pretending it away. It loosens its hold when you are clear about what you stand for. Name what that is: your conscience, your faith, the people you protect. Then step down from the chariot and walk toward what is coming.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, Sthenelus sees Aeneas and Pandarus charging and urges Diomedes to retreat in the chariot. Diomedes refuses: he will not shrink from the fight but will go to meet them on foot, for Pallas Athena does not let him be afraid.

aspects.love: Friends may be warning you off a person or a reconciliation. Listen, and then consult your own heart. If you are clear and unafraid, go forward simply and honestly, without strategies or armour, and meet the other person as you are.
aspects.work: Colleagues may advise caution about a proposal or a confrontation. Weigh their reasons, but if your conscience is settled, act. Go directly, on foot as it were: no manoeuvring, no padding, just a clear statement of what you will do and why.
aspects.home: Someone at home needs you to face a difficulty everyone else is avoiding: a hard conversation, a debt, an old wound. If you are the one with the steadiness for it, do not wait for permission. Walk toward it calmly.
aspects.health: Facing a test, a treatment or a result can bring a fear that tells you to turn the chariot round. Go to meet it. Bring what steadies you: a companion, a prayer, a reason to be well. Fear shrinks when you walk toward it with clear eyes.
aspects.journeys: You stand at the edge of a big decision and part of you wants to flee. If you know this step is right, take it without waiting for perfect conditions. Leave the chariot. Your own feet and conviction are enough for the first stretch of ground.

entries.message: A friend's caution is kind, but it is not your counsel today. Go forward on your own two feet; what stands behind you will not let you shrink.
entries.reflect: What do you stand for that is larger than your fear?

entries.greek: ἐχθρὰ δέ μοι τοῦ δῶρα, τίω δέ μιν ἐν καρὸς αἴσῃ.
entries.english: His gifts are hateful to me: I value him no more than a splinter.
entries.reading:
The embassy has eaten and drunk in Achilles' hut. Odysseus has recited, item by item, the treasure Agamemnon offers: tripods, gold, horses, women skilled in handiwork, a daughter in marriage, seven cities by the sea. Achilles listens and then answers with contempt. His gifts are hateful to me. I value him no more than a splinter. What he wanted was never on the list: an acknowledgement of the wrong, from the man himself, face to face.

You may have been offered amends that leave you colder than before. Someone who hurt you is trying to pay the debt in things, favours, money, sudden kindness, while never quite saying what they did. Your anger is not unreasonable. Gifts that skip the apology can feel like a second insult, as if your dignity had a price.

But the oracle shows you the whole of Achilles' story. His refusal was just, and it was also the beginning of his greatest grief; while he sat in his hut, his dearest friend went out to die. Say clearly what you need, which may be words rather than gifts. Then be careful not to let pride hold your door shut so long that the cost falls on those you love.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, Agamemnon sends Odysseus, Ajax and Phoenix to offer Achilles lavish gifts if he will return to battle. Achilles answers Odysseus that Agamemnon's gifts are hateful to him and that he values the man at no more than a splinter; he will not fight for him again.

aspects.love: A partner may be trying to make up for a wrong with presents or extra attention, without ever naming it. Tell them, gently but plainly, that you need the words. And be honest with yourself about whether you are holding out for repair, or for victory.
aspects.work: An employer or associate offers compensation that seems designed to make a grievance disappear. You have every right to decline if it does not address the real issue. Say what would; and consider whether refusing everything serves you, or only your anger.
aspects.home: Old family injuries are often paid off in gifts: help with the house, money at Christmas, but never an apology. If this stings, say what you need. If they cannot give it, decide what relationship is still possible, rather than letting contempt become your only answer.
aspects.health: Resentment held long enough becomes a weight the body carries: a tight jaw, broken sleep. You need not accept a false apology, but you can lay the grudge down for your own sake. Refusing gifts is one thing; refusing peace is another.
aspects.journeys: A tempting offer may be trying to buy you back into a place or role you left for good reason. Weigh it on more than its size. If the thing that drove you away is unchanged, no list of treasures will make the return sit right with you.

entries.message: No gift can mend a wound the giver will not name. But guard against a refusal so proud that it costs you what you love.
entries.reflect: What would a true repair look like to you, and have you told anyone?

entries.greek: μοῦνον τηλύγετον πολλοῖσιν ἐπὶ κτεάτεσσι,
entries.english: an only son, born late, heir to great wealth.
entries.reading:
Phoenix is an old man now, and he tells Achilles a story from his youth. He quarrelled bitterly with his own father and fled across the broad lands of Hellas, a fugitive with nothing. He came to Peleus, and Peleus welcomed him and loved him as a father loves an only son, born late, heir to great wealth. He made him rich and gave him a people to rule. And Phoenix, in turn, took the little boy Achilles on his knee and fed him, and the child spluttered wine down his tunic.

The line holds the deepest kind of welcome: not merely kindness to a stranger, but love lavished as if on the one child a family had waited years for. Perhaps you have received something like this, from a mentor, a step-parent, a friend's family, a community that took you in when your own door was closed. Or perhaps you have given it.

Phoenix recalls it for a reason. He wants Achilles to soften, to remember that he too was carried and cherished. The card asks the same of you. Before you harden toward someone, remember the people who made room for you when you had nothing. Their love is yours to pass on.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, old Phoenix reminds Achilles of his past: after fleeing his own father he came to Peleus, who welcomed him and loved him as a father loves an only son, born late and heir to great wealth, and made him rich. Phoenix then recalls how he raised the infant Achilles, as part of his plea for Achilles to relent.

aspects.love: Some loves are given without measure: the kind that treats you as precious simply because you are there. Recognise it if you have it. If a partner or friend loves you like this, do not take it as your due; return it in daily, visible care.
aspects.work: A mentor may have opened doors for you that you could never have opened alone. Honour that by doing the same for someone newer, someone who arrives with little. The generosity of those who raised you up is meant to flow onward, not to stop with you.
aspects.home: Families are made by welcome as much as by blood. If you have taken someone in, or been taken in, cherish it. If a relative is coming to you as a fugitive from a quarrel elsewhere, receive them as Peleus received Phoenix.
aspects.health: Remember how you were cared for as a child or in illness: held, fed, kept warm. Offer yourself a little of that tenderness now. And if someone near you is weak, let them feel what it is to be valued without having to earn it.
aspects.journeys: If you are leaving one home for another, you may find a welcome warmer than you expect. Accept it humbly. And if you are settled, be ready to open your door to someone arriving with nothing; you may be the Peleus in their story.

entries.message: You were taken in and loved beyond what you could repay. Remember that, and let it soften what you are holding hard.
entries.reflect: Who once made room for you as if you were their own, and how might you pass that on?

entries.greek: νῦν μὲν δὴ μάλα πάγχυ κακὸς κακὸν ἡγηλάζει,
entries.english: Look at that: here is one wretch leading another.
entries.reading:
Odysseus is home at last, and no one knows him. Dressed in filthy rags, leaning on a staff, he walks toward the town with the faithful swineherd Eumaeus. At the spring where the townsfolk draw their water, they meet the goatherd Melanthius, driving the best of his goats down for the suitors' dinner. He looks at the pair and jeers. Look at that, here is one wretch leading another; god always brings like to like. Then he kicks the beggar on the hip. Odysseus wonders whether to strike him dead on the spot, and endures it.

The words of this line belong to a sneerer, and you should hear them as such. Someone may be judging you by the company you keep, or by how you look in a lean season: your humble friend, your unglamorous work, your plain clothes. They lump you together and laugh, sure they know your worth.

The oracle asks two things of you. First, do not abandon the faithful friend walking beside you to win the scoffer's approval; one loyal swineherd is worth a hundred goatherds. Second, hold your temper as Odysseus did. Your true standing does not need to be proved at the roadside spring. In time your conduct will speak, and it will speak louder than any kick.
entries.context: In Odyssey 17, the swineherd Eumaeus is leading Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, into town. At the spring they meet the goatherd Melanthius, who insults them, crying that here is one wretch leading another, for god always brings like to like. He then kicks Odysseus, who restrains himself.

aspects.love: Someone may mock your choice of partner or friend as beneath you. Look at the substance: loyalty, kindness, honesty walking at your side. Do not let a sneer at the spring persuade you to let go of a faithful hand.
aspects.work: In a humble role, or working alongside people others overlook, you may be treated with contempt. Keep your dignity and your patience. Those who judge by appearances are often the ones driving the suitors' goats, serving someone else's greed.
aspects.home: A relative may look down on the way you live, the friends you bring home, the work you do. You do not have to answer every jibe. Be steady and courteous, and let the integrity of your household answer for itself over time.
aspects.health: When you are unwell or worn down, you may feel you look like a beggar in rags, and someone's careless remark can wound. Hold on to what you know of your own worth. Your condition is not your identity, and you need not defend it to the unkind.
aspects.journeys: Returning somewhere in reduced circumstances, or arriving as a newcomer, you may be judged harshly. Do not rush to prove yourself. Keep your faithful companions near, observe quietly, and wait for the right moment to show who you are.

entries.message: Contempt says more about the one who sneers than the one sneered at. Keep your company and your temper; the rags are not the man.
entries.reflect: Whose company are you tempted to be ashamed of, and what has that friend truly given you?

entries.greek: καί κε τὸ βουλοίμην, καί κεν πολὺ κέρδιον ἦεν
entries.english: That is what I would wish, and it would have been far better.
entries.reading:
Paris was strutting at the front of the Trojan line in a leopard skin, challenging the best of the Greeks, until he saw Menelaus leap down from his chariot. Then he shrank back among his comrades like a man who has come upon a snake in a mountain glen. His brother Hector turns on him. I wish you had never been born, he says, or had died unmarried. That is what I would wish, and it would have been far better.

Sometimes we arrive at this place: looking at a person, a choice, a whole chain of events, and wishing it simply did not exist. You may be feeling this about someone close to you, or about something you yourself began. The wish is honest. Hector is not wrong that much grief has come from Paris' choices. But a wish against the past has no spear in it. It wounds the one it is aimed at and leaves the war exactly where it was.

What is striking is what comes next. Stung by his brother's words, Paris offers to settle the war in single combat. Say your hard truth once, cleanly. Then put your strength into what can still be changed: tomorrow's choice, not yesterday's.
entries.context: In Iliad 3, Paris shrinks back into the Trojan ranks on seeing Menelaus. Hector rebukes him, wishing that Paris had never been born or had died unmarried; that, he says, is what he would wish, and it would have been far better than being a disgrace and a thing despised.

aspects.love: You may be wishing you had never met someone, or never said a certain thing. Let yourself feel the regret, but do not live there. Ask what this relationship, as it now is, requires: an ending, an apology, or a fresh and more honest start.
aspects.work: A decision made months ago now looks like a mistake, and you catch yourself wishing it undone. Name what went wrong, plainly, once. Then turn the regret into a plan: what can be salvaged, corrected or learned, starting with the next task on your desk.
aspects.home: Anger at a family member who caused harm can harden into wishing they were not part of your life. That wish may be honest, but spoken aloud it can wound for years. Speak the harder truth that is useful instead: what must change, and how.
aspects.health: Regret about past habits, choices or neglect can sit heavily on the body. You cannot go back and live it differently. You can begin today, with one decision that would make the wiser version of you glad.
aspects.journeys: Looking back on a move or a path taken, you may wish you had chosen otherwise. The road behind cannot be unwalked. Ask instead where you can go from here, and what this ground, unchosen as it was, makes possible.

entries.message: Wishing it had never happened is honest, and it changes nothing. Say the wish once, then turn to what can still be done.
entries.reflect: If you stopped wishing it had never happened, what could you begin to do about it?

entries.greek: τῷ κέ τοι ἀγλαΐας γε διασκεδάσειεν ἁπάσας,
entries.english: Then he would scatter all your fine show to the winds.
entries.reading:
At the spring where the townsfolk draw their water, Melanthius has just kicked a beggar for sport. The swineherd Eumaeus does not strike back. Instead he lifts his hands and prays to the nymphs of the spring, whom Odysseus once honoured with rich offerings: let my master come home. Then, he tells the goatherd, he would scatter all your fine show to the winds, the swagger you carry about the town, while bad herdsmen ruin the flocks.

Every life has some fine show in it: the image we present, the clothes, the confidence, the story of how well things are going. This card asks what lies behind yours. You may be spending effort on looking prosperous, capable or above it all, while the real flock, your work, your relationships, your health, your word, is quietly being neglected. Or you may be watching someone else do this, and feeling powerless against their arrogance.

Either way, the line carries a sober promise: show built on neglect does not last when the true reckoning arrives. If it is yours, turn back to the flocks while there is still time to mend them. If it is another's, do as Eumaeus did. Pray, keep faith, and leave the scattering to a greater hand.
entries.context: In Odyssey 17, after Melanthius has insulted and kicked the disguised Odysseus, Eumaeus prays to the nymphs of the spring that Odysseus may come home. Then, he tells Melanthius, his master would scatter all the fine show that the goatherd so insolently parades about town while the flocks are ruined.

aspects.love: Grand gestures, perfect occasions, a confident public face: none of these hold a relationship together if the daily care is absent. Look behind the display. Give your attention to the small, unseen kindnesses that are the real flock in love.
aspects.work: There may be a gap between how your work looks and how it actually is. Close it before someone else notices. Substance is what survives scrutiny; polish without it will be scattered the moment a serious eye falls upon it.
aspects.home: A household can look impressive from the road while its foundations crack: money stretched, relationships thin, chores neglected. Spend less on appearances for a while and more on what truly keeps a home: time, honesty, attention.
aspects.health: It is possible to look well while running yourself down. Look honestly at the real state of your body and mind, beneath the show of coping. Tend that, and let appearances follow, rather than the other way round.
aspects.journeys: Before a big change, ask whether you are choosing it for how it will look or for what it will truly give you. Choices made for display scatter quickly. Choose what will hold its value when no one is watching.

entries.message: Show built on neglect cannot stand when the master comes home. Tend the flock, not the finery.
entries.reflect: If all your fine show were scattered tomorrow, what would remain that you could be proud of?

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ ἤτοι τάδε πάντα καταφλέξω πυρὶ κηλέῳ
entries.english: But I will burn all these things in blazing fire,
entries.reading:
Andromache was weaving when she heard the cry from the walls. She had been at her loom deep in the house, working flowers into a purple web, and had told her maids to set a cauldron on the fire so that Hector would have a hot bath when he came home from the fighting. Now he lies naked by the Greek ships, and she stands among the Trojan women thinking of all the fine soft clothing in the chests, made by women's hands for him. But I will burn all these things in blazing fire, she says.

This is a line of grief, and the oracle does not soften it. It is drawn when something has ended that you had prepared for lovingly: a person gone, a plan undone, a future you were weaving that will never be worn. The things remain, folded in the chest, and you do not know what to do with them.

Andromache's answer is fierce and ancient. She does not hoard them, nor throw them away. She makes an offering of them, a fire in his honour that all Troy can see. There may be something in your life that needs this kind of rite. Choose your fire, and let it be an act of honour, not of waste.
entries.context: At the end of Iliad 22, Andromache laments Hector, whose body lies naked by the Greek ships. She thinks of the fine clothes woven for him that lie in the palace and says she will burn them all in blazing fire, since he will never be wrapped in them, so that they may be an honour to him before the Trojans.

aspects.love: After the end of a love, by death or parting, the things you shared can become hard to live among. You need not keep everything, nor discard it in anger. Choose a way to release some of it with ceremony, so that the letting go is itself a form of love.
aspects.work: A project you poured yourself into has been cancelled or overtaken. Rather than leaving it to gather dust, close it properly: write down what it taught you, thank those who worked on it, and then set it aside with honour. Endings done well make room.
aspects.home: A house after a loss is full of objects that carry someone. Decide together, as a family, what to keep and what to release. A small shared rite, a fire, a gift, a donation, can turn the sorting into a way of remembering rather than of erasing.
aspects.health: Grief lives in the body; it needs somewhere to go. Weeping, writing, walking, a ceremony of your own making: these are your blazing fire. Do not keep the sorrow folded in a chest for ever. Give it form, so that it can begin to move.
aspects.journeys: Before you can move on, there may be something to burn behind you: an old identity, a cherished plan that will not now happen. Mark its ending deliberately. Then you can step forward without dragging the unworn clothes of the past behind you.

entries.message: Some things can only be honoured by letting them go. Give them to the fire, and let the flame say what you cannot.
entries.reflect: What are you keeping folded away that would be better honoured by being let go?

entries.greek: οὐδέ κεν ὧς ἔτι θυμὸν ἐμὸν πείσειʼ Ἀγαμέμνων
entries.english: not even so would Agamemnon win over my heart,
entries.reading:
Not if he gave me ten times as much, says Achilles, or twenty times; not all the wealth that flows into Orchomenus, or into Egyptian Thebes with its hundred gates; not if his gifts were as many as the grains of sand and dust. Not even so would Agamemnon win over my heart.

There is something magnificent in that refusal. Achilles is saying that his heart, the seat of his will and passion, cannot be bought. You may be under pressure now to agree to something you do not want, and the pressure is coming as an offer that keeps growing. More money, more flattery, more reasons. The line tells you that you are entitled to say no, and that no sum changes a refusal that truly comes from the heart.

But it holds a question too, for the very next words show what Achilles is really waiting for: that the outrage done to him be paid back in full. Ask yourself what would actually move you. If the answer is nothing at all, look closely. A heart that cannot be bought is integrity; a heart that cannot be reached is a prison. Know which of the two you are guarding.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, Achilles rejects the embassy sent by Agamemnon. Listing riches beyond count, he declares that not even so would Agamemnon win over his heart until he has paid back in full the outrage that grieves him.

aspects.love: No one can buy your affection, and you should be wary of anyone who tries. Equally, ask whether you are trying to win someone with offerings rather than honesty. Hearts are moved by being seen and respected, not by a lengthening list of gifts.
aspects.work: You may be offered more and more to accept a role, a merger or a compromise you dislike. A rising price does not alter a sound refusal. Decline clearly if your conscience says no, and do not let the size of the offer make you doubt your own judgement.
aspects.home: Relatives sometimes try to buy agreement: help with a deposit if you choose the school they prefer, an inheritance if you live as they wish. Love them, and keep your decisions your own. A home built on purchased consent will never feel like yours.
aspects.health: Others may press you toward choices about your body with promises of quick rewards. Your consent is your own. Take advice from those you trust, but do not let persuasion or pressure decide for you what only your own heart and good counsel can.
aspects.journeys: A tempting opportunity elsewhere may be dressed up in greater and greater rewards. If your heart is not in the move, no amount will make it right. Wait for a reason that answers your deeper wish, not only your ambition.

entries.message: Your heart is not a market. Nothing worth having can be bought from you against your will, and you should not try to buy it from anyone else.
entries.reflect: What would genuinely move your heart, if gifts cannot?

entries.greek: ἔσθλʼ ἀγορεύοντες, κακὰ δὲ φρεσὶ βυσσοδόμευον.
entries.english: speaking kind words, but plotting evil deep in their hearts.
entries.reading:
Telemachus walks into the place of assembly with a spear in his hand and two swift dogs at his heels, and Athena has poured such grace over him that everyone turns to look. The suitors crowd round him at once, all smiles, speaking kind words. Yet they had sent a ship to lie in wait and kill him on his voyage home, and they are plotting evil deep in their hearts still. Telemachus does not linger. He slips out of their throng and goes to sit with Mentor, Antiphus and Halitherses, the old friends of his father's house.

This line is a warning, and a quiet one. Someone around you is warmer than they have any reason to be. The praise is a little too ready, the interest in your plans a little too keen. You may not have proof, only a sense that the words and the hands do not match. The oracle tells you to trust that sense.

You need not make a scene; Telemachus did not. Be courteous, give little away, and do not stay in the crush of false friends. Go and sit with the people who have stood by you through the hard years. Their plain company is your safest ground.
entries.context: In Odyssey 17, Telemachus, newly home from his voyage, walks into the assembly place. The suitors throng around him speaking kind words, but plotting evil deep in their hearts; he avoids them and sits with Mentor and the old friends of his father.

aspects.love: A new admirer, or an old friend suddenly attentive, may be saying everything you want to hear. Go slowly. Watch whether their actions match their words over time, and keep close the people who loved you before you had anything worth wanting.
aspects.work: Flattery from a rival or an unexpectedly helpful colleague may be cover for a different aim. Stay polite, but share your plans cautiously. Seek advice from mentors who have shown their loyalty over years, rather than from those who have only just discovered your worth.
aspects.home: Within a wider family, someone may be smiling while working against you: over a will, a property, the care of an elderly parent. Do not accuse without evidence, but keep careful records, speak openly with those you trust, and make no promises in the crowd.
aspects.health: Be wary of anyone who offers easy, flattering answers about your health, especially for a price. Seek out plain-speaking, long-trusted sources of advice. Kind words that ask nothing of you may be hiding what they really want from you.
aspects.journeys: As you weigh a big change, some voices may be urging you on for their own benefit. Look behind the enthusiasm. Talk the decision through with old friends who have nothing to gain, and let their sober counsel weigh heavier than the crowd's applause.

entries.message: Pleasant faces may hide a plan against you. Be courteous, give little away, and sit with the friends who have proved themselves.
entries.reflect: Whose warmth toward you feels out of proportion, and what might they want?

entries.greek: οὔ τοι ἀπόβλητʼ ἐστὶ θεῶν ἐρικυδέα δῶρα
entries.english: The glorious gifts of the gods are not to be thrown away.
entries.reading:
Hector has just torn into his brother: Paris the handsome, the woman-mad, whose lyre and flowing hair and Aphrodite's favours would be worth nothing once he lay in the dust. Paris does not deny the charge. Your heart is always as hard as an axe, he answers. But do not cast the lovely gifts of golden Aphrodite in my teeth. The glorious gifts of the gods are not to be thrown away, and no one could choose them for himself.

It is a surprisingly wise reply from a man not often wise. You may have been made to feel ashamed of something that came to you unearned: beauty, charm, a talent, an ease with people, good fortune. Others resent it, or you resent it yourself, and you have half a mind to hide it or squander it so that no one can accuse you of having it.

The oracle says keep the gift, but do not stop there. Notice what Paris does next. Stung and steadied at once, he offers to stand in single combat for the whole war. A gift is not an excuse; it is a responsibility. Hold what you were given without apology, and then use it for something that costs you, and serves more than yourself.
entries.context: In Iliad 3, after Hector scorns him for his good looks and Aphrodite's favour, Paris replies that the glorious gifts of the gods are not to be thrown away, for no one can choose them for himself. He then offers to settle the war by single combat with Menelaus.

aspects.love: Perhaps you are easy to love, or love easily, and others have called it shallow. Do not discard your warmth to seem serious. Give it faithfully to the people who matter, and let your gift deepen into loyalty rather than remain mere charm.
aspects.work: A natural talent may have brought you further than others think fair. Stop apologising for it, and start using it where it counts: on the difficult task, the neglected project, the colleague who needs your particular ability. Gifts proven in hard service quiet envy.
aspects.home: In families, one child is often called the lucky one. If that is you, refuse both shame and smugness. Use what came easily to you to make life easier for the others, and the gift will become a blessing to the whole house.
aspects.health: If you were given a strong constitution, do not waste it through neglect or bravado. If you were not, honour the strengths you do have. Either way, the body you were given is a gift, not something to be thrown carelessly away.
aspects.journeys: An opportunity has fallen into your lap that you did not earn by effort. Do not refuse it out of false modesty or fear of what others will say. Accept it, and then prove worthy of it by what you do once you are under way.

entries.message: You did not choose your gifts, and you need not apologise for them. Do not throw away what the gods gave; put it to worthy use.
entries.reflect: Which of your gifts have you been ashamed of, and what would it look like to use it well?

entries.greek: δαιμόνιοι, μαίνεσθε καὶ οὐκέτι κεύθετε θυμῷ
entries.english: Fools, you are mad, and you no longer hide what is in your hearts.
entries.reading:
A footstool flies across the hall. Eurymachus has hurled it at the ragged beggar, who ducks; it strikes the wine-steward on the right hand, and the jug rings on the floor as he falls back groaning in the dust. The shadowy hall erupts. Into the uproar Telemachus speaks: Fools, you are mad, and you no longer hide what is in your hearts. You have eaten and drunk too much. Some god is stirring you. Go home and sleep.

This card is drawn when something hidden is coming into the open. Perhaps people around you have been behaving with practised courtesy, and now, in a moment of excess or anger, the mask has slipped. What you are seeing is not a strange exception. It is what was always there, kept quiet by restraint. Believe it.

Or perhaps the mirror turns toward you. When you are tired, overfull, frightened or furious, what comes out of your heart? Telemachus' counsel is simple and sound for both: the night is over, the feast has turned ugly, and nothing good will be decided now. Go home. Sleep. Tomorrow, act on what you saw tonight, with a clear head.
entries.context: In Odyssey 18, Eurymachus hurls a footstool at the disguised Odysseus; it misses and strikes the wine-steward, and the suitors break into uproar. Telemachus rebukes them: they are mad and can no longer hide that they have had too much food and wine; some god is stirring them, and they should go home to bed.

aspects.love: An argument or a careless night may have shown you a side of someone that frightened or saddened you. Do not explain it away. Take it seriously, talk about it in sober daylight, and let what you learned guide what you decide.
aspects.work: Under pressure, a colleague or a whole group has shown its true attitudes: contempt, greed, carelessness. Note it quietly. You now know something useful about the ground you stand on, and you can plan accordingly rather than hoping it was a passing mood.
aspects.home: Family gatherings, with their food and wine and old tensions, can unmask feelings everyone usually hides. If a scene erupts, be the one who calls time: suggest everyone rest, and deal with what was revealed when tempers have cooled.
aspects.health: Excess, whether of drink, work or worry, loosens the hold you keep on yourself. Notice what spills out when you are overextended. It may be telling you to rest, to cut back, or to face something you have been holding down.
aspects.journeys: A moment of strain may reveal the true character of a place, a group or an arrangement you were considering. Do not ignore it because the first impression was pleasant. What emerges under pressure is what you would be living with.

entries.message: When people lose their restraint, they show you what was always there. Believe what you see, and go home to bed.
entries.reflect: What did you glimpse when the restraint fell away, in them or in yourself?

entries.greek: τοῦ μὲν φθίνοντος μηνός, τοῦ δʼ ἱσταμένοιο,
entries.english: as one month wanes and the next begins.
entries.reading:
A beggar sits by the swineherd's fire and swears an oath. By Zeus, by this table of hospitality, by the hearth of noble Odysseus: your master will return, as one month wanes and the next begins. The swineherd shakes his head. He has heard such tales from travellers before. But the beggar is Odysseus himself, and the oath is truer than his host can know.

Homer sets the homecoming at a curious moment, the dark days when the old moon has thinned to nothing and the new has not yet shown its sliver. It is a time when the night sky looks empty. Nothing seems to be happening. And yet it is precisely there, at the hinge between months, that the turning occurs.

You may be in such a season now: one thing waning, the next not yet visible, and an anxious sense that you are stuck. The oracle reads it otherwise. The darkness between moons is not absence but passage. Something is ending as it should, and something is beginning below the horizon. Finish what is waning with care. Keep your lamp lit. And do not mistake a dark sky for a closed door.
entries.context: In Odyssey 14, the disguised Odysseus swears to the doubting swineherd Eumaeus that Odysseus will return within this very year, as one month wanes and the next begins, and will punish those who dishonour his wife and son. Eumaeus does not believe him.

aspects.love: A relationship may be passing from one phase into another, and the in-between feels uncertain and dark. Do not rush to name it or to end it. Some loves are renewed only after an old form wanes; give the new moon time to show itself.
aspects.work: One project, role or season of work is finishing while the next has not appeared. Use the gap well: close the old work cleanly, rest a little, and prepare. The quiet days between tasks are often when the next opening is quietly being made.
aspects.home: Family life has its turnings: a child moving from one stage to another, a household reshaping itself around a new need. If home feels unsettled, see it as passage rather than failure. Mark the change gently, and let everyone find their new place.
aspects.health: Bodies move in cycles, and recovery often has its dark days before any visible improvement. Do not judge your progress by a single moonless night. Keep steady, rest, eat well, and give the turning time to show itself.
aspects.journeys: You are at a threshold: the old way thinning, the new not yet clear. This is a natural time to prepare rather than to force a leap. Gather what you need, and be ready to move when the first sliver of light appears.

entries.message: Change comes at the turning, in the dark between one month and the next. What feels like nothing happening may be the hinge itself.
entries.reflect: What in your life is waning, and what might be beginning that you cannot yet see?

entries.greek: οὐκ ἄν τοι χραίσμῃ…
entries.note: One of two lines that begin the same way: Iliad 11.387 or 3.54.
entries.english: It would be no help to you…
entries.reading:
The papyrus breaks off after a few words, and two scenes in the Iliad begin the same way. In one, Diomedes sits with an arrow through his foot and mocks the archer who shot him from behind a grave-pillar: your bow would be no help to you if you faced me in armour, man to man. In the other, Hector scorns his brother on the battlefield: your lyre, your hair, your looks, the gifts of Aphrodite, would be no help to you once you lay in the dust. Both are spoken to Paris. Both say the same hard thing.

Each of us has a way of meeting the world that has served us well: charm, wit, distance, the knack of striking from safety. This card suggests that what lies in front of you will not be won that way.
