What works from a distance may fail at close quarters. You may sense this already, and keep reaching for the old bow anyway.

The line does not ask you to discard your gifts. It asks you to see clearly what this particular fight requires. Perhaps it is presence rather than cleverness, honesty rather than charm, coming close rather than keeping safe. Find out what will truly help. Then go and get it.
entries.context: The papyrus line begins with words found in two places in the Iliad, so the identification is uncertain. At Iliad 11.387 Diomedes, shot in the foot by Paris, taunts him that his bow and arrows would be no help to him in open combat; at Iliad 3.54 Hector tells Paris that his lyre and Aphrodite's gifts would be no help when he lay in the dust. Both are said to Paris.

aspects.love: Charm and clever words may have carried you through difficulties before. This time they will not help. Your partner or friend needs something plainer: your full presence, an honest admission, a willingness to stay in the hard conversation rather than retreat behind wit.
aspects.work: The skills that won you your place may not be the ones this new challenge needs. Rather than leaning harder on them, name the gap honestly. Ask for training, advice or a partner whose strength complements yours, and meet the task at close quarters.
aspects.home: At home you may be trying to solve a problem from a distance: with money, with messages, with arrangements made by others. It would be no help. What the family needs is for you to come in through the door, sit down and be part of what is happening.
aspects.health: Familiar comforts, the distracting habit, the quick fix, the way you usually push through, may no longer help with what you are facing. Be willing to try something different, and seek advice that tells you what actually works rather than what you hoped to hear.
aspects.journeys: The plan you made assumes conditions that may not hold. Before committing, ask what would really help you where you are going: skills, allies, resources. Do not set out relying on gifts that look fine at home but will be no use in the field.

entries.message: The tools you rely on most may be the ones that fail you in this fight. Find out what will truly help, and set the rest down.
entries.reflect: What have you been relying on that this situation will not reward?

entries.greek: μήτε τι τὸν ξεῖνον στυφελίζετε μήτε τινʼ ἄλλον
entries.english: Do not mistreat the stranger, nor anyone else
entries.reading:
The hall is in uproar. A footstool has been thrown, a servant knocked to the floor, and Telemachus has told the suitors to their faces that they are mad. Anger is gathering. Then Amphinomus stands, the most decent of the suitors, the one whose words pleased Penelope best. Friends, he says, no one should answer a just rebuke with fury. Do not mistreat the stranger, nor anyone else among the servants in this house. Let us pour a libation and go home.

It is the right word at the right moment, and it works; the suitors drink and disperse. You may be in a group where cruelty or carelessness toward someone weaker has become normal: a newcomer mocked, a junior worker bullied, an outsider shut out. The oracle asks you to be the one who speaks for them, calmly, without grandstanding.

But there is a sorrow folded into this line. Amphinomus had been warned, by the beggar himself, to leave that house before the reckoning. He spoke well, and stayed, and died with the rest. Kind words in bad company are not enough. Speak up for the stranger, and then ask honestly whether you belong in that hall at all.
entries.context: In Odyssey 18, after Telemachus has rebuked the suitors for their brawling, the suitor Amphinomus calls on them not to answer a just rebuke with anger. He tells them not to mistreat the stranger or any of the servants in Odysseus' house, but to pour a libation and go home.

aspects.love: If your friends treat someone badly, a newcomer to the group or a partner they disapprove of, your quiet word can change the mood. Say it. And if the cruelty is constant, consider whether this is a circle you want to keep.
aspects.work: In a workplace where juniors, cleaners or temporary staff are treated with contempt, be the senior voice that sets a different tone. A single calm intervention can shift a culture. But if the place cannot change, think carefully about how long you will stay.
aspects.home: In the household, notice who is treated as less: a carer, a new partner, a child who does not fit. Insist on courtesy toward everyone under your roof. The way a home treats its most vulnerable member reveals its true character.
aspects.health: Treat your own body as you would a stranger who needs kindness: no rough handling, no contempt for its weaknesses. And if a group or habit around you encourages harm, speak up for yourself, then step away from it.
aspects.journeys: You may have been the moderating voice in a situation for a long time, hoping to soften something that will not soften. Your decency is real. But the line asks whether it is time to pour the last cup and go home.

entries.message: Decency needs a voice in every crowd. Say the fair word, and then make sure your feet follow it out of the hall.
entries.reflect: Where are you speaking kindly, but staying in a company you know you should leave?

entries.greek: αἰσχρόν τοι δηρόν τε μένειν κενεόν τε νέεσθαι.
entries.english: It is shameful to wait long and go home empty-handed.
entries.reading:
The Greeks have just stampeded for the ships, shouting, hauling the hulls down to the sea, ready to sail for home after nine years of war. Odysseus goes among them with the king's sceptre and turns them back, one by one. Then he speaks to the assembly, and he does not pretend. Nine years have rolled round, he says; I do not blame any man for chafing beside the beaked ships. Even one month away from wife and home is hard. But it is shameful to wait long and go home empty-handed.

You may be very tired of something: a long effort, a slow relationship, a goal that seems always one season away. Part of you is already running for the ships. The oracle honours that weariness first. It is real, and it is not weakness.

Then it asks you to stand still for a moment. You have given years to this; leaving now would mean leaving with nothing to show. Odysseus reminds the army of the omen they all saw at Aulis, the reason they came. Recall yours. If the reason still lives, stay and finish. If it has truly died, go with honour. But do not let mere weariness decide what years of work deserve.
entries.context: In Iliad 2, after Agamemnon's test of the army sends the Greeks rushing for the ships, Odysseus addresses the assembly. He admits that nine years is a long time to wait, but says it is shameful to wait long and go home empty-handed, and urges them to stay and see whether Calchas' prophecy of victory comes true.

aspects.love: A long-standing relationship may feel stuck, and you are tempted to walk away. Before you do, remember why you chose it, and whether that reason is still present. If it is, invest once more; it would be a shame to leave just before the harvest.
aspects.work: After a long effort, a qualification, a business, a slow climb, you may be close to giving up. Look honestly at how near the end might be. Persistence now may turn years of sowing into a harvest you can carry home.
aspects.home: Family undertakings, from caring for an elderly parent to raising a difficult teenager, can feel endless. Acknowledge how tired you are, and ask for help. Then consider what remains to be done, and see it through, so the long years are crowned rather than wasted.
aspects.health: Recovery, training or a change of habit may be taking far longer than you hoped. Do not abandon it simply because it has been slow. Remind yourself of the reason you began, and give it one more steady season.
aspects.journeys: You may be ready to abandon a long-planned venture, or to come home from a place that has not yet delivered. Weigh it carefully. If the promise that drew you is still real, stay and see it through; leaving empty-handed may trouble you longer than another year would.

entries.message: You have waited too long to leave with nothing. Remember why you came, and let that reason, not your weariness, decide.
entries.reflect: Is the reason you began still alive, or are you staying only because you have stayed so long?

entries.greek: μὴ παῖδʼ ὀρφανικὸν θήῃς χήρην τε γυναῖκα·
entries.english: Do not make your child an orphan, and your wife a widow.
entries.reading:
At the Scaean gate Andromache runs to meet her husband, and behind her comes a nurse carrying their baby son, bright as a star. She has lost everyone: her father and seven brothers killed by Achilles, her mother dead soon after. Hector, she says, you are father and mother and brother to me, and my husband too. Stay here on the wall. Do not make your child an orphan, and your wife a widow.

Hector answers that shame will not let him hang back like a coward. He goes, and the poem never lets us forget the price. This is one of the hardest lines in Homer, and the oracle gives it to you in earnest. You may be facing a choice where duty, ambition or honour pulls you toward a risk, and someone who depends on you is asking you to stay.

The card does not say Hector was wrong, nor that Andromache was right. It says her voice deserves a full hearing. Before you go out onto the plain, look at the faces at the gate. Count what your choice would cost them, not only what it might win. If there is a way to serve honour without leaving them alone, choose it.
entries.context: In Iliad 6, Andromache meets Hector at the Scaean gate with their infant son. Having lost her father and brothers to Achilles, she tells Hector that he is everything to her and begs him to stay on the wall and not make his child an orphan and his wife a widow. Hector answers that shame will not let him hold back.

aspects.love: Your partner may be pleading with you not to take a risk: a dangerous job, a reckless habit, a fight you feel bound to pick. Their fear is not weakness or control. Hear it fully, and look for the course that honours both your conscience and their love.
aspects.work: Ambition is calling you toward long hours, danger or upheaval. Before you go, count the cost at home, in time and presence as well as money. A career built while children grow up without you may win glory at a price you can never repay.
aspects.home: Those who depend on you need you present and whole. If you are their shelter, think carefully before exposing yourself to harm that could be avoided. Sometimes staying on the wall is the braver and more loving choice.
aspects.health: If you are driving your body toward danger, ignoring warnings for the sake of pride, think of those who love you. Your wellbeing is not only your own concern; it holds up other lives too. Take the advice that keeps you with them.
aspects.journeys: A big decision may take you far from those who rely on you, or into real hazard. Talk it through with them before deciding, not after. Find out what they can bear, and whether there is a way to go that does not leave them unprotected.

entries.message: Those who love you are asking you to count what your courage would cost them. Hear them, before honour decides alone.
entries.reflect: Who stands at the gate of your decision, and have you truly heard what they are asking?

entries.greek: ἔσται ταῦτα Σκάμανδρε διοτρεφές, ὡς σὺ κελεύεις.
entries.english: It shall be so, Scamander, nursling of Zeus, just as you command.
entries.reading:
The river is full of the dead. Achilles has driven half the Trojan army into the eddies of Scamander and is cutting them down in the water, until the stream is so choked with bodies it can barely reach the sea. Then the river takes the form of a man and speaks from a deep whirlpool: drive them out onto the plain and do your killing there. Achilles answers with perfect courtesy. It shall be so, Scamander, nursling of Zeus, just as you command. But he adds that he will not stop killing Trojans. Moments later he leaps back into the stream, and the river comes at him in a roaring flood.

This is a line of outward agreement, and it holds up a mirror. You may be saying yes to a warning you are not really heeding. Someone, or your own body, or the world around you, is telling you that what you are doing has gone too far, that the channel is choked. And you have answered politely, adjusted a little, and carried on.

The oracle asks for a truer yes. Words of agreement cost nothing, and the river can tell the difference. If you have been told enough, show it in what you do, before the water rises.
entries.context: In Iliad 21, the river Scamander, choked with the bodies of Trojans Achilles has killed, rises in human form and tells him to drive them out of his stream. Achilles answers that it shall be so, Scamander, nursling of Zeus, as he commands, but says he will not stop killing Trojans until he has met Hector.

aspects.love: A partner may have told you, perhaps more than once, that something you do is hurting them. Agreeing in the moment is easy. Show them, in changed behaviour over weeks, that you really heard; otherwise the next conversation will come as a flood.
aspects.work: You may be complying with feedback on paper while keeping your old ways in practice. That gap will be noticed. Either make the change in earnest, or have an honest conversation about why you disagree; a hollow yes is the most dangerous answer of all.
aspects.home: Someone in the household has asked you to stop or change something, and you said of course. Look at whether you have. Promises made to keep the peace and then quietly broken wear away trust far faster than an open disagreement would.
aspects.health: Your body may be sending a clear message: too much, too long, too hard. Acknowledging it and carrying on is not listening. Make the real change, the rest, the reduction, the appointment, before the warning becomes a crisis.
aspects.journeys: You may have agreed to slow down, reconsider or wait, while privately pressing ahead. If you still believe in the course, say so honestly and take counsel. If the warning is sound, change direction in fact, not just in words.

entries.message: When even the river is choking on what you are doing, a polite yes is not enough. Change course in deed, not only in word.
entries.reflect: Where have you said yes to a warning while carrying on exactly as before?

entries.greek: δυσμενέσιν μὲν χάρμα, κατηφείην δὲ σοὶ αὐτῷ;
entries.english: a joy to your enemies, and a shame to yourself?
entries.reading:
Paris sailed across the sea and brought Helen home from a distant land, and after her came the whole Greek army. Now, the moment Menelaus appears, Paris melts back into the ranks. Hector's question stings: you brought a great harm to your father, your city and all your people, a joy to your enemies and a shame to yourself. Will you not stand and face the man whose wife you took? There is a particular insight in Hector's words. He does not only call Paris a coward. He shows him who profits from his cowardice. Every time Paris slips away, the Greeks laugh and the Trojans hang their heads.

When this card comes, look honestly at a pattern of avoidance in your own life: a problem you created and keep stepping around, a consequence you will not face, an apology you will not make. Each time you shrink from it, you hand a small victory to whatever works against you, a rival, a bad habit, the voice that says you will never change. And you lose a little respect for yourself.

The way through is simple, though not easy. Turn round. Face the thing you set in motion. The laughter on the other side stops the moment you stand your ground.
entries.context: In Iliad 3, Hector rebukes Paris for slipping away from Menelaus. He reminds him that he brought Helen from a far land, a great harm to his father, his city and his people, a joy to their enemies and a shame to himself, and asks whether he will not stand and face Menelaus.

aspects.love: If you caused a rift and keep avoiding the conversation that would mend it, the distance grows, and those who never wished you well may enjoy watching it. Go and face the person you hurt. Your own dignity returns the moment you stop hiding.
aspects.work: A mistake of yours is being quietly worked around rather than owned. Rivals notice, and your standing suffers more from the avoidance than from the error itself. Name it, take responsibility, and present a plan; you will deny your critics their satisfaction.
aspects.home: Choices of yours have brought difficulty to the household, and you have left others to carry the consequences. Step forward and share the load. Children and partners respect someone who faces what they caused far more than someone who disappears.
aspects.health: Putting off a health matter you know you need to address only strengthens the problem; every delay is a small gift to it. Make the appointment, change the habit, face the result. Self-respect grows from the first honest step.
aspects.journeys: You may have started something, a move, a commitment, a public plan, and now want to slip away from it. Consider who would be pleased if you did, and what it would cost your sense of yourself. If it is right, return to it and stand firm.

entries.message: Ask who is glad when you flinch. Then stand where your choice will no longer hand them the day.
entries.reflect: Who or what is quietly glad each time you avoid this?

entries.greek: τοῦδʼ αὐτοῦ λυκάβαντος ἐλεύσεται ἐνθάδʼ Ὀδυσσεύς.
entries.english: Within this very year, Odysseus will come home.
entries.reading:
Eumaeus has heard it all before. Wanderers come to Ithaca with stories of Odysseus seen alive, here or there, and Penelope gives them a cloak and weeps, and nothing comes of it. So when the old beggar at his fire swears by Zeus, by the table of hospitality and by the hearth of Odysseus himself that the master will come home within this very year, the swineherd will not be moved. Leave off swearing, old man, he says, and drink your wine in peace. The irony, which Homer lets us savour, is that the beggar is Odysseus. The man Eumaeus has given up hoping for is sitting at his own hearth, eating his bread.

You may be guarding your heart in the same way. You have hoped for something before, a return, a reconciliation, a turning, and been let down so often that hope itself feels foolish. Your caution is earned; the oracle respects it. But it asks you to notice what disappointment can do. It can make us so practised at disbelief that we fail to recognise good when it has already crossed the threshold.

Keep your faithfulness, as Eumaeus kept his master's herds through twenty years. And look again, carefully, at who is sitting by your fire.
entries.context: In Odyssey 14, Odysseus, disguised as a wandering Cretan, swears by Zeus, the table of hospitality and Odysseus' own hearth that Odysseus will come home within this very year. The swineherd Eumaeus, who has been deceived by travellers' tales before, refuses to believe him.

aspects.love: If you have been hurt by broken promises, you may now distrust even sincere ones. Notice whether someone close to you is offering steady, quiet faithfulness that you have been too guarded to see. The love you wait for may look humbler than you imagined.
aspects.work: Repeated letdowns, promised promotions, delayed payments, deals that fell through, have made you cynical. Keep your realism, but do not let it blind you to genuine signals. Look at the evidence before you, not only at the history behind you.
aspects.home: Someone in the family may be trying to come back to you: an estranged relative, a child who drifted, a parent who failed you. Their return may arrive in rags, imperfect and unconvincing. Be cautious, but leave the door open and keep a seat by the fire.
aspects.health: After many disappointments with treatments or plans, it is natural to stop hoping. Stay realistic, and keep doing the faithful daily things. Improvement can arrive quietly, and small signs are worth noticing rather than dismissing as more travellers' tales.
aspects.journeys: You may have given up on a change you once longed for. The line asks whether it has really gone. Keep your house in order, as Eumaeus did, and stay alert; the opening you stopped believing in may present itself in an unexpected disguise.

entries.message: You have been let down by promises before, and your caution is earned. But do not let old disappointment blind you to what may already be sitting at your fire.
entries.reflect: What good thing might you be failing to recognise because you have learned not to hope?

entries.greek: οὐδὲν σοί γʼ ὄφελος, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἐγκείσεαι αὐτοῖς,
entries.english: They are no use to you, since you will not lie wrapped in them.
entries.reading:
Fine, soft garments lie folded in the chests of Hector's palace, woven by the women of the house through long afternoons. Andromache thinks of them while her husband's body lies naked by the Greek ships, far from his parents, left for the dogs. They are no use to you, she says to him, since you will never lie wrapped in them. These are the plainest words in her lament, and the most devastating. All that careful weaving has lost its purpose in a single afternoon.

This card is for the moment you finally admit that something you made for the future will not be used: the room prepared, the business plan, the house for two, the skills learned for a role that disappeared. Often we keep such things exactly as they were, as if keeping them could keep the future possible. It cannot, and some part of you knows it.

Andromache does not stop at the bitter truth. In the same breath she gives the clothes a new purpose: they shall be an honour to him before the men and women of Troy. What can no longer serve the one it was meant for can still serve memory, and the living. Admit what is lost. Then ask what it can become.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Andromache mourns Hector, killed by Achilles and lying unburied by the Greek ships. Of the fine clothes woven for him, she says she will burn them, for they are no use to him since he will not lie wrapped in them; instead they shall be a mark of honour before the Trojans.

aspects.love: After a parting, you may still be holding things meant for a shared life: plans, gifts, a picture of the years ahead. Acknowledge, gently, that they will not be used as intended. Then let them become something else: a lesson, a memory honoured, room for a new kind of love.
aspects.work: Skills, contacts or work prepared for a goal that has vanished can feel wasted. They are not useless, only unassigned. Take stock of what you built, and ask where else it could do you honour or serve someone who needs it now.
aspects.home: A home may hold rooms or objects prepared for someone who is gone or never came. There is no hurry to change them. But in your own time, consider how they might serve the living household, so that the house remembers without being frozen.
aspects.health: You may be grieving a version of your body, or a life it was supposed to allow. Name that loss honestly; it is real. Then look for what your body can still do, and give your care to that, rather than to clothes you will not now wear.
aspects.journeys: Plans for a move or venture that cannot now happen may still be packed in the hallway. Unpack them honestly. Some things will need to be given away; others may serve a different path. Clearing the old hope makes space to choose a new one.

entries.message: Some of what you made for the future will never be used as you meant it. Say so honestly. Then let it serve another purpose: memory, honour, the living.
entries.reflect: What are you keeping ready for a future that is not coming, and what could it become instead?

entries.greek: τῷ δέ κε νικήσαντι γυνὴ καὶ κτήμαθʼ ἕποιτο·
entries.english: Let the woman and the treasure go to the one who wins.
entries.reading:
For nine years two armies have bled on the plain, and now a herald runs up to old Priam with a simpler plan: let the two men at the heart of it fight alone. Paris against Menelaus. The woman and the treasure go to whoever wins, and everyone else goes home. Priam shudders when he hears it, and still he mounts his chariot and goes down to swear.

This card comes when something in your life has dragged on far past its use: a dispute, a rivalry, a question you and another keep circling without ever settling. The line offers a way out. Narrow it down. Find the one decisive conversation, the one clear test, and agree in advance that you will both abide by what it shows. Most long wars survive because no one will name the terms.

But notice what is being handed over. Helen is listed beside the treasure, as if she were cargo. If the thing you are contesting is really a person, their love, their loyalty, their choice, then no contest can award it. Settle what can be settled, honestly and soon. Leave people free to choose for themselves.
entries.context: In Iliad 3, the herald Idaeus summons Priam to the plain to swear oaths with the Greeks. He explains that Paris and Menelaus will fight for Helen, and that the woman and the treasure will go to the winner, while everyone else makes peace. Priam shudders, but goes.

aspects.love: If two people are pulling at one heart, yours or someone else's, do not let it become a duel with a prize. A person is not the treasure that goes to the winner. Step back, speak plainly, and let the one being fought over make the choice.
aspects.work: A negotiation or rivalry has gone on too long and cost too many. Propose a single clear measure: a trial, a figure, a deadline, and agree on what follows from it before anyone begins. Terms named in daylight save a season of skirmishes.
aspects.home: A family argument has been running for years over the same few things: an inheritance, a room, a grievance. Gather everyone, name exactly what is in dispute, and decide together how it will be resolved, so the rest of the household can finally make peace.
aspects.health: You have been fighting the same small battle with yourself for months, half-trying and half-avoiding. Choose one fair test, a set period of real effort, and agree with yourself in advance to accept what it teaches you about what helps.
aspects.journeys: Two possible paths have been warring inside you, and the indecision is costing more than either choice would. Set the terms: what would make you go, what would make you stay. Then let one clear moment decide, and honour it like an oath.

entries.message: A long quarrel can end in a single honest test, if the terms are named before it begins. Only be sure that what you are fighting over is a thing, and not a person.
entries.reflect: What long-running struggle in your life could be settled by one honest test, and what are you afraid it might show?

entries.greek: οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη· εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω,
entries.english: Rule by many is no good thing: let there be one ruler.
entries.reading:
The army has broken. Agamemnon tested his men by suggesting they go home, and they took him at his word, running for the ships with a roar like surf on a beach. Odysseus snatches up the king's sceptre and goes through the camp, turning them back one by one. To the loudest he says: we cannot all be kings here. Rule by many is no good thing. Let there be one.

The line comes to you when there are too many hands on the steering oar. Perhaps a project or a household has a dozen opinions and no one able to say yes or no. Perhaps the crowd is inside you: a voice for every option, each with a vote, so that nothing is ever chosen. The result looks like freedom and feels like a stampede to the shore.

Homer is not praising tyranny; the same scene shows Odysseus using that sceptre too roughly. The wisdom here is clarity. Somebody must hold the oar, and everyone must know who it is. Choose that person, or choose to be that person, and the scattering will stop.
entries.context: In Iliad 2, after Agamemnon's test causes the army to flee for the ships, Odysseus goes through the ranks restraining them. He tells common soldiers who shout that they cannot all be kings, that rule by many is no good thing, and that there should be one ruler, to whom Zeus has given sceptre and law.

aspects.love: A relationship cannot be steered by friends, parents and past partners all calling advice from the shore. Listen kindly, then close the circle. The decisions about your love belong to the two of you, and the more voices you admit, the less you hear each other.
aspects.work: A team where everyone has a veto and no one has the final word drifts in circles. Ask plainly who owns this decision. If it is you, take it with courage; if it is someone else, give them your best counsel and then let them steer.
aspects.home: Children and households settle when they know who is holding the oar. Agree between the adults which of you decides what, and stop undoing each other's rulings. A home with one clear voice on each matter is calmer than one with many loud ones.
aspects.health: You may be following five sets of advice at once and keeping none of them. Choose one trusted guide or one sensible plan and give it a fair season. Too many counsellors leave the body confused about what it is meant to be doing.
aspects.journeys: Before a big change, everyone you know will have an opinion about it. Hear them, but remember there can be only one captain of this voyage. Write down your own reasons, and when the shouting starts again, read them back to yourself.

entries.message: When everyone steers, the ship goes nowhere. Decide who decides, and let that voice be heard above the shouting.
entries.reflect: In the matter that is troubling you, who is actually allowed to decide, and does everyone know it?

entries.greek: εἰδώλων δὲ πλέον πρόθυρον, πλείη δὲ καὶ αὐλή,
entries.english: The porch is full of ghosts, and the courtyard full of them too,
entries.reading:
The suitors are feasting in Odysseus' hall, and suddenly they cannot stop laughing; their jaws seem borrowed, their meat is spattered with blood, their eyes fill with tears they do not feel. Only the seer Theoclymenus sees clearly. Night is wrapped around their heads, he cries, the walls drip red, and the porch and courtyard are crowded with ghosts hurrying down into the dark. The young men laugh at him and tell him to go outside, if it is so gloomy in here.

This is a grave card, and it does not soften. Something in your life is giving off signs that all is not well, and part of you has noticed. The house is loud, the cups are full, and it is easy to call the one who worries a fool. Ask yourself who your Theoclymenus is: a friend, a dream, a tightness in your own chest that will not go away.

The ghosts on the threshold are not a sentence passed on you. They are a picture of where the present road leads if nothing changes. Unlike the suitors, you can still put down the cup, walk out to the courtyard, and choose another way.
entries.context: In Odyssey 20, Athena stirs the suitors to wild, unnatural laughter at their feast. The seer Theoclymenus sees a vision of their doom: night about their heads, walls dripping with blood, and the porch and courtyard full of ghosts hurrying to the darkness below. The suitors only laugh at him.

aspects.love: If someone who loves you has said, more than once, that something is wrong between you, do not treat them as the gloomy guest at the feast. The jokes that keep the room cheerful can also keep it blind. Ask them what they see, and listen to the end.
aspects.work: The figures look festive but something underneath feels wrong: a pattern of shortcuts, a dealing no one quite explains. Do not wave away the colleague who is uneasy. Go through the courtyard yourself and look at what is gathering there before it fills the house.
aspects.home: A household can be noisy with life and still be heading for trouble no one names. If there are quiet signs, a withdrawn child, a debt not spoken of, a drink too many, look at them steadily now while the doors are still open.
aspects.health: The body sends its seers too: a tiredness that does not lift, a mood that has darkened for weeks. Do not laugh them out of the room. Take the warning seriously enough to seek proper counsel, and let it turn you before the hall grows darker.
aspects.journeys: If the plan you are about to carry out leaves you uneasy whenever you are alone with it, that unease is worth more than the applause around you. Before you go further, sit with it in a quiet place and ask what it is trying to show you.

entries.message: When the warning comes, the danger is in laughing at it. Look at what you have been refusing to see.
entries.reflect: What warning have you been laughing off, and whose voice is it really in?

entries.greek: ἠράμεθα μέγα κῦδος· ἐπέφνομεν Ἕκτορα δῖον,
entries.english: We have won great glory: we have killed the noble Hector.
entries.reading:
Hector lies dead in the dust, and Achilles turns to the army with a shout of triumph. Sing the victory song, he tells them; we have won great glory; we have killed the noble Hector, whom the Trojans prayed to like a god. It is the summit of the Iliad's fighting, the thing Achilles came for. And in the next breath he pierces the dead man's ankles, ties him to his chariot, and drags his head through the dirt.

This card arrives at, or near, a real success. Perhaps you have beaten a rival, won an argument, overcome something that loomed like a hero over your life for years. Feel it. You earned it, and the line gives you leave to sing. But it also shows how close triumph lies to cruelty, and how quickly the winner can become the one who shames himself.

So celebrate, and then stop. Do not drag the defeated around the walls; do not keep proving, to yourself or anyone, how thoroughly you won. Honour what you overcame. In the end Achilles himself had to learn this, when an old father came to his tent to ask for the body back.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Achilles has just killed Hector. He calls the Greeks to sing the victory song and return to the ships, saying they have won great glory and killed noble Hector, whom the Trojans prayed to as a god. He then ties Hector's body to his chariot and drags it in the dust.

aspects.love: You may have won the argument, or won someone back from a rival. Let the victory song be short. The partner who lost a point needs to keep their dignity, and nothing poisons love like a winner who keeps reminding the other that they lost.
aspects.work: A deal closed, a competitor beaten, a promotion won: enjoy it and thank those who fought beside you. Then resist the urge to humiliate the other side. Markets and offices are small, and the person you drag through the dust may be across the table again.
aspects.home: If a long family struggle has finally gone your way, do not parade the outcome at every gathering. Let the old opponent keep their place at the table. A household recovers from a defeat far faster than from a victory used as a whip.
aspects.health: You have beaten something hard: a habit, an illness, a long dark season. Mark it gladly. Then be gentle with the self who struggled, rather than scorning who you used to be. That person carried you to this day.
aspects.journeys: You have reached the place you fought to reach. Before you rush on to the next conquest, pause and give thanks for what it cost. Make your arrival a song, not a parade of the beaten, and you will travel on lighter.

entries.message: You have won. Now the harder test begins: what you do with your victory will decide what it means.
entries.reflect: Now that you have won, what would it look like to be generous to what you defeated?

entries.greek: ὡς καὶ ἐμοὶ τόδε ἔργον ἀέξεται, ᾧ ἐπιμίμνω.
entries.english: so my work too grows and prospers, the work I keep at.
entries.reading:
In a hut on a high field, a swineherd feeds a ragged stranger and talks about his absent master. Eumaeus built the pig-yard himself, stone by stone, with a fence of oak stakes split from the heartwood, without asking the queen or the old king for help. He grumbles that a good master would have rewarded him by now with a house and a wife. And yet, he says, the god makes my labour thrive; my work grows, the work I keep at.

This is a card of steady increase. You may be doing something no one is watching: tending a craft, a family, a small business, a slow recovery. The person whose praise you were working for may be far away, or may never come. The line tells you the growth is real anyway. Count the herd; it is larger than it was.

Notice, too, that Eumaeus is speaking to his master without knowing it. Faithful work is often seen by someone we cannot recognise. Do not stop because the reward is late. The keeping-at is itself the blessing, and it is building something that will still be standing when the master comes home.
entries.context: In Odyssey 14, the swineherd Eumaeus receives Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, in his hut. He speaks of his absent master, who would have rewarded his faithful work with a house and land, as a kind master does for a servant whose labour the god makes prosper, so too his own work grows, the work he keeps at.

aspects.love: Love that lasts is mostly tending: the daily kindness, the remembered detail, the mended quarrel. If it feels unnoticed, keep at it anyway. The bond is growing stronger than you can see, the way a herd grows while the herdsman is busy with the fences.
aspects.work: Your patient work is paying off, even if the recognition has not arrived. Keep building your pig-yard stone by stone. Write down what you have made this year; the list will show you a prosperity you have been too close to notice.
aspects.home: You keep the household running in ways nobody mentions: meals, repairs, the remembering of birthdays. That labour is holding the family together. Keep at it, and ask for help plainly when you need it, without waiting for a master who may be long in coming.
aspects.health: Small daily habits, a walk, an earlier night, a meal cooked rather than bought, are the work that grows. You may not see the change from one week to the next. Look back over a season and you will find the god has made it thrive.
aspects.journeys: You may be tempted to leave a place because the reward has been slow. Weigh that carefully. What you have built here by staying is real, and it may be closer to bearing fruit than it looks from inside the hut.

entries.message: Faithful work grows quietly, like a well-kept herd. Keep at it; the god is already making it prosper.
entries.reflect: What have you been quietly keeping at, and how much has it actually grown since you began?

entries.greek: οὐδʼ εἴ μοι τόσα δοίη ὅσα ψάμαθός τε κόνις τε,
entries.english: not even if he gave me gifts as many as the grains of sand and dust.
entries.reading:
Three envoys sit in Achilles' hut with an offer of staggering size: tripods, gold, horses, women, cities, a king's daughter in marriage. Achilles listens to it all, and then answers like a wave breaking. Not if he gave me ten times, twenty times as much. Not if he gave me gifts as many as the grains of sand and dust. He would not take Agamemnon's treasure until the outrage had been paid in full.

This card comes when someone is trying to make up for a wrong with something other than the truth. A larger offer, a gift, a promotion, a smoother apology. And you feel, rightly, that what was taken from you is not that kind of thing. Your refusal has dignity. Some debts are paid only by being seen.

Yet Homer does not let Achilles off lightly. His refusal, held too long, costs him the life of the friend he loves most. So stand by what cannot be bought, and still keep one door open. Ask what would truly mend this, and say it aloud. A no that names its own conditions can become a yes; a no made of pure sand only buries you.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, Achilles answers the embassy sent by Agamemnon with a sweeping refusal: not even if Agamemnon gave him gifts as many as the grains of sand and dust would he win him over before paying back the bitter outrage.

aspects.love: If you have been hurt and the other person is offering presents and grand gestures instead of honesty, you are right not to be bought. Tell them what you actually need: an acknowledgement, a change. But do not let pride turn a fair refusal into a wall that walls you in.
aspects.work: Money is being offered to smooth over something that was really about respect. You may decline it. Before you do, say clearly what would put the matter right. A refusal that only grows more absolute will cost you more than it costs them.
aspects.home: A relative is trying to make amends with gifts rather than words. Hold your ground on what matters, but name it: the apology, the truth about what happened. Families mend when the wound is spoken of, not when it is covered in sand.
aspects.health: Do not trade what is essential to you, your rest, your peace of mind, your honest limits, for any amount of reward. Some prices are too high however generous the offer sounds. Know what your well-being is not for sale for.
aspects.journeys: A tempting offer may be pulling you towards a change that would cost your integrity. Grains of sand are many, but they slip through the fingers. Stay true to what you know, and wait for a door you can walk through with your honour intact.

entries.message: Some things cannot be bought back, and you are right to know it. Only make sure your refusal is guarding your honour and not your wound.
entries.reflect: What would genuinely repair the wrong that was done to you, if gifts cannot?

entries.note: Only the opening survives: "So he spoke, praying…", words that begin several lines in Homer.

entries.greek: μηκέτι παῖδε φίλω πολεμίζετε μηδὲ μάχεσθον·
entries.english: Fight no more, dear sons, and stop your battle.
entries.reading:
Hector and Ajax have fought all afternoon: spears through shields, boulders hurled, blood drawn on both sides. Neither will yield. As the light fails and they draw swords to close, two heralds step in and hold their staffs between them. Fight no more, dear sons. Zeus loves you both; you are both great warriors; and night is coming, and it is good to obey the night. The two men part. Hector gives Ajax a silver-studded sword, and Ajax gives Hector a purple belt.

Drawn for your question, this line steps between you and a struggle that has gone on long enough. It may be a rivalry, a disagreement with someone you respect, or a battle with yourself that neither side can win outright. The heralds do not say who was right. They say: you have both proved yourselves, and it is getting dark.

Accept the interruption. There is no dishonour in ending a contest that has become a matter of exhaustion rather than truth. Better still, offer something to the one you fought, a word of recognition, a fair acknowledgement. Rivals who part with gifts often find, later, that they were never really enemies.
entries.context: In Iliad 7, Hector and Ajax fight a long duel. As night falls and they are about to close with swords, the heralds Idaeus and Talthybius hold their staffs between them, and Idaeus tells them to fight no more, for Zeus loves them both and both are warriors. The two exchange gifts and part.

aspects.love: Two people who love each other can fight to a standstill over the same point for years. Tonight, let someone hold a staff between you. Say what you admire in the other, and put the quarrel down unfinished. Morning often shows it was smaller than it looked.
aspects.work: A professional rival is as strong as you are, and neither of you is gaining. Consider calling it even. A respectful truce, perhaps even a collaboration, can bring you more than another round. Exchange something of value and part as equals.
aspects.home: Two members of the family are locked in a standoff, and the rest of you are tired of watching. You may be the herald here. Step between them gently, remind them that they are both loved, and help them part for the night with something kind said.
aspects.health: Stop fighting your body as though it were an enemy to be beaten. Struggle has its place, but so does nightfall. Call a truce with yourself: rest, eat, sleep, and let tomorrow bring its own strength.
aspects.journeys: You have been wrestling a decision so long that you are both worn out, you and the choice. Let night fall on it. Step away for a while, and when you return you may find the matter has quietly resolved itself into something you can live with.

entries.message: A fight can end without a winner and still end with honour. When night falls on the struggle, put the sword down and exchange gifts.
entries.reflect: If you stopped fighting tonight, what gift of respect could you offer your opponent?

entries.greek: ἄλκιμος ἔσσʼ, ἵνα τίς σε καὶ ὀψιγόνων ἐὺ εἴπῃ.
entries.english: Be brave, so that those born in years to come may speak well of you.
entries.theme: Words for Those Not Yet Born
entries.reading:
A stranger with a spear sits in the hall, and the young man of the house, Telemachus, is the only one who welcomes him. The stranger is Athena in disguise, and she does not flatter. You are no longer a child, she tells him. Look how tall and fine you have grown. Remember Orestes and the name he won. Be brave, so that those born in years to come will speak well of you.

This card is a summons. It may find you, like Telemachus, sitting among people who have taken over a part of your life while you watched, too young or too uncertain to act. You have been waiting to feel ready. Athena does not wait for that feeling; she simply tells him he is grown, and the next morning he calls an assembly and books a ship.

Ask how your present choice will look from far off, to a grandchild, a student, a friend not yet met, your own older self. Courage is rarely a single great blow; mostly it is the next uncomfortable step taken on time. Take it, and let the story that is told of you begin with this.
entries.context: In Odyssey 1, Athena, disguised as Mentes, counsels the young Telemachus to seek news of his father and to deal with the suitors. She reminds him of the fame Orestes won by avenging his father, and urges him, tall and fine as he is, to be brave so that people in later times will speak well of him.

aspects.love: Love asks for courage too: to say the true thing, to commit, or to leave what is not right. Imagine how you would want this time to be told by those who come after you. Then speak or act in a way that story would honour.
aspects.work: You have been acting younger than you are at work, waiting for permission. Athena's word is that you have grown. Step forward in the meeting, put your name to the idea, ask for the role. Courage shown now becomes the reputation others repeat later.
aspects.home: Your children, or the children of your family, are watching how you meet trouble. What they see will become their idea of bravery. Stand up for what is right in the household, steadily and kindly, and you will be giving them a story to live by.
aspects.health: It takes courage to face what you have been avoiding: an appointment, a habit, a fear. Be brave for the sake of the person you will be in ten years, who will either thank you for starting now or wish that you had.
aspects.journeys: You stand on the edge of a bold choice. You will not feel entirely ready, and Telemachus did not either. Choose the path you would be proud to describe to someone born long after this day, and set out.

entries.message: Courage now becomes the story others tell later. Act today as someone you would be glad to be remembered as.
entries.reflect: How would you want someone, years from now, to describe what you did at this moment?

entries.greek: στήλῃ κεκλιμένος ἀνδροκμήτῳ ἐπὶ τύμβῳ
entries.english: leaning against a pillar on a tomb built by men's hands.
entries.reading:
Diomedes is having his greatest day. He has struck down a Trojan captain and kneels to strip the bronze from his chest. Behind the old grave-mound of Ilus, founder of Troy, Paris leans against a carved pillar with his bow drawn. He waits for the moment Diomedes bends, and looses an arrow straight through his foot, pinning it to the ground. Then he laughs aloud.

This card warns of a blow from cover. When you are flushed with success and busy gathering what you have won, you are least watchful of your flank. Someone may resent your rising, and they will not come at you openly. Keep your eyes up a little longer than feels necessary.

It is also a mirror. Paris hides behind a monument built by other men's hands, an ancestor's honour, and uses it as a shield to strike without risk. Ask whether you ever do the same: criticising from behind tradition, or a title, or an anonymous distance. Diomedes, wounded, called the arrow a scratch from a coward. Whichever side of the pillar you are on, choose to fight in the open.
entries.context: In Iliad 11, Paris takes aim at Diomedes with his bow, leaning against a pillar on the tomb of Ilus, the ancient elder of Troy. While Diomedes is stripping the armour from a fallen enemy, Paris shoots him through the foot.

aspects.love: If you feel undermined in love by small barbs, a friend's sly remark, a family member's well-aimed jibe, notice who is speaking from cover. Name it calmly and openly. And if you have been sniping instead of saying what hurts, step out and say it face to face.
aspects.work: A success may stir resentment in someone who will not confront you directly. Do not gloat while you collect your reward. Make sure your work is documented and your allies informed, and treat a sudden small wound as information rather than a disaster.
aspects.home: In families, old loyalties are sometimes used as shields: what our father would have wanted, how things have always been done. Watch for criticism that hides behind the ancestors. Answer it in the open, gently, with what is true now.
aspects.health: A small injury or strain often comes when we are absorbed and careless, crouched over the task in front of us. Look up, stretch, notice your surroundings. Do not let a moment of triumph become the moment you forget to guard yourself.
aspects.journeys: As you move into new territory, not everyone you leave behind will cheer. Expect a sting or two from those who prefer you where you were. Do not stop to strip every prize from the field; keep moving, and keep your guard.

entries.message: While you stoop to gather the spoils, watch who is leaning in the shadows with a bow. And never become the one who shoots from behind the past.
entries.reflect: Where are you most exposed at the moment, and where might you be the one hiding behind a pillar?

entries.greek: ἔρχεο· πάρ τοι ὁδός, νῆες δέ τοι ἄγχι θαλάσσης
entries.english: Go: the road lies open before you, and your ships are close to the sea.
entries.reading:
The Greek kings sit in a dark assembly after a day of defeat, and Agamemnon, weeping like a spring running down a black rock, proposes that they all sail home. Young Diomedes rises and answers him to his face. If your heart is so set on going, then go. The road lies open, your ships are drawn up close to the sea. The rest of us will stay until Troy falls; and if they leave too, Sthenelus and I will fight on alone.

This is a card of real permission, offered without softness. The way out of your situation is not blocked. The ships are there; no one will hold you back. That is both a relief and a challenge, because it removes your excuse. If you stay now, it is your choice.

So test your wish to leave. Agamemnon did not, in the end, want to sail; he wanted to be told the defeat was not his fault. Is that your wish too? If you truly need to go, go cleanly, without bitterness. If what you need is courage to remain, look at Diomedes, and let his stubborn faith steady your own.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, Agamemnon, despairing after defeat, proposes that the Greeks sail home. Diomedes rebukes him: if his heart is set on going, let him go, the road is open and his ships stand by the sea; the rest of the Greeks will stay until Troy is taken, and even if they leave, Diomedes and Sthenelus will fight on.

aspects.love: You may be weighing whether to leave a relationship. The road is open, and that is your right. But ask honestly whether you want to go, or want the other person to fight harder to keep you. Those are different needs, and each asks for a different conversation.
aspects.work: You can leave this job, this project or this partnership; nothing binds you but your own word. Before you resign, notice who is resolved to stay and see it through. Either join them with your whole heart or walk to the ships without looking back.
aspects.home: A family member may be threatening to leave, or you may be. Say the free thing calmly: the door is open, and you will be loved either way. Removing the drama from departure often lets people see clearly whether they really wish to go.
aspects.health: You are allowed to give up a regime, a commitment or a way of living that is not serving you. Just be sure you are setting it down for a reason, not out of one bad day's despair. Sleep on it, then decide with a clear head.
aspects.journeys: The ships are near the sea and the way is clear. If your heart is set on a move or a departure, nothing outside you stands in the way. The only question left is whether you are going towards something, or only running from a hard night.

entries.message: You are free to go. Before you take the road, look at who is staying, and ask whether you truly want to leave or only want to be asked to stay.
entries.reflect: If no one would stop you or blame you, would you still want to go?

entries.greek: ψευστήσεις, οὐδʼ αὖτε τέλος μύθῳ ἐπιθήσεις.
entries.english: You will be proved a liar, and you will not bring your words to pass.
entries.theme: Do Not Swear on a Dare
entries.reading:
Even Zeus was once made a fool. On the day Heracles was to be born, he announced proudly to the gods that a child of his blood born that day would rule all who lived around him. Hera, smiling, needled him: you will turn out a liar, you will never make that word come true. Swear it, then. And Zeus, stung, swore a great oath without seeing the trap. Hera flew to Argos, hurried another child into the world early and held back Heracles' birth, so the kingship went to the wrong boy. Zeus seized Ate, the spirit of blindness, by her shining hair and flung her out of heaven.

This line is spoken by a deceiver, and the card reads it as a warning. Someone, or something in you, is daring you to prove yourself: you will never do it, you always back down. The jab is designed to make you commit before you think.

Do not swear on a dare. Your word is worth keeping precisely because you give it slowly. When you feel the heat of being doubted, pause, ask who gains from your promise, and decide in your own time.
entries.context: In Iliad 19, Agamemnon, making peace with Achilles, tells how even Zeus was blinded by Ate. When Zeus announced that a man of his blood born that day would rule his neighbours, Hera, planning deceit, told him he would prove a liar and not fulfil his word, and tricked him into an oath that let her delay Heracles' birth.

aspects.love: A partner or a past love may be saying, you will never change, you never follow through. The words sting and tempt you into grand vows. Answer instead with small, steady actions over time. Promises made to win an argument rarely survive the argument.
aspects.work: Watch for the colleague or competitor who doubts you publicly in order to steer you into a commitment: a deadline, a figure, a public pledge. Take the doubt calmly, ask for time, and set terms that serve the work rather than your wounded pride.
aspects.home: Family members know exactly which words make us swear rash things. If someone says, you will never manage it, do not bind yourself on the spot. Let the remark pass, think it over, and give your word only when you are sure you can keep it.
aspects.health: Do not start a punishing new regime just because someone mocked you, or because you are angry with yourself. Oaths sworn in a flush of shame tend to fail and leave you lower than before. Choose a kind, achievable promise and keep that.
aspects.journeys: If someone is betting you will never go through with a move or a big change, that is not a reason to go. Let your decision rest on your own reasons, weighed carefully, so that no one can claim they tricked you into it.

entries.message: When someone tells you that you will never keep your word, beware of rushing to prove them wrong. Haste to defend a boast is how the wise are tricked.
entries.reflect: Who, or what, has been goading you lately into promising more than you have thought through?

entries.greek: μήτηρ δʼ αὖθʼ ἑτέρωθεν ὀδύρετο δάκρυ χέουσα
entries.english: And on the other side his mother wept and wailed, shedding tears.
entries.reading:
Hector stands alone before the Scaean Gate, waiting for Achilles like a snake coiled at the mouth of its den. On the wall above, his old father has torn his grey hair and begged him to come inside. Then, on the other side, his mother wails and weeps. Hecuba loosens her robe and holds out the breast that once fed him: Hector, my child, pity me, if ever I comforted you; fight him from within the walls. Hector hears it all, and does not move.

This card is about the voices that love you, and what they ask. You may be facing a decision that frightens the people closest to you, and their fear is reaching you as tears, pleading, perhaps anger. It is tempting to harden yourself against it, or to give in simply to make the crying stop.

Do neither too quickly. Hecuba's plea was not foolish; it was love seeing clearly what lay ahead. Listen to the whole of it. Let it change you if it is right. And if you still must go out through the gate, go knowing what you are leaving and what it costs those who watch from the wall.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Hector waits alone outside the walls of Troy for Achilles. Priam has begged him from the wall to come inside, tearing his grey hair; then on the other side his mother Hecuba weeps and wails, baring her breast and pleading with him to fight from within the walls. Hector does not yield.

aspects.love: Someone who loves you is begging you not to do a thing you feel you must. Before you answer, sit with them, let them say everything, and say back what you heard. Even if you decide the same, the hearing itself is a gift they will remember.
aspects.work: A career risk you are considering frightens your family. Their fear is not a veto, but it is information. Ask what they see that you might not, and whether there is a way to fight this battle from inside the walls before you go out alone.
aspects.home: You may be the one on the wall, pleading with a grown child or a partner who will not listen. You cannot hold them inside. Say your love plainly and fully, once, then let them choose; a tearful last word is better than a cold silence.
aspects.health: If those around you are worried about your health and you keep waving them away, their tears may be seeing something you are not. Let them speak, and consider getting proper advice, not to please them, but because love can sometimes see further than pride.
aspects.journeys: A departure you are planning is painful for someone who loves you. Do not slip away to avoid their grief. Hear it, honour it, and if you still go, leave behind a clear account of why, so that what you leave is understanding rather than only an empty gate.

entries.message: Before you go out to meet what you must face, let yourself hear the love that is pleading with you. Then choose with your eyes open.
entries.reflect: What are the people who love you most afraid of for you, and have you truly let yourself hear it?

entries.greek: οὐδʼ εἰ πεντάετές γε καὶ ἑξάετες παραμίμνων
entries.english: not even if you stayed here five years, or six, to ask
entries.reading:
Telemachus has sailed to sandy Pylos with one question: what became of my father? Old Nestor, the king who has seen three generations, welcomes him warmly and begins to remember. So many sufferings at Troy, so many dead: Ajax, Achilles, Patroclus, his own son Antilochus. Not even if you stayed here five years, or six, could you ask about all the woes the Greeks endured there.

The card comes to the asker who is drowning in the past. You may be trying to understand everything before you allow yourself to move: every cause of an old hurt, every detail of what went wrong, every version of what others said. The archive is endless, and like Nestor's memory it will gladly keep you at its hearth for years.

The line gently names the trap. There is always more to hear. Even Nestor, in the end, cannot tell Telemachus where Odysseus is; he sends him on to Sparta. Do the same with your search. Honour the old stories, but stop waiting for a complete account. Ask the question that matters most now, accept whatever partial answer comes, and take the next road.
entries.context: In Odyssey 3, Telemachus visits Nestor at Pylos to ask news of his father. Nestor recalls the sufferings of the Greeks at Troy and the heroes who died there, saying that not even if Telemachus stayed five years or six to ask could he hear all their woes; he would grow weary and go home first.

aspects.love: You may be going over a past relationship endlessly, asking why in a hundred forms. Five years, or six, would not be enough to hear it all. Choose the one question that matters, find what answer you can, and let the rest of the story stay in the past.
aspects.work: More research, more data, more meetings will not make the decision for you. You have enough of the picture already. Name the single question the work truly depends on, answer it as well as you can, and act on that.
aspects.home: Family histories are full of old griefs, and you could spend years unpicking them. Honour the elders' memories and listen kindly, but do not let the past become a place you live. Ask what you need to know in order to move forward, and then move.
aspects.health: Reading endlessly about what might be wrong rarely brings peace. You will never know every possibility. Ask the right person the right question, take sensible counsel, and let the rest of the worrying wait outside the door.
aspects.journeys: You may be gathering advice from every quarter before a big decision, and every elder has a long tale to tell. Listen, but know that no amount of hearing will make the choice for you. Take what you need, then set sail.

entries.message: You will never hear the whole story, and you do not need to. Ask the one question you came for.
entries.reflect: What is the one thing you most need to know, beneath all the other things you have been asking?

entries.greek: ὣς φάτο, καὶ Παιήονʼ ἀνώγειν ἰήσασθαι.
entries.english: So he spoke, and ordered Paeon the healer to heal him.
entries.reading:
Ares, god of war, has been wounded by a mortal. Diomedes, guided by Athena, drove a spear into his belly, and the god bellowed like ten thousand men and fled to Olympus. There he sits beside Zeus, showing his immortal blood and complaining. Zeus looks at him darkly: you are the most hateful to me of all the gods, for strife and battle are always dear to you. And yet, he says, you are my child. So he spoke, and ordered Paeon the healer to heal him. The wound closes as quickly as milk curdles under fig juice.

This card is for the one who feels they do not deserve recovery. Perhaps the harm you are carrying was partly of your own making: a fight you picked, a recklessness you knew better than. You expect a lecture, and you may get one. But the line does not stop at the scolding. It moves, in the same breath, to the healer.

Let both be true. Hear the honest word about what led you here, and then accept the help that is offered. You are not cast out for your faults. You are still a child of the house, and the house sends for Paeon.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, Ares, wounded by Diomedes with Athena's help, flees to Olympus and complains to Zeus. Zeus scolds him as the most hateful of the gods for his love of strife, but because Ares is his own son he orders Paeon, the gods' healer, to cure him, and the wound closes at once.

aspects.love: You may have hurt someone, or been hurt in a quarrel you started. Expect hard words, and accept them. But do not refuse the reconciliation that follows. People who love you can be angry with you and still want you well.
aspects.work: A mistake of your own has cost you, and a superior is not pleased. Take the rebuke without excuses. Then accept the support, training or second chance on offer. Being corrected is not the end of your standing; often it is the first step in its repair.
aspects.home: Someone in the family, perhaps you, is a troublemaker, always in some battle. Even so, they belong. Speak honestly about their behaviour, and in the same conversation make sure they know the household will still look after them.
aspects.health: Whatever led to your present ailment, blame does not speed recovery. Note the lesson, without punishing yourself, and turn to the healers available to you. Let yourself be cared for, as if healing were your right, because it is.
aspects.journeys: You may be retreating from a venture that wounded you, half ashamed of having rushed in. Go home, tell the truth about what happened, and let yourself recover fully before you decide what comes next. The wound closes faster when it is shown.

entries.message: You can be rebuked and still be mended. Healing is not a prize for the blameless; it is given because you belong.
entries.reflect: Where are you refusing help because you feel you brought the trouble on yourself?

entries.greek: ταῦτά τοι, ὦ δύστηνε, τελευτήσω τε καὶ ἔρξω.
entries.english: All this, unhappy one, I will carry out and do for you.
entries.reading:
At the edge of the world of the dead, before any of the great ghosts can come forward, a young man appears whom no one has missed. Elpenor, the youngest of the crew, not brave in battle, not wise in counsel, had drunk too much on Circe's island, slept on the roof, and fallen to his death as they left. They sailed without burying him. Now he begs Odysseus to go back, to burn his body with his armour and set the oar he rowed with on his grave. All this, unhappy one, Odysseus says, I will carry out and do for you.

This card asks about the small, unglamorous promises. There is someone, or something, you have left unfinished: a debt of honour, a duty to a person who can no longer ask, a farewell you skipped in the rush to move on. It is not grand. No one would blame you for forgetting it.

And yet Odysseus, with the whole voyage before him, really does go back to Aeaea and raise that mound. Do the same. Return and finish the thing. Planting one oar over a forgotten friend will settle more in you than many larger victories.
entries.context: In Odyssey 11, at the edge of the Underworld, the ghost of Elpenor, the young comrade who fell from Circe's roof and was left unburied, begs Odysseus to return to Aeaea, burn his body with his armour and raise a mound with his oar upon it. Odysseus answers with this line, promising to do it all.

aspects.love: Perhaps there is a past relationship you left without a proper ending, an apology or a thank-you owed. You need not reopen what is closed. But a respectful word, or a quiet private farewell, can lay something to rest that has been following you.
aspects.work: There is a loose end you have been ignoring: a colleague you promised to help, a small piece of work left half-done when you moved on. Go back and finish it. People remember who keeps their word in small matters long after they forget the large ones.
aspects.home: A promise to an elder or someone now gone is still waiting: a grave to tend, a story to write down, an object to pass on as they asked. Keep it. Families are held together by such quiet acts of fidelity.
aspects.health: Grief that was never given its rites can sit in the body like a stone. If there is a loss you hurried past, allow yourself a ceremony of your own: a visit, a letter, a day set aside. Let the oar be planted.
aspects.journeys: Before you sail on to the next chapter, make one return voyage to finish what you left undone. It may delay you, as it delayed Odysseus. It will also send you on with a clearer conscience and a lighter ship.

entries.message: Keep the promise that no one can force you to keep. That is where your faithfulness is truly measured.
entries.reflect: Whom have you left unburied in your haste to move on, and what would it take to go back?

entries.greek: πῶς ἐθέλεις ἅλιον θεῖναι πόνον ἠδʼ ἀτέλεστον,
entries.english: How can you wish to make my labour vain and come to nothing?
entries.reading:
For a moment there is a chance of peace. The duel is over, and Zeus muses aloud that perhaps the war could end here, Troy left standing, Helen returned. Hera blazes up. How can you wish to make my labour vain and come to nothing? She has worn out her horses gathering the Greek host against Priam. Rather than see her toil wasted, she offers Zeus her own three dearest cities to destroy whenever he likes, if only Troy may fall.

This line is spoken by a goddess in fury, and it is offered to you as a mirror. You may have poured years into something: a plan, a grudge, a relationship, a cause. Now there is a quiet chance to let it end differently, and every part of you protests: but all that work. The feeling is real and deserves respect. It is not always wise.

Notice what Hera is willing to pay so as not to lose her effort. Ask what you are willing to sacrifice for the same reason. Sometimes your labour should be carried through. But sometimes the best use of it is to let it have taught you, and choose peace.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, after the duel between Paris and Menelaus, Zeus teasingly proposes that the war might end in friendship and Troy be spared. Hera, who has toiled to gather the Greek army against Priam, protests furiously with this line, and Zeus gives way and lets the war resume.

aspects.love: You have invested years in this bond, and the thought of them coming to nothing is painful. That alone is not a reason to stay or to keep fighting for it. Ask whether the love is alive now, not whether the past effort deserves a reward.
aspects.work: A project has swallowed money and time, and abandoning it feels like wasting all of it. Weigh honestly what finishing will cost, not only what you have already spent. Sometimes a well-made decision to stop is the real return on your labour.
aspects.home: You may have worked hard for a family plan, a house, a move, a way of doing things, that others no longer want. Before insisting, ask what you would sacrifice to keep it on course. Effort spent is not a debt that others must repay by obeying.
aspects.health: You may keep pushing through a training plan or a punishing schedule because you have already suffered so much for it. Your body does not owe your past effort anything. Adjust, ease off, or change course if that is what wisdom asks now.
aspects.journeys: You have travelled far towards a goal, and turning back feels like failure. Pause and look at the road ahead with fresh eyes. If it no longer leads anywhere you want to be, then the miles behind you were the lesson, not the destination.

entries.message: The fear that your effort will be wasted is not a reason to finish what should not be finished. Count the cost of completing it, not only the cost of stopping.
entries.reflect: If you had not already spent so much on this, would you still choose to continue it?

entries.greek: ὄψιμον ὀψιτέλεστον, ὅου κλέος οὔ ποτʼ ὀλεῖται.
entries.english: Late it comes, and late it is fulfilled, but its fame will never die.
entries.reading:
At Aulis, before the fleet ever sailed, the Greeks were sacrificing beside a spring under a fine plane tree when a blood-red serpent slid from under the altar. It climbed to a nest high in the branches and devoured eight sparrow chicks, then caught their mother as she fluttered crying about it. Nine in all. Then Zeus turned the serpent to stone. Calchas the seer read the sign: nine years of war, and in the tenth, Troy would fall. Late it comes, and late it is fulfilled, but its fame will never die.

Drawn for you, this line speaks to a long wait. Something you hoped for has taken far longer than you thought, and the years have felt like those swallowed sparrows, eaten one by one. You may be wondering whether the promise was ever real.

The oracle answers that some things are made slowly because they are meant to last. Odysseus recalls this sign in the ninth year, when the army is ready to give up. He is telling them to hold on through the last stretch. Do the same. The lateness of a good thing is often the measure of how long it will endure.
entries.context: In Iliad 2, as the Greek army nearly abandons the war, Odysseus reminds them of the portent at Aulis, where a serpent devoured eight sparrow chicks and their mother and was turned to stone. He recalls how the seer Calchas declared it a sign from Zeus, late in coming and late in fulfilment, meaning that they would fight nine years and take Troy in the tenth.

aspects.love: A love that is slow to arrive, or slow to mature, is not lesser for it. If you have waited long, keep faith. What grows over many seasons tends to have deep roots, and is more likely to be remembered with joy.
aspects.work: The reward for your work is late, and you may have stopped believing in it. Hold on through the hardest stretch, which is often the last. Achievements that take years are frequently the ones whose name endures long after quicker successes fade.
aspects.home: Family healing, a reconciliation or a long-sought home, may be coming far more slowly than you hoped. Do not abandon it in the ninth year. Keep tending the hearth; the tenth may yet bring what all the waiting was for.
aspects.health: Your recovery or strength is returning more slowly than you wished. That pace may be what makes it lasting. Keep on with patient care, and judge your progress by the seasons rather than the days.
aspects.journeys: A move or a change you planned long ago keeps being delayed. Do not take the delay as a sign it was never meant to be. Keep yourself ready. When late things finally come, they often arrive whole and stay.

entries.message: What comes slowly can come to stay. The delay is not a denial; it is the length of the thing.
entries.reflect: What would change in how you are waiting if you believed the delay was part of the thing's strength?

entries.greek: πρίν κεν ἀνιηθεὶς σὴν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἵκοιο.
entries.english: You would grow weary and go home to your own country first.
entries.reading:
Nestor sits by the shore at Pylos, a cup in his hand and a hundred griefs in his memory. He tells young Telemachus that the sufferings at Troy were so many that even if the boy stayed five or six years to hear them, he would grow weary first and sail back to his own country before the telling was done. The old man is not complaining. He is simply naming a truth about grief: it is longer than any one listener.

This card gives you permission. You may have been sitting a long time at someone else's hearth of sorrow: caring for a friend's pain, carrying a community's troubles, living inside a hard history that is not wholly yours. You may feel guilty that you are tired. Nestor expects it. Any honest guest grows weary and longs for home.

So go home, at least for a while. Your own country, your own fields and rooms and people, are waiting for you to return and tend them. Leaving before the tale is finished is not a betrayal of those who suffered. It is the only way the listener can live to listen again.
entries.context: In Odyssey 3, Telemachus at Pylos asks old Nestor for news of his father. Nestor begins by saying that the sufferings of the Greeks at Troy are so many that if Telemachus stayed five or six years to hear them all, he would grow weary and sail home before the telling was done.

aspects.love: You may have been carrying a partner or friend through a long grief, listening night after night. It is not a failure of love to feel worn out. Ask for rest, or for others to share the listening, so that you can come back to them with your heart refreshed.
aspects.work: Some work involves endless troubles: complaints, crises, other people's hardship. You will never hear them all to the end. Set an hour for going home each day, and keep it, so the work does not quietly consume your own country.
aspects.home: Perhaps you have been away in spirit, caught up in a parent's or sibling's troubles, while your own household waits. Return. Sit at your own table and attend to the people under your roof; they need you whole, not worn thin by distant griefs.
aspects.health: Weariness is telling you something true. You cannot absorb every sorrow and stay well. Go back to simple restoring things, sleep, food, quiet, your own familiar places, before you are too tired to recover easily.
aspects.journeys: You have been abroad, literally or figuratively, for a long time. If you are longing for home, that longing may be wiser than your plans. You do not have to see out every chapter; you may return before the story is over.

entries.message: You are allowed to grow weary of sorrow and go home. Not every story has to be heard to the end.
entries.reflect: Whose sorrow have you been sitting with so long that you have forgotten your own home?

entries.greek: ἐλθεῖν, ὄφρʼ ἔνθεν θυμοφθόρα φάρμακʼ ἐνείκῃ,
entries.english: to go there, and bring back poisons that destroy the life,
entries.reading:
Telemachus has stood up in the assembly and announced that he will take a ship and go in search of news of his father. That evening the suitors lounge at his table, eating his flocks, and they laugh. One young lord jeers: perhaps he means to sail to fertile Ephyra and bring back poisons that destroy the life, to drop in the wine bowl and kill us all. Another adds that he may drown at sea like his father, and leave them the trouble of dividing his goods.

This card comes when your intention has been met with ridicule. You have said aloud that you mean to change something, and those who benefit from things as they are have made a joke of it. Notice what the joke is. They are not laughing at your weakness. They are laughing about their own destruction, and the laughter is thin.

Do not argue with them, and do not shrink. Telemachus said nothing more; he went down to the shore that night and slipped away on a dark ship. Let your actions answer the mockery. And keep the details of your plans away from those who sneer at them.
entries.context: In Odyssey 2, Telemachus announces that he will sail to Pylos and Sparta for news of his father. The suitors mock him at their feast, one jeering that he may go to fertile Ephyra to fetch deadly poisons and drop them in the wine bowl to destroy them all.

aspects.love: If someone mocks your hopes in love, or your wish to leave a situation that diminishes you, hear the fear behind it. People who sneer at our growth often fear being left behind. Keep your counsel, and move quietly towards what is right for you.
aspects.work: Colleagues laugh at your new idea, or your plan to go out on your own. Their jokes may reveal that they see its threat to the old arrangement. Say less, work more, and let results do the answering when the time comes.
