aspects.home: In some households, every attempt to change is met with teasing. That teasing keeps everyone in place. Recognise it for what it is, refuse to be shamed, and take your steps without announcing each one to the table.
aspects.health: When you try to change a habit, someone nearby may joke about it: the new diet, the early nights, the giving up of drink. Do not let mockery undo your resolve. It often comes from people who feel judged by your choice, not from anything wrong with it.
aspects.journeys: You have spoken of a voyage or a big decision, and the response has been ridicule. Take that as a cue to plan in private. Prepare your ship quietly, choose your companions carefully, and leave at the hour that suits you, not them.

entries.message: When people jeer at your plan, listen to the joke closely. Mockery often tells you exactly what they are afraid you can do.
entries.reflect: What does the scorn of others reveal about the power they suspect you have?

entries.greek: ἆνερ ἀπʼ αἰῶνος νέος ὤλεο, κὰδ δέ με χήρην
entries.english: Husband, you have died young and left me a widow
entries.reading:
The body of Hector has come home at last. It lies on a carved bed in Priam's palace, singers stand around it leading the dirge, and the women of Troy answer with their wailing. Andromache comes first. She takes her husband's head between her hands, the head of the man who killed so many and who lifted their baby son in his arms on the wall, and she begins: Husband, you have died young, and left me a widow.

This is one of the darkest lines in Homer, and the card does not pretend otherwise. It may come to you in grief: for a person, a marriage, a hope or a future that ended long before its time. You may have been told to be strong, to look on the bright side, to move on. Andromache does none of these things. She speaks, out loud, in front of everyone, exactly what has been taken from her.

That is what the oracle offers you now. Not comfort, but the dignity of lament. Say what was lost and how young it was. Hold its face in your hands. Grief spoken among others is lighter than grief carried alone, and in speaking it you keep faith with what you loved.
entries.context: In Iliad 24, Priam brings Hector's body home to Troy. As the singers lead the dirge, Andromache, holding Hector's head in her hands, begins her lament with these words: he has died young and left her a widow in the halls, with their son still an infant.

aspects.love: If a love has ended, by death, by parting, or by quiet erosion, allow yourself to name it truthfully. Do not hurry into the next thing to escape the ache. Speak to a friend, write it down, weep if you need to. Mourning is love that still has somewhere to go.
aspects.work: A career, a business or a vocation may have been cut short before its time. It is right to grieve that, not only to make plans. Acknowledge what you built and what you hoped, and let the loss be spoken before you set your hand to new work.
aspects.home: When a family suffers a loss, people often fall silent to protect one another. Silence can leave each one grieving alone. Gather, as the women of Troy did, and let the dirge be shared: memories told, names spoken, tears allowed.
aspects.health: Unspoken grief weighs on body and mind alike. If sorrow has settled in you, give it form, in words, in ritual, in the company of others, and do not be ashamed to seek help in carrying it. Lament is not weakness; it is a way of staying alive.
aspects.journeys: A change you did not choose has forced you onto a new road, and with it a sense of a life ended too early. Before you set out, stop and mourn what you are leaving. Those who grieve honestly at the threshold walk more freely afterwards.

entries.message: Some losses come too soon, and nothing makes them right. Give your grief its voice; the lament is how love goes on speaking.
entries.reflect: What loss in your life has never been properly mourned out loud?

entries.greek: ᾗ περ δὴ φρονέω τε καὶ ὡς τετελεσμένον ἔσται,
entries.english: as I truly think, and as it will surely come to pass.
entries.reading:
The embassy has made its speech, and the cups are set down. Odysseus has laid out Agamemnon's treasures with all his famous skill. Achilles, before he says anything else, tells them how he means to answer: bluntly, as I truly think and as it will surely come to pass, so that you do not sit here cooing at me one after another. For I hate that man as I hate the gates of Hades who hides one thing in his heart and says another.

Drawn for your question, this line asks for plain speech. Perhaps there is a conversation in which you have been softening, hinting, letting the other person believe something you do not think is true. Perhaps you are on the receiving end of polished words and long for someone to simply tell you how things stand.

Achilles' answer is harsh, and the card does not ask you to imitate his temper. It asks you to imitate his honesty. Say what you think. Say what you believe will actually happen. Gentleness belongs in how you say it, not in hiding what is meant. People can build on a clear no far better than on a misty maybe.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, Odysseus leads an embassy to Achilles, offering Agamemnon's gifts if he will return to battle. Achilles begins his reply by saying he must speak out bluntly, as he truly thinks and as things will be, because he hates the man who hides one thing in his heart and says another. The identification of this line in the papyrus is probable but marked as uncertain.

aspects.love: Hints and hopeful silences are wearing your love thin. Tell your partner, or the one you care for, what you truly feel and what you truly expect. It may be hard to hear, but honesty spoken gently is the ground real closeness is built on.
aspects.work: Do not let a negotiation drift along on flattering phrases. State your real position and your honest view of how things will go. Colleagues and clients trust the one whose word matches their mind, even when they do not like the answer.
aspects.home: Families often keep the peace by not saying things. If something needs saying at home, say it simply, with love, and without sarcasm. One clear conversation can clear a fog that has hung over the house for months.
aspects.health: Be honest with yourself and with anyone helping you about how you really are. Do not tell the doctor, or your own mirror, that all is well when it is not. Plain truth about the body is the first step towards caring for it properly.
aspects.journeys: If you have already decided to go, or to stay, stop letting others believe the matter is still open. Tell them clearly. Plans built on false hope fall apart; plans built on plain words can be prepared for together.

entries.message: Speak what you truly think and what you truly see coming. A plain word now is kinder than a sweet one that hides the heart.
entries.reflect: Where are you saying one thing while holding another in your heart?

entries.greek: μή μοι οἶνον ἄειρε μελίφρονα πότνια μῆτερ,
entries.english: Do not bring me honey-sweet wine, my lady mother,
entries.reading:
Hector comes straight from the battlefield into the city, sweat and blood still on him. At the palace his mother runs to meet him, takes his hand and offers him honey-sweet wine: pour some to Zeus, she says, and drink yourself, for wine restores a weary man's strength. Hector refuses. Do not bring me honey-sweet wine, lady mother, lest you sap my strength and I forget my courage. And he will not pour to Zeus with unwashed hands, spattered with gore.

This card comes when comfort is being offered at a moment you need to stay sharp. It may be a kind person's offer of rest, a pleasure that would ease the strain, a distraction that would take the edge off. None of it is bad. Hecuba loves her son. But Hector knows that if he sits down in her hall, he may not stand up again for the fight.

So say no, warmly. Explain if you can. Keep your hands to the task until it is done and you have washed. The wine will still be sweet at evening, and you will have earned the right to pour it to the gods.
entries.context: In Iliad 6, Hector returns from battle to Troy to ask the women to pray to Athena. His mother Hecuba offers him honey-sweet wine to pour to Zeus and to restore his strength; Hector refuses with this line, saying it would weaken him and make him forget his courage, and that he will not pour libations with unwashed hands.

aspects.love: Someone dear may want to soothe you, to make the hard thing easier by persuading you to stop. Thank them, and tell them truly why you must keep going for now. Love can understand a refusal that is explained with care.
aspects.work: At a crucial point in a task, the temptation to celebrate early or rest too soon is strong. Hold off. Finish the push, then take the reward. A drink before the work is done often costs more than the work itself.
aspects.home: Family members sometimes show love by pressing comforts on us: stay, rest, have another. When you need to remain focused, refuse gently and honour the gesture behind it. Promise to return to their table once the work is finished.
aspects.health: A comfort you reach for under strain, a glass, a sweet, a screen, a long lie-in, may be quietly draining your strength. Notice which comforts help and which make you forget your courage. Choose the ones that restore rather than dull.
aspects.journeys: On the eve of a demanding change, people will offer every reason to delay and be comfortable a while longer. Their care is real. Keep your resolve; you can rest when you have washed off the road and arrived.

entries.message: A loving comfort can be the wrong thing at the wrong hour. Refuse it gently, finish what you came to do, and drink later.
entries.reflect: Which comfort, offered with love, would weaken you right now if you accepted it?

entries.greek: ὕστατα καὶ πύματα νῦν ἐνθάδε δειπνήσειαν·
entries.english: Let this be the last time, the very last, that they dine here.
entries.theme: The Last Time They Dine Here
entries.reading:
For three years the suitors have eaten their way through Odysseus' house: his oxen, his sheep, his wine. Now the herald Medon comes to the threshold of Penelope's chamber, and before he can speak she turns on him. Have they sent you to tell the maids to stop their work and cook another feast for them? I wish they would never court me again, never gather anywhere again. Let this be the last time, the very last, that they dine here.

This line is a cry of exhaustion. It belongs to anyone who has watched something consume their life season after season: a dependence, a draining relationship, an arrangement that feeds others at your expense. Penelope cannot yet stop the feasting. She can only wish, fiercely, for it to end.

Do not underestimate that wish. To name the end aloud is to stop pretending you can bear it forever. Penelope is about to hear worse news, and she will grieve, pray and sleep; but from this point the poem bends towards the day the hall is cleared. Let your enough be spoken. Then begin, quietly, to prepare for the last meal.
entries.context: In Odyssey 4, the herald Medon comes to tell Penelope that the suitors are plotting to ambush and kill Telemachus on his way home. Before he can speak, she bitterly asks whether they have sent him to order her maids to prepare a feast, and wishes that this might be the very last time they dine in the house.

aspects.love: If a relationship keeps taking far more than it gives, and you have quietly put up with it, this card asks you to name your limit. You need not act tonight. But say, at least to yourself, this cannot go on, and begin to plan with that truth in hand.
aspects.work: You may be subsidising others' comfort with your labour or your money: covering for colleagues, carrying a partner who contributes little. Decide where the last feast will be. Set a date, a condition, a change, and begin quietly preparing for it.
aspects.home: Guests who have overstayed, relatives who treat your home as theirs, habits that consume the household's peace: the time for endless hospitality may be over. Say kindly but clearly what will change, and when, and then hold to it.
aspects.health: A habit or pattern has been feasting on your health for too long. Your weariness of it is a turning point. Let today's meal be the last of that kind, or as close to it as you can manage, and gather the help you need to keep it so.
aspects.journeys: You are tired of a situation that devours your time and spirit. The wish to be done with it is the beginning of change. Start preparing the road away from it, even if the day of leaving is not yet in sight.

entries.message: There comes a point when you know a thing must end. Say it, even if only to yourself; the saying is the first stone of the wall.
entries.reflect: What in your life has been feeding on your household for too long, and have you said enough out loud?

entries.greek: οὐ χρὴ παννύχιον εὕδειν βουληφόρον ἄνδρα
entries.english: A man who must give counsel should not sleep the whole night through.
entries.reading:
Agamemnon sleeps in his hut, and a Dream sent by Zeus stands at his head, wearing the face of wise old Nestor. Its first words are a reproach any leader would accept: a man who must give counsel should not sleep the whole night through, with so many people in his care. Then comes the lie. Arm the Greeks at once; today you will take Troy. Agamemnon wakes, believes, and leads his army into a day that ends in disaster.

This card is a warning. Something is urging you to act right now: a sudden conviction at three in the morning, a person who speaks with borrowed authority, a voice that begins with a truth you cannot argue with and ends with a promise too good to be true. The first half disarms you. The second half is the hook.

You are right to take your responsibilities seriously. You are not obliged to believe every promise that comes wrapped in that seriousness. Rise, yes; think, yes. But before you call the army to arms, check the face of the messenger, sleep on the promise one more night, and ask someone awake and honest what they see.
entries.context: In Iliad 2, Zeus sends a deceptive Dream to Agamemnon in the likeness of Nestor. Standing over the sleeping king, the Dream rebukes him that a counsellor responsible for so many should not sleep all night, then falsely promises that he can take Troy that very day.

aspects.love: Be wary of anyone who stirs you with flattering urgency: now or never, this is destiny. They may start with something true about your loneliness and end with a promise no one can keep. Let real love prove itself slowly and in daylight.
aspects.work: A tempting opportunity arrives with pressure to decide at once and the authority of a trusted name. Check it carefully. A plausible rebuke followed by a dazzling promise is a classic shape of deception. Sleep on it, and seek an independent opinion.
aspects.home: Worries that come in the small hours about the family often feel like commands. Some are real duties; some are dreams in disguise. Write them down, and look at them again in the morning before you act on any of them.
aspects.health: Night-time anxiety can wear the face of good sense and tell you dramatic things about your body or your life. Do not make big changes on the strength of a sleepless hour. Rest if you can, and take your concerns to a clear-headed person by day.
aspects.journeys: If a sudden conviction is driving you to uproot everything immediately, pause. True callings tend to survive a week of reflection; false dreams dissolve under it. Give the plan time to show which it is before you summon the ships.

entries.message: Not every voice that wakes you in the night is your friend. A true rebuke can carry a false promise; test the urgency before you act on it.
entries.reflect: What urgent voice has been pushing you lately, and does its promise hold up in daylight?

entries.greek: δαιμόνιʼ οὐ μὲν καλὰ χόλον τόνδʼ ἔνθεο θυμῷ,
entries.english: Strange man, it is not right to nurse this anger in your heart.
entries.reading:
The Trojans are dying around the walls, and the war is being fought over one man. That man, Paris, is at home in his fine chamber, turning over his shield and breastplate and handling his curved bow, while Helen sits among her maids at their work. Hector strides in, spear in hand, and speaks with a brother's anger: strange man, it is not right to nurse this anger in your heart. The people are perishing; get up, before the city burns.

Hector offers Paris a generous excuse, that he is sulking from injured pride, and Paris half takes it. The card asks you to look beneath your own version of it. Perhaps you are withdrawn from something that needs you, and you have a good reason: someone wronged you, or no one appreciates you, or you are still getting ready. Look closely. Is it anger, or is it comfort?

Polishing armour indoors feels like preparation. It is not the fight. The sweet surprise of this scene is that Paris agrees, arms himself, and runs out through the city like a stallion that has snapped its tether. You can do the same. Put the bow on your shoulder and go.
entries.context: In Iliad 6, Hector finds his brother Paris idling in his chamber, polishing his armour beside Helen, while the Trojans die around the walls in a war fought on his account. Hector rebukes him with this line and urges him back into battle.

aspects.love: You may be holding back from someone, nursing a slight while the bond suffers. The resentment may be real, but it has become a reason to avoid the harder work of repair. Put the grievance down for a day, and go towards the person.
aspects.work: Endless preparation, research, polishing the plan, can be a comfortable hiding place from the real battle. Others are working on what you started. Step out, take your part, and let the effort you have been refining finally be used.
aspects.home: A family member may be sulking in their room while the household struggles. Like Hector, speak frankly but offer them a way back with their dignity intact. Sometimes people need only an honourable reason to rejoin the fray.
aspects.health: Anger turned inward can keep you shut indoors, inactive and resentful. If you notice you are brooding more than living, get up and move. Fresh air and simple action will do more for your spirits than one more hour of rehearsing the wrong.
aspects.journeys: You keep saying you are not quite ready to make the change, but your gear has been polished for months. Readiness is a feeling that often arrives only after you start. Leave the chamber and set out; you will learn the rest on the road.

entries.message: Your grievance may be real, but it is also a hiding place. Leave the bedchamber; the fight that is yours is going on without you.
entries.reflect: What are you polishing at home instead of carrying out into the field?

entries.greek: τίς δʼ οἶδʼ εἴ κέ ποτέ σφι βίας ἀποτίσεται ἐλθών,
entries.english: Who knows whether he may come one day and repay their violence?
entries.reading:
In the bright hall at Pylos, Telemachus pours out his despair. The suitors waste his house and plot against him, and the gods have given him no strength to make them pay. Old Nestor listens, and then says something simple: who knows whether he may come one day and repay their violence, alone or with all the Greeks behind him? Telemachus can hardly bear to hope. Even if the gods willed it, he says, it would never happen.

The card comes to you in the position of the powerless. Someone has wronged you, or wronged many, and nothing you can do seems able to set it right. Bitterness tells you it will always be so. Nestor will not promise anything. He only refuses to let the door be bolted: who knows?

That small question is enough to stand on. It does not ask you to plot revenge, which is not yours to arrange. It asks you to stop deciding that the story is over. The poem itself answers that Odysseus does come home. In the meantime, Telemachus does his part: he travels, learns, grows. Do the same, and leave the rest of the reckoning in wiser hands.
entries.context: In Odyssey 3, Telemachus tells Nestor of the suitors' outrages and laments that the gods have given him no power to punish them. Nestor answers with this line: who knows whether Odysseus may one day come home and pay them back for their violence, alone or with all the Achaeans.

aspects.love: If you have been hurt and the one who hurt you seems to face no consequence, resist making their fate your project. Life has many ways of balancing accounts. Put your care into your own healing, and leave room for what you cannot see.
aspects.work: An unfairness at work may seem permanent: a credit stolen, a dishonest colleague prospering. Keep doing honest work and keep good records. Circumstances change, and those who behave badly are often found out, though rarely on the timetable we would choose.
aspects.home: A family injustice may feel as though it will never be acknowledged. Do not give up hope entirely, but do not wait on it either. Live well, tend those who are kind to you, and let the future speak for itself.
aspects.health: Holding on to the conviction that wrongs will never be righted can sour mind and body alike. Ease your grip on the grievance. Leaving the door open to justice, without keeping watch at it day and night, is a kind of release.
aspects.journeys: You may be tempted to leave a place because you feel powerless against those who harm it. Before you go, ask whether your absence serves you or simply concedes the field. Who knows what may yet return to set things right.

entries.message: You cannot see every road by which justice comes. Leave the door of the future unbarred, and do your own part in the meantime.
entries.reflect: Where have you decided that a wrong will never be answered, and how is that belief shaping you?

entries.greek: ἄξομαι ἀμφοτέροις ἀλόχους καὶ κτήματʼ ὀπάσσω
entries.english: I will find wives for them both, and give them possessions.
entries.reading:
Out in the courtyard, away from the noise of the suitors, a beggar draws two old servants aside: Eumaeus the swineherd and Philoetius the cowherd. He has heard them pray for their master's return. Now he tells them who he is, and to prove it he pulls back his rags to show the scar a boar's tusk left on his thigh when he was a boy. If the gods let me overcome the suitors, he says, I will find wives for you both and give you possessions and houses near my own, and you will be companions and brothers to my son. The two men throw their arms around him and weep.

This is a card of loyalty rewarded. Perhaps you have stayed faithful to a person, a cause or a place through a long absence, when it would have been easier to go over to the side that was feasting. The line says your faithfulness has been noticed by the one who matters.

It may also be asking you to be the one who rewards. Who has kept your house while you were away? Draw them aside, show them your scar, tell them plainly what they mean to you, and make them family.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, Odysseus, still disguised, takes the faithful swineherd Eumaeus and cowherd Philoetius outside and reveals himself to them. He promises that if the gods let him overcome the suitors, he will give each of them a wife, possessions and a house near his own, and treat them as Telemachus' companions and brothers.

aspects.love: A friend who stood by you during a hard and hidden time deserves more than private gratitude. Tell them, openly, how much their loyalty has mattered, and draw them closer into your life. Steadfast companions are rarer than gold, and should be treated as kin.
aspects.work: Your patient loyalty in a difficult workplace is closer to being recognised than you think. Meanwhile, look around: who has supported you quietly? Share credit, recommend them, and make sure that when good fortune comes, they share in it.
aspects.home: In every family there are those who keep things running during absences and crises. Name them. A spoken thank-you, a gift, a place of honour at the table: these say, you are one of us, and make the bonds of the household stronger.
aspects.health: Think of those who helped you through illness or a dark season without being asked. Their care was part of your healing. Let them know, and let yourself receive gratitude too for the times you were the faithful one who stayed.
aspects.journeys: As you move into a new phase, bring along those who were loyal to you in the old one. Do not leave the faithful behind in the courtyard. Change is easier with trusted companions, and they have earned their place on the road.

entries.message: Faithfulness that waited in the dark will be seen. Recognise those who stood by you, and let yourself be recognised.
entries.reflect: Who has stayed faithful to you when no one was watching, and have you told them what it means?

entries.greek: τόξου πειρώμεσθα καὶ ἐκτελέωμεν ἄεθλον.
entries.english: Let us try the bow, and see the contest through.
entries.reading:
One by one the suitors have tried to string Odysseus' great bow, and one by one they have failed. Leodes, the gentlest of them, puts it down with blistered hands and warns that it will break their hearts. Antinous sneers at him, then calls for a fire to be lit and a cake of fat to be brought. Let us warm the bow and grease it, he says. Let us try the bow, and see the contest through. They warm it and grease it and strain at it, and still not one of them can bend it.

On the surface this is a card of persistence. A test is before you, and the line says, do not abandon it. That is true, and worth holding on to.

But look at who is speaking and what he does. Antinous does not grow stronger; he tries to soften the bow. Ask whether you are doing the same: changing the terms, finding a trick, lowering the bar until you can clear it. Some tests cannot be cheated, because they are measuring whether this thing is truly yours. If it is, the bow will bend to you in time. If it is not, no amount of grease will make it so.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, the suitor Leodes has failed to string Odysseus' great bow. Antinous scorns him and orders the goatherd Melanthius to light a fire and bring a cake of fat, so that the young men can warm and grease the bow, try it again and finish the contest.

aspects.love: If you keep trying to win someone by finding new tricks, new ways to soften their resistance, pause. Love is not a bow to be greased into bending. If the bond is truly yours, it will answer honest effort; if not, cleverness will not change that.
aspects.work: Finish the trial you have begun, but do it honestly. If you find yourself bending rules or massaging figures to pass a test, stop. The work that lasts belongs to the one who could do it without the warming fire.
aspects.home: In family matters, you may be trying to force an outcome by changing the rules each time it fails: new conditions, new arguments. Step back and ask whether this outcome is truly yours to claim, or whether you are straining at someone else's bow.
aspects.health: Keep at the effort, but be wary of shortcuts that promise to make the hard part vanish. Real strength is built slowly. Keep to the steady way, and let the test show you honestly where you are.
aspects.journeys: Persevering with a challenging plan is good; contorting it to fit what you want can be a sign it is not meant for you. If every attempt needs a new trick, listen to that, and consider whose bow you are trying to string.

entries.message: Seeing a trial through is right. Bending the trial so that you can pass it is not; the bow will only yield to the hands it belongs to.
entries.reflect: Are you trying to become equal to the test, or trying to make the test easier?

entries.greek: οὐ γάρ τις νέμεσις φυγέειν κακόν, οὐδʼ ἀνὰ νύκτα.
entries.english: There is no shame in running from ruin, even by night.
entries.reading:
The Trojans have broken through the wall, and the Greek kings, wounded and leaning on their spears, walk down among the ships. Agamemnon has lost heart for the third time in the war. Let us drag the nearest ships down to the sea, he says, moor them out in deep water, and when night comes launch the rest. There is no shame in running from ruin, even by night. Better to flee and escape than be caught.

Odysseus' answer is fierce. If the men see the ships going down to the water, they will stop fighting and look back, and the whole army will be destroyed. Diomedes, wounded himself, urges them to go back to the battle and at least put heart into the others.

This card asks you to tell retreat from flight. Agamemnon's principle is not wrong: sometimes leaving is wise, and no one should die for pride. But his way is wrong: secret, panicked, abandoning those who trust him. If you need to step back, do it in daylight, with others informed and cared for. And check that it is ruin you are escaping, not merely fear. Often the line holds if the leader does.
entries.context: In Iliad 14, with the Trojans breaking through the Greek wall, Agamemnon despairs and proposes launching the ships at night and fleeing, saying there is no blame in escaping ruin even by night. Odysseus immediately rebukes him for the suggestion, and Diomedes urges the leaders back to the battle.

aspects.love: If you are considering leaving a relationship, do it honestly and openly, not by slipping away at night. The way you leave matters as much as whether you leave. Speak face to face, and do not abandon the other person to discover it alone.
aspects.work: There may be no disgrace in withdrawing from a failing venture. But a leader who quietly prepares an escape while others keep fighting destroys their trust. Share your thinking, and if you go, go in a way that protects those who relied on you.
aspects.home: In a crisis at home, the urge to escape can be overwhelming. Before you leave, physically or in spirit, ask who is depending on you to stay at your post. A short, honest pause is wiser than a sudden flight that leaves others exposed.
aspects.health: Stepping back from a punishing commitment to protect your health is wise and nothing to be ashamed of. Do it calmly and with a plan, telling those it affects, rather than collapsing out of it in exhaustion when you can no longer stand.
aspects.journeys: Moving away from danger can be right. Be sure that what you are fleeing is truly ruin and not only a hard patch. If you must go, plan the departure clearly, and do not let fear choose the hour for you.

entries.message: Retreat can be wise. Flight in the dark, chosen in panic and hidden from those who depend on you, rarely is.
entries.reflect: Are you thinking of retreat because it is wise, or because you are frightened and tired?

entries.greek: παντοίης ἀρετῆς μιμνήσκεο· νῦν σε μάλα χρὴ
entries.english: Remember all your courage. Now, above all, you must
entries.reading:
Three times Hector has run around the walls of Troy, and three times Achilles has run after him, the whole of the gods watching. Then Hector stops. He asks only that whoever wins will give back the other's body. Achilles refuses with contempt, and then says the line that tells Hector the chase is over: remember all your courage; now, above all, you must be a spearman and a bold fighter. There is no escape for you any longer.

The man who speaks is pitiless, and the card does not pretend he is kind. Yet the words themselves carry a hard truth that anyone may one day need. There are moments when the running stops. The thing you have circled for months, the conversation, the reckoning, the illness, the loss, is in front of you, and no further lap of the walls will change it.

When that hour comes, what is left is everything you have been. Remember it: every hard thing you have already survived, every skill, every love that made you. Hector, at the last, draws his sword and charges like an eagle, resolved not to die without a struggle. No card can promise you the outcome. This one promises that you can meet it as yourself.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Hector, facing Achilles at last before the walls of Troy, asks that the winner return the loser's body. Achilles refuses any pact and, with this line, tells Hector to remember all his prowess, for now he must be a spearman and bold warrior, since there is no escape left to him.

aspects.love: A conversation you have long avoided can no longer be postponed. Gather your courage, remember why this bond matters, and say what must be said. Whatever follows, you will have met it with your whole heart rather than circling it.
aspects.work: The deadline, the decision or the confrontation is here, and there is no way around it. Draw on every skill and experience you have built. Stand and do your best work now; you are more prepared than your fear allows you to feel.
aspects.home: A family crisis has arrived that cannot be fled. Call on every reserve you have, and on those who love you. Face what is before you steadily; a household finds its strength when someone stops running and turns to meet the trouble.
aspects.health: When illness or difficulty can no longer be ignored, courage means facing it with clear eyes and good help. Remember the times you have already come through hard seasons. Bring all of yourself to the task of caring for your body now.
aspects.journeys: The decision you have circled for so long is now in front of you. Stop the circling. Bring together everything you know and value, choose, and step forward. Whatever comes, you will have faced it rather than fled.

entries.message: There is no escape left, and so there is only this: gather every strength you have ever had, and meet it standing.
entries.reflect: If you stopped running from the thing you fear, what strengths would you bring to meet it?

entries.greek: χήρην ἐν μεγάροισι· πάϊς δʼ ἔτι νήπιος αὔτως,
entries.english: a widow in the halls; and the child is still only a baby.
entries.reading:
Andromache has not heard the news. She is at her loom in the inner room, weaving a purple cloak strewn with flowers, and she has told her maids to set a great cauldron on the fire so Hector can have a hot bath when he comes home from the fighting. Then the wailing reaches her from the wall. The shuttle falls from her hand. She runs, sees the body dragged through the dust, and faints. When she can speak, her first thought is not only for herself: a widow in the halls, and the child is still only a baby.

This card comes to those standing in the aftermath of a blow. The loss may be large or small: a death, a separation, a failing business, a dream given up. In the middle of your own sorrow, the line turns your eyes to whoever is most vulnerable now. A child, an elderly parent, a friend who relied on what has gone, or the small, young part of yourself that does not understand what happened.

Tend to them. Make the practical arrangements. Keep the fire under the cauldron, even if the one it was heated for is not coming. Grief and care can live in the same hands.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Andromache, hearing the cries from the wall, runs out and sees Achilles dragging Hector's body behind his chariot. When she recovers from her faint she laments that Hector has gone to the house of Hades, leaving her a widow in the halls and their son still a baby.

aspects.love: After a loss or a breaking-up, some of those around you are more vulnerable than they seem: children, friends, the partner who will be alone. Grieve, but also look out for them. Small, steady acts of care can carry others through the worst.
aspects.work: When something at work collapses, think of those most affected: the new colleague, the dependent client, the supplier who relied on you. Take time to put arrangements in place that protect them; it is part of ending things honourably.
aspects.home: If a household has been struck, think first of the children and the frail. Keep their routines as steady as you can, tell them the truth at the level they can bear, and make sure they know who will look after them.
aspects.health: Grief takes a toll on the body, and it is easy to neglect yourself while caring for others. Treat yourself as one of the vulnerable ones too. Eat, sleep, accept help, and remember that tending the small child inside you is part of tending the house.
aspects.journeys: If change is forced on you by loss, plan with an eye to those who depend on you. Ask what they need from the next chapter, not only what you need. A decision taken with them in mind will carry you all more safely.

entries.message: When loss strikes, look first to the small ones it leaves exposed. Grief that turns into care is grief that keeps the house standing.
entries.reflect: Who, in or around you, is most exposed by what has happened, and what do they need from you now?

entries.greek: ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν μή πω καταδύσεο μῶλον Ἄρηος
entries.english: But do not go into the struggle of war just yet.
entries.reading:
Patroclus is dead, and Achilles lies in the dust, tearing his hair. He will go out at once, he says, and kill Hector. His mother rises from the sea to comfort him. She does not tell him he is wrong. She reminds him only that his own splendid armour is now on Hector's shoulders, stripped from the body of his friend. But do not go into the struggle of war just yet. At dawn I will come back with new arms from Hephaestus himself.

This card is a hand on your arm. You may be burning to act: to answer a wrong, defend someone, launch yourself at a problem that has already cost you dearly. The urge is honourable. But you are not yet equipped. Something essential, your strength, your information, your allies, your calm, is not in your hands tonight.

Waiting does not mean doing nothing. While Achilles waits, he goes to the edge of the trench unarmed and shouts three times, and the sound alone turns back the enemy so that his friend's body can be brought home. Do what can be done bare-handed now. Then rest. The better armour is being forged, and it will be yours at dawn.
entries.context: In Iliad 18, Achilles, grieving for Patroclus, vows to return to battle at once to kill Hector. His mother Thetis agrees the cause is good, but reminds him that Hector now wears his armour, and tells him not to enter the fighting until she returns at dawn with new arms from Hephaestus.

aspects.love: You are ready to have it out, to defend your love or confront a wrong. Wait. Speak when you are calm and know what you need to say. In the meantime, a single word of support or presence can protect what matters until you are ready.
aspects.work: You want to answer a setback with an immediate bold move. Give it a day. Gather the facts, the allies and the resources you lack. Meanwhile, make your presence felt in smaller ways, so that ground is held while you prepare.
aspects.home: Anger over a family hurt may push you to act tonight. Hold back until you have rested and thought. Take care of the immediate needs, those that keep everyone safe and fed, and let the larger reckoning wait until morning.
aspects.health: If you are eager to return to full strength after injury or illness, do not rush back before you are ready. Let healing finish its work. Do what you can lightly now, and save the full effort for when your armour is restored.
aspects.journeys: A big move tempts you to leave immediately. Make sure your preparations are complete first. Arrange what is needed, wait for the right moment, and when it comes, step out equipped, not merely eager, with the road ahead of you.

entries.message: Your cause is right, but your armour is in the enemy's hands. Wait for dawn, and go out properly equipped.
entries.reflect: What do you still need before you go out to this fight, and what can you do while you wait for it?

entries.greek: αἶψα γὰρ ἐν κακότητι βροτοὶ καταγηράσκουσιν.
entries.english: For in hardship, mortals grow old before their time.
entries.reading:
In the firelit hall, Penelope sits across from a ragged old beggar who has told her he once met Odysseus. She calls the old nurse Eurycleia to wash his feet, and as she does so she says, almost to herself: by now my husband must have hands and feet like these, for in hardship, mortals grow old before their time. She does not know that her husband is sitting in front of her. Minutes later the nurse's fingers find the old scar on his leg, and she drops his foot into the basin with a clang.

This card speaks of what trouble does to us. You may feel older than your years: worn by worry, by loss, by a long struggle, or by caring for others. You may look in the mirror and not quite recognise yourself. The line does not deny it; hardship ages us, and Homer says so plainly.

But look at the scene. The aged stranger is the very man she has waited for. What matters most about him has not been worn away, and someone who loves him knows him by touch. Be gentle with what life has done to you and to those around you. Beneath the weathering, the self you are is still there to be found.
entries.context: In Odyssey 19, Penelope asks the old nurse Eurycleia to wash the feet of the disguised beggar, unaware that he is Odysseus. She remarks that Odysseus must by now look as this man does, for in misfortune mortals quickly grow old; moments later, Eurycleia recognises her master by his scar.

aspects.love: You or your partner may have been changed by hard years. Do not mistake weariness for the loss of love. Look past the lines and the tiredness for the familiar scar, the gesture or the laugh that is still unmistakably theirs, and let them see yours.
aspects.work: Long strain at work can make you feel ground down and much older than you are. Notice it, and take it seriously. Seek work that restores rather than only consumes you, and remember that the person you were before this hardship has not vanished.
aspects.home: Family members who have been through difficulty may seem changed, distant or older. Be patient. Wash their feet, as it were: small acts of care can bring the familiar person back into view and remind them they are known.
aspects.health: If trouble has aged you, honour what it has cost and give yourself the rest and care you would give anyone in that state. Recovery may not undo every mark, but much that seems lost can return as the burden lightens.
aspects.journeys: Long wandering leaves its mark, and you may return from a hard chapter barely recognisable to yourself. Give it time. In familiar places, among people who know you, the truest parts of you will be found again.

entries.message: Hardship marks the face and bends the back, but the one who loves you will still know you by your scar.
entries.reflect: What part of you has hardship hidden, and who would still recognise it?

entries.greek: οὐκ ἔσθʼ οὗτος ἀνὴρ διερὸς βροτὸς οὐδὲ γένηται,
entries.english: That man is not alive, and never will be born,
entries.reading:
The line begins like a death notice: that man is not alive, and never will be born. But listen to the rest of the sentence. On a Phaeacian beach, the shipwrecked Odysseus has crept out of the bushes, naked but for a leafy olive branch, crusted with brine, terrible to look at, like a mountain lion driven by hunger. The girls who were playing ball by the river flee in every direction. Only Nausicaa stands still, because Athena has put courage in her heart. She calls them back: no man lives, or will ever be born, who could come to this land bringing war. The gods love us. This is some poor wanderer, and every stranger comes from Zeus.

This card arrives when fear has outrun the facts. Something new has appeared on your shore, wild and alarming in its first moment: a person, a situation, a change. Your instinct, and perhaps everyone else's, is to scatter.

The line asks you to be Nausicaa. Hold your place long enough to see what is actually there. You may be safer than you feel; what looks like a threat may be someone half-drowned asking for help. Be steady, be generous, and let your courage call the others back.
entries.context: In Odyssey 6, the shipwrecked Odysseus appears, naked and salt-caked, before the princess Nausicaa and her maids, who flee in fright. Nausicaa calls them back, telling them that no man lives or will ever be born who could come to the land of the Phaeacians bringing war, for they are dear to the gods.

aspects.love: A new person may have arrived in your life looking nothing like what you expected: rough round the edges, in difficult circumstances. Do not run at first sight. Look again with calm eyes. Some of the best friendships begin with one person staying when the others fled.
aspects.work: A change at work, a new arrival, a merger, an unfamiliar task, is causing alarm all around you. Keep your head. Gather the facts before joining the panic. Your steadiness may help others see that what arrived is no enemy, and may even be an opportunity.
aspects.home: When something unexpected appears at home, a guest, a confession, a sudden need, the household may scatter in fear or judgement. Be the one who calms the others. Ask what is needed, offer what you can, and remind everyone that this house has room for kindness.
aspects.health: Fear can turn a passing alarm into a monster. If something about your body or mind has frightened you, stand still a moment and look clearly, with proper counsel if you need it. Many things are less dangerous than they first appear.
aspects.journeys: You may be arriving somewhere new and feel like the salt-crusted stranger in the bushes, or meeting one. Remember that most shores hold more welcome than threat. Approach with courtesy, accept hospitality, and let first fears give way to what is truly there.

entries.message: The thing that has made everyone scatter is not the danger they think. Stand your ground, look again, and you may find a stranger in need of kindness.
entries.reflect: What has frightened you at first sight that might, on a second look, be asking for your kindness?

entries.greek: ναὶ δὴ ταῦτά γε τέκνον ἐτήτυμον οὐ κακόν ἐστι
entries.english: Yes, my child, this is true; it is no bad thing
entries.reading:
A mother rises from the sea and kneels beside her son in the dust. Achilles has just sworn to go back to the war and avenge Patroclus, knowing it will cost him his life, and Thetis does not argue. Yes, my child, this is true, she says; it is no bad thing to defend your friends from ruin. Then comes the hard half of her answer: your armour is gone, stripped from Patroclus and now worn by Hector. Wait for me until dawn, and I will bring you new arms from the forge of Hephaestus.

Drawn for your question, this line is a yes, and a real one. Whatever you have resolved to do, to stand up for someone, to answer a wrong, to return to a fight you left, it is worthy, and you do not need to defend it any longer. But the yes carries a condition. Something you relied on is no longer in your hands. Perhaps another now holds it; perhaps it was lost in the very trouble that has stirred you.

So do not go out bare-chested in your grief. Give it one night. Let the right means be made for you, then go, and go wholeheartedly.
entries.context: In Iliad 18, Achilles declares that he will go back to battle and avenge Patroclus even if it costs him his life. Thetis replies with this line, agreeing that it is good to defend his hard-pressed comrades from destruction, but warns that his armour is now in Hector's hands.

aspects.love: Your wish to stand by someone you love is good and true. Before you step in, ask whether you are equipped for what they need: patience, knowledge, a calm voice. Love armed with the right tools does more than love rushing out in anger.
aspects.work: The project or stand you are planning is sound. Check, though, whether the resources you counted on are still yours; a colleague may have taken the plan, or the budget may have moved. Secure fresh means before you announce the charge.
aspects.home: A family matter calls you to defend someone, and you are right to answer. Talk first with the elder or the wiser one in the house, as Achilles did with his mother. One quiet conversation at the hearth may forge what you lack.
aspects.health: Your resolve to face something in your body or mind is brave and right. Do not go to it unprotected. Gather the help, rest and advice you need before the hard day, and let the waiting night be part of the remedy.
aspects.journeys: The change you have decided on is a good one. Something you thought you would take with you, savings, a companion, a certainty, may no longer be there. Pause long enough to replace it, then set out at dawn without looking back.

entries.message: Your cause is good, and the gods say so. Before you run out to fight for it, look at what you are carrying.
entries.reflect: What do you need to have in your hands before you can rightly step into this fight?

entries.greek: οὔ οἱ νῦν ἔτι γʼ ἔστι πεφυγμένον ἄμμε γενέσθαι,
entries.english: Now there is no way left for him to escape us,
entries.reading:
Three times the two men have circled the walls of Troy, past the springs where Trojan wives once washed their bright clothes, and still Achilles cannot close the gap. Then, far above, Zeus lifts his golden scales and Hector's day sinks. Athena comes down to Achilles and tells him: now there is no way left for him to escape us. Stand here and catch your breath.

This is a hard line to receive, because it is spoken over a good man's doom, and the goddess then wins the fight by a trick. Yet drawn for you it speaks plainly. You have been pursuing something for a long time, a result, an answer, a person's decision, and you have worn yourself thin with running. The oracle says the matter has already been weighed elsewhere. The outcome you have chased is now within reach, and your frantic effort is no longer what will decide it.

So stand still. Let your lungs fill. And when the meeting comes, meet it cleanly and with open eyes. A victory that needs deception or cruelty to finish it is one you will carry for the rest of your life; let yours be one you can look at.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, after Zeus weighs the fates and Hector's sinks, Apollo abandons him. Athena comes to Achilles and tells him that now Hector cannot escape them, even if Apollo grovels before Zeus, and bids him stand and rest while she persuades Hector to fight.

aspects.love: A long uncertainty with someone is reaching its end, and you no longer need to pursue or persuade. Let them come to the moment of truth in their own time. When it comes, be honest rather than clever; what you win by pressure you will not keep.
aspects.work: The deal, post or result you have chased is close to settled. Stop sending one more message and one more reminder. Prepare yourself instead for the final meeting, and make sure you arrive rested and fair-minded, not breathless.
aspects.home: An old household question is about to be resolved. You have argued it round and round like the circuit of the walls. Step back now, let the facts speak, and when it is settled, be generous to whoever loses.
aspects.health: You have been running on nerves for a long stretch. The pressure is nearly over; let your body know it. Sit, breathe slowly, eat properly. The last stage will ask for a steady hand, not more speed.
aspects.journeys: A decision you have pursued for months is, in truth, already made; the scales have tipped. You need not keep gathering reasons or circling the walls one more time. Pause before the final step, check that you act from clear sight rather than exhaustion, and then go.

entries.message: The long chase has turned. What you have pursued can no longer slip away, so stop running and breathe before the last step.
entries.reflect: Now that it cannot escape you, how do you want to be when you finally reach it?

entries.greek: χαλκοῦ τε χρυσοῦ τʼ ἀπολυσόμεθʼ, ἔστι γὰρ ἔνδον·
entries.english: We will ransom them with bronze and gold, for there is plenty inside.
entries.reading:
An old king leans over the wall and pleads. Priam is begging Hector to come inside, and in his fear he counts his missing sons: Lycaon and Polydorus, whom he cannot find in the city. If they are alive among the Greeks, he says, we will ransom them with bronze and gold, for there is plenty inside. The treasure is real. The hope is not. Both boys are already dead by Achilles' hand, and the father does not know.

This line asks you to look gently at something you are still planning to buy back. A friendship that ended, a chance that passed, a version of yourself or of someone you love that is no longer there. You keep the gold ready in the storeroom: the apology, the effort, the money, the perfect plan. But some things are past ransom, and the waiting is costing you.

Notice, too, where Priam's real plea is going. He is speaking to the son who is still alive, still outside, still within reach of a voice. Mourn what is gone, truly and without hurry. Then turn your love and your riches to the living who can still hear you.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Priam begs Hector from the walls not to face Achilles alone. He speaks of his sons Lycaon and Polydorus, whom he cannot find in the city, and says that if they are alive among the Greeks he will ransom them with bronze and gold, of which there is plenty in the house; he does not know that both are already dead at Achilles' hands.

aspects.love: You may be keeping yourself ready for a love that has already ended, rehearsing what you would offer if they returned. Let it be mourned. The tenderness you hold in reserve belongs now to the people still at your side.
aspects.work: Money and effort poured into reviving a venture that is truly finished will not bring it back. Count honestly what is lost. Your resources are better spent on the work that is still alive and needs you.
aspects.home: Someone in your family is quietly waiting for a person or a past that will not return. Do not argue with their hope; sit with them in it. Then help them see the ones still under the roof.
aspects.health: Part of you may be waiting to get back a strength or ease you once had. Grief for that is real and allowed. Then ask what this body, as it is now, needs from you, and give that generously.
aspects.journeys: Do not go back to a place or a plan to recover what time has already taken. If you travel, travel toward the living: the person you can still visit, the door you can still open.

entries.message: Some losses cannot be bought back with any treasure. Grieve them, and spend your gold on the one still standing at the gate.
entries.reflect: What are you still hoping to buy back, and who near you could be helped by that love today?

entries.greek: πῖνέ τε, μηδʼ ἐρίδαινε μετʼ ἀνδράσι κουροτέροισιν.
entries.english: Drink, and do not quarrel with men younger than yourself.
entries.reading:
In the smoky hall at Ithaca the great bow lies on the table, and one by one the young suitors have failed to string it. Then a ragged old beggar asks for a turn. Antinous, the boldest of them, answers with threats and a cautionary tale about a drunken Centaur, and finishes with this: drink, and do not quarrel with men younger than yourself. He calls it advice. It is fear. The beggar is Odysseus, the bow is his own, and Antinous knows something in that old frame might bend it.

You may be hearing this voice now, from outside or from within. You are too old for this, too late, out of your depth among the quick and confident. Sit down, enjoy what you have, leave the contest to others. The line asks you to notice how eagerly that counsel is offered and by whom.

Yet notice also what Odysseus does. He does not quarrel. He does not shout down the young men or plead his case. He waits, lets the right people hand him the bow, and then lets his hands speak. Do not argue for your place. Take it quietly when it comes.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, the disguised Odysseus asks to try the bow. Antinous, alarmed, scolds him as a drunken beggar, recalls how the Centaur Eurytion was maimed for drunken folly, threatens to ship him to the cruel King Echetus, and ends by telling him to drink in peace and not compete with younger men.

aspects.love: Someone may be telling you, kindly or not, that you are past the age for romance or too set in your ways for a new friendship. You need not argue with them. Simply stay open, and when the moment comes, step forward without asking permission.
aspects.work: Younger rivals may be crowding the floor and dismissing your experience. Do not waste breath in quarrels over who deserves a turn. Keep your skill ready, wait for the opening, and let your work answer for you.
aspects.home: At family gatherings you may be treated as the one who should sit back and be pleased. If you still have something to offer, offer it calmly and without resentment. Patience at the table can carry more weight than a raised voice.
aspects.health: Do not let anyone talk you out of strength you still have because of the number of your years. Test yourself sensibly and with good advice, as Odysseus tested the bow, rather than accepting a seat by the fire too early.
aspects.journeys: You may be told a big change is for the young. Weigh that honestly, but do not let another's nervousness decide for you. A late start, made with steady hands, can still send the arrow through every axe.

entries.message: When someone hurries to keep you in your seat, ask what they fear you will do if you stand.
entries.reflect: Whose comfort is served by you staying in your seat?

entries.greek: πῇ φεύγεις μετὰ νῶτα βαλὼν κακὸς ὣς ἐν ὁμίλῳ;
entries.english: Where are you running, turning your back like a coward in the crowd?
entries.theme: The Old Man in the Chariot
entries.reading:
One arrow from Paris strikes a horse in the head, and old Nestor's chariot is pinned in the middle of the plain while Hector's horses thunder toward him. Diomedes sees it and shouts to Odysseus: where are you running, turning your back like a coward in the crowd? Odysseus, of all men, does not hear, and races on to the ships. So Diomedes wheels round alone, lifts the old man into his own chariot, and turns to face the charge.

This card asks you to look at the field around you. Is there someone pinned down, an older person, a struggling colleague, a friend in a mess, while everyone moves on with their own escape? It is easy to run with the many; nobody blames a face in the crowd. But the line says you can see, and seeing makes you responsible.

It has a second edge. You may be the one shouting while others hurry past without hearing. If so, do not wait for help to turn round. Diomedes acted alone and it was enough. Whether you are the caller or the one called, the counsel is the same: stand, turn your horses, and help.
entries.context: In Iliad 8, Zeus turns the battle against the Greeks, and Nestor is trapped when Paris shoots one of his horses. As Hector charges at him, Diomedes shouts to Odysseus with this line, asking where he is fleeing and urging him to stay and save the old man; Odysseus does not hear and runs on to the ships, so Diomedes rescues Nestor alone.

aspects.love: A friend or partner may be struggling while you are absorbed in your own hurry. You have perhaps heard their call and told yourself you did not. Turn back. Being the one who stops will matter more to them than anything you are rushing toward.
aspects.work: When a project fails, people scatter to protect themselves. Someone, perhaps a junior or an older colleague, will be left holding the blame. Stand next to them. Loyalty under pressure is remembered long after the deadline is forgotten.
aspects.home: An elder in your family may be stranded by illness, age or loneliness while the rest are busy. If no one else answers, do not wait for a committee. Go yourself, as Diomedes did, and bring them in.
aspects.health: If you are the one pinned down, call out plainly and keep calling; someone will hear. If you are well, notice who around you is not, and offer more than a passing word on your way somewhere else.
aspects.journeys: A change ahead may tempt you to rush out with the crowd and leave someone behind. Before you go, ask who depends on you. Your departure can still happen, but perhaps with them beside you in the chariot.

entries.message: Someone near you is stranded while the crowd runs past. You will long remember whether you stopped.
entries.reflect: Who in your life is stuck in the middle of the field right now, and what would stopping for them cost you?

entries.greek: αἲ γὰρ ἐμοὶ τοιόσδε πόσις κεκλημένος εἴη
entries.english: If only such a man might be called my husband,
entries.reading:
He came out of the bushes naked, caked with brine, holding a leafy branch, and the maids scattered screaming. Only Nausicaa stood her ground. Now Odysseus has bathed in the river, Athena has poured grace over his head and shoulders, and the princess watches him sit on the shore shining. He seemed so wretched before, she tells her maids; if only such a man might be called my husband.

The line holds two lessons, and both may be for you. The first: worth often arrives in poor clothes. A person, a chance, an idea you met at its roughest may show its real nature once it has rested and been cared for. Do not judge it by the moment it crawled out of the sea. And if you are the shipwrecked one, take heart: you will not always look the way you look now.

The second lesson is in how the story ends. Nausicaa's wish does not come true. Odysseus is going home to his own wife, and she lets him go with grace, asking only that he remember her. Admire freely, then, and hope openly. But hold your wish with an open hand.
entries.context: In Odyssey 6, after Odysseus has bathed in the river and Athena has made him tall and handsome, Nausicaa marvels at the change. She tells her maids that he who seemed so wretched now looks like a god, wishes aloud that such a man might be her husband and stay among them, and orders them to give him food and drink.

aspects.love: Someone you overlooked may look quite different now. Let yourself feel the admiration. But remember Nausicaa, and do not build a whole future on one shining afternoon; let what is real reveal itself before you name it.
aspects.work: A candidate, partner or proposal that came to you badly presented, salt-stained and stammering, may be the best on offer. Give it the bath and the clean clothes, which is to say a proper hearing, before you decide. Worth often hides under brine.
aspects.home: A family member who has been through a rough season, washed up and silent, may be ready to be seen afresh. Notice how they have changed and say so aloud, as Nausicaa did to her maids. People grow into the way they are looked at.
aspects.health: If you feel battered and unrecognisable, wash, rest and eat before you pass judgement on yourself. Odysseus did not change his nature on that riverbank; he only recovered it. Give yourself the same chance, and recovery will show you to yourself again.
aspects.journeys: A new place may receive you warmly once you have found your feet. Accept its kindness. Yet be clear in your heart whether you are staying or passing through, and be honest with those who hope you will stay.

entries.message: What first came to you salt-crusted and wild may be worth more than it looked. Look again once the sea has been washed off.
entries.reflect: What or whom did you dismiss at first sight that deserves a second look?

entries.greek: οὐρανῷ ἐστήριξε κάρη καὶ ἐπὶ χθονὶ βαίνει·
entries.english: Her head strikes the heavens while she walks upon the earth.
entries.reading:
The truce is broken, and for the first time in the poem the armies advance. Among the powers driving them on goes Strife, sister of the war god. Homer gives her one of his most haunting pictures: she rises only a little at first, and soon her head strikes the heavens while she walks upon the earth, throwing hatred into the crowd and swelling the groans of men.

This card arrives when something is growing. Perhaps it is a disagreement that began over very little, a remark, a missed message, a question of whose turn it was, and is now taking up the whole sky of your days. Strife is like that. She feeds on every step forward, every answer given in heat, until no one remembers how small she once was.

The line gives you a clear counsel. Look at your own part in her growth. Are you adding to her stride with each reply? You may not be able to shrink her by yourself, but you can stop lifting her. Speak while she is still small enough to be spoken to, or step aside and let her walk past without your shoulders under her.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, after the truce is broken, the armies advance into battle for the first time in the poem. The narrator describes the gods who drive them on, among them Strife, sister and comrade of Ares, who rises small at first but soon has her head in the heavens while she walks the earth, spreading conflict and grief among men.

aspects.love: A small irritation between you and someone you love has been growing taller with each exchange. Name it now, kindly and specifically, before it fills the house. The first word of peace is easier while the quarrel is still small.
aspects.work: Office friction that began as a minor slight is spreading through the team. Do not feed it with gossip or sharp messages. Address it directly with the person concerned, or let it pass entirely; half-measures make it grow.
aspects.home: A family dispute may be passing from one person to the next, gathering size. Refuse to carry it further. You can listen without taking sides, and that alone can stop Strife from walking through every room.
aspects.health: Inner conflict grows like outer conflict. A worry you have entertained every night may now loom over everything. Bring it down to earth by writing it out or speaking it to someone; seen at its true size, it may shrink.
aspects.journeys: A change you are weighing has become tangled in arguments with others about it, and the quarrel now looms larger than the choice. Separate the two. Ask what you would decide if no one were fighting over it, and act from that quieter place.

entries.message: A quarrel begins at the height of a word and ends with its head among the clouds. Meet it while it still walks at your ankle.
entries.reflect: If you remember how this conflict began, how much of its present size have you helped to build?

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ οὐ Ζεὺς ἄνδρεσσι νοήματα πάντα τελευτᾷ·
entries.english: But Zeus does not bring every plan of men to fulfilment.
entries.theme: The Promise You Could Not Keep
entries.reading:
In the tent, beside the body, Achilles remembers a day in his father's house. He had told Menoetius, the father of Patroclus, that he would bring his son home to Opoeis, rich with a share of Troy's plunder. He meant every word. Now the son lies washed and still on the bier, and Achilles says the hardest thing he knows: but Zeus does not bring every plan of men to fulfilment.

You may be standing over a promise like that. You said you would protect someone, finish something, bring a person or a project safely home. You meant it, and it did not happen. And because you meant it, you have been treating the failure as a crime of your own. This line, from the mouth of the greatest of warriors, says otherwise. Mortals plan; the outcome is held in larger hands than yours.

That does not make the loss smaller. Achilles weeps all night, and he is right to. But grief honours the promise; guilt only poisons it. Let yourself mourn what you hoped to give. Then, as Achilles does, find what can still be done in its name: the rites, the care, the faithful remembering.
entries.context: In Iliad 18, Achilles mourns over the body of Patroclus and laments to the Myrmidons. He recalls promising Patroclus' father Menoetius that he would bring his son home with a share of the plunder from Troy, and says with this line that Zeus does not fulfil all men's plans, for both of them are fated to die at Troy.

aspects.love: You may have promised someone a future that did not come: a marriage that ended, a friendship that faded, a move that never happened. You were not a liar. Plans fail. Tell them, or tell yourself, that the intention was true.
aspects.work: A target you committed to has fallen through, through no simple fault of yours. Own your part honestly and stop carrying the rest. Then ask what you can still deliver that keeps faith with the people who trusted you.
aspects.home: Perhaps you promised a parent or a child something you could not provide in the end: a house, a reunion, a safe return. Speak of it openly at home; silence turns sorrow into shame. Families can bear broken plans far more easily than broken trust.
aspects.health: Your body may not have kept the plans you made for it. That is not a moral failure. Grieve the hoped-for recovery or strength, and then treat yourself with the tenderness Achilles showed the body of his friend.
aspects.journeys: A homecoming or venture you planned for someone else did not happen as you hoped, and Opoeis waited in vain. Do not punish yourself by refusing every new road. Carry their memory with you, and let your next step be taken in their honour.

entries.message: You made a promise in good faith that life would not let you keep. Call what you carry grief, not guilt.
entries.reflect: If you forgave yourself for the outcome, what would remain for you to do in honour of the promise?

entries.greek: νεῦσε δέ οἱ λαὸν σόον ἔμμεναι οὐδʼ ἀπολέσθαι.
entries.english: He nodded his promise that the people would be safe and would not perish.
entries.reading:
The Greeks are penned behind their ditch, Hector's fires are in sight, and Agamemnon stands on the black hull of Odysseus' ship and weeps. He does not pray for victory now. He asks only that his men escape with their lives. Zeus pities the tears and nods his promise that the people would be safe and would not perish. At once an eagle sweeps over, a fawn in its talons, and drops it beside the altar where the Greeks used to sacrifice. The men see the sign and turn back to fight.

This card comes to someone who has been praying, in words or in worry, for others. Your family, your team, a friend in trouble. You may have stopped hoping for the best outcome and begun asking simply that no one be lost. The oracle answers: that prayer is heard.

Notice its shape, though. Zeus does not promise that the day will go well; the Greeks still suffer hard fighting before the end. What he promises is survival, and the sign gives them courage. So take this answer as Agamemnon's men did. Let the eagle steady your heart, and then go back to the wall with your people.
entries.context: In Iliad 8, with the Greeks driven back to their ships by Hector, Agamemnon weeps and prays to Zeus to let at least his men escape with their lives. Zeus pities him and nods his promise that the army will be saved, and at once sends an eagle with a fawn in its talons, which it drops by his altar.

aspects.love: If you have been afraid of losing someone dear, this line is gentle. The bond will hold through the trouble ahead. It may not be easy, but it will not perish; let that knowledge make you braver in how you love them.
aspects.work: A hard season may lie ahead, but the people and the core of the enterprise will come through it. Tell your colleagues what you have perceived. A leader's steadiness is the eagle the others need to see.
aspects.home: Your household may face a stretch of real difficulty, but you need not fear its ruin; the nod has been given. Gather everyone and speak plainly of what will be protected. Children and elders alike take courage from a calm face at the hearth.
aspects.health: Your worry for someone's wellbeing, or your own, can loosen its grip a little. The line does not promise an easy road, only that what matters most will be preserved. Rest in that, and keep doing the sensible things.
aspects.journeys: A risky passage ahead may be rough, yet those travelling with you will arrive. Watch for small signs of favour along the way, an eagle over the altar, a kindness from a stranger, and take them as encouragement, not as permission to be careless.

entries.message: Your prayer for the people in your care has been heard. Not triumph, but safety: they will not perish.
entries.reflect: Which of your fears for others can you now lay down, so that your strength goes into helping them?

entries.greek: μὴ ὄφελες λίσσεσθαι ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα
entries.english: You should never have pleaded with the noble son of Peleus,
entries.reading:
The envoys come back through the dark to Agamemnon's hut and report the refusal: Achilles will not fight, not for tripods, horses, cities, nor a king's daughter. Silence falls on the leaders. Then Diomedes, the youngest of them, speaks: you should never have pleaded with the noble son of Peleus. He was proud enough before; your gifts have made him prouder. Let him stay or go as he pleases. Now let us eat and drink, take our rest, and at first light draw up the army.

You may have been pleading with someone for some time, offering more each round, waiting for them to return, to commit, to approve, to come to your aid. Each offer has only confirmed their sense of their own importance, and your own sense of helplessness. The oracle says: stop asking.

This is not a call to bitterness. Diomedes even grants that Achilles will fight again when his own heart moves him. It is a call back to yourself and to those who are actually beside you. Feed your strength. Sleep. Then at dawn do the work with the people who showed up, and let the proud one find his own way back.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, the embassy returns from Achilles with his refusal to fight. In the silence that follows, Diomedes tells Agamemnon that he should never have begged Achilles with countless gifts, since he was proud enough already and is now prouder, and urges the Greeks to rest and fight on without him.

aspects.love: If you have been courting someone's attention with ever greater efforts, notice how little it has moved them. Withdraw your pleading without slamming any door. Spend your warmth on those who return it, and let the other come if they choose.
aspects.work: A client, manager or partner may be holding out for more because your offers keep rising. Stop bidding against yourself. Make your plan with the team you already have, and let them see you can manage without them.
aspects.home: A relative may be refusing to join in, and every invitation you press on them becomes another chance to say no. Leave the door open, stop the persuading, and make the family meal good for those at the table.
aspects.health: You may have been waiting for a person or a single remedy to rescue you. Turn to the plain things within your reach: food, rest and the support that is actually present. Strength gathered there will carry you further.
aspects.journeys: Do not delay a decision while you wait for one proud person's blessing. If they have refused you twice, take that as the answer and stop sending envoys. Rest tonight, consult those who are actually with you, and move at first light.

entries.message: Pleading with the proud only feeds their pride. Go back to your own fire, eat, sleep, and at dawn fight with those who are here.
entries.reflect: What would change if you stopped waiting for this person to say yes?

entries.greek: οἶνός σε τρώει μελιηδής, ὅς τε καὶ ἄλλους
entries.english: The honey-sweet wine has gone to your head, as it does to others,
entries.reading:
The beggar asks for the bow, and Antinous rounds on him: the honey-sweet wine has gone to your head, as it does to others who gulp it down. It is a strange accusation. Odysseus is the only sober man in that hall; the suitors have been feasting and drinking his stores for years. And the next day, when the first arrow flies, it will find Antinous himself with a golden cup lifted to his lips.

So this line comes as a mirror with two faces. First: when someone dismisses you as foolish, carried away, not thinking straight, ask whether they are describing themselves. Often the one who cries drunkenness is the one most drunk on comfort, on power, on the sweet wine of other people's goods. Do not let that charge shake your sense of what you see.

But the oracle does not let you off entirely. Wine harms anyone who drinks without measure, says Antinous, and in that he is right. Is there something honey-sweet in your life, a pleasure, a praise, a habit, a hope, that you have been gulping until it clouds your judgement? Drink, if you drink, by the mixing bowl, slowly, and keep your eyes clear for the bow.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, the disguised Odysseus asks the suitors to let him try the bow, to test whether his old strength remains. Antinous, fearing he may succeed, rebukes him with this line, saying the sweet wine has harmed him as it harms anyone who gulps it without measure, and begins the tale of the Centaur Eurytion.

aspects.love: If a partner or friend accuses you of being swept away, listen once, honestly. Then look at the accuser. Passion can cloud judgement, but so can jealousy and comfort. Measure your feelings by your conduct, not by their words.
aspects.work: Success can go to the head like wine, yours or a colleague's. If you have been told you are overreaching, check your figures soberly. If you find you are clear and right, proceed calmly and let the results correct them.
aspects.home: A pleasant habit in the household, late nights, rich meals, easy spending, may be slowly clouding everyone's judgement. Name it without blame and ask what moderation would look like. The house will feel clearer for it.
aspects.health: This line asks plainly about measure: in drink, in food, in idle distractions, in anything sweet you reach for to soften the day. No need for shame. Notice how much and when, and mix it with water.
aspects.journeys: Before a big decision, be sure you are not being carried by the flush of a good evening, a flattering offer or a rush of excitement. Sleep on it. Choose with the sober mind of the morning.

entries.message: Be wary of the voice that calls you drunk. Then, honestly, look at what sweetness you have been gulping without measure.
entries.reflect: What sweet thing in your life is harder to put down than you would like to admit?

entries.greek: ἔρξον ὅπῃ δή τοι νόος ἔπλετο, μὴ δʼ ἔτʼ ἐρώει.
entries.english: Do as your mind is set on doing, and hold back no longer.
entries.reading:
On Olympus, Zeus watches Hector run and pities him. He wonders aloud whether to snatch him from death once more. Athena will not have it; this man's end has long been settled, she says. And Zeus, who wavers but does not refuse what is fated, gives her leave: do as your mind is set on doing, and hold back no longer. At once she darts down from the peaks of Olympus to the plain.

This is a sombre line, spoken over the death of a noble enemy, and the card does not pretend otherwise. But drawn for you it carries a clear release. Some part of you has been waiting for permission, from a parent, from an authority, from your own softer heart, to do something you have long known must be done. A conversation that ends a chapter, a resignation, a final break, a beginning that closes other doors.

Notice that Zeus does not stop pitying Hector; he simply stops letting pity hold up what is right. You may do the same. Carry the tenderness with you. Be sure, in a quiet hour, that your resolve is one you could defend before the gods. Then, like Athena from the summit, move swiftly and do not look back.
