entries.context: In Iliad 22, as Achilles chases Hector around the walls of Troy, Zeus wonders aloud whether to save Hector. Athena objects that his death is long fated, and Zeus yields, telling her with this line to act as she intends and delay no longer; she darts down from Olympus to the plain.

aspects.love: A conversation you have rehearsed for months, a confession, a proposal, or an ending, has been held back by fear of the pain it will cause. Pity is right; paralysis is not. Speak gently, and speak soon.
aspects.work: You know what decision needs making, and every week of hesitation costs more than the decision itself. Gather your facts once more if you must, then act. Leaders who wait too long lose the trust they were protecting.
aspects.home: A family arrangement needs to change, and you have both the standing and the knowledge to change it. Like Zeus, you may pity those it will unsettle; let the pity shape how you act, not whether. Do it kindly and firmly; delay is making everyone more anxious.
aspects.health: You have long known which step your wellbeing needs: a visit you keep postponing, a habit given up, a burden put down. Stop negotiating with yourself and asking for one more day. Make the first move now, while your resolve is fresh and swift.
aspects.journeys: The way ahead has been clear in your mind for some time, and you have only been waiting for leave to go. Consider it given. Book the passage, give notice, tell those who need to know. The waiting is wearing you out more than the going will.

entries.message: You have already decided. Delay has become a choice of its own; go now and do what your mind is set on.
entries.reflect: Whose permission have you been waiting for, and what if this line is it?

entries.greek: ἄμφω γὰρ πέπρωται ὁμοίην γαῖαν ἐρεῦσαι
entries.english: For both of us are fated to redden the same earth.
entries.reading:
Achilles has given up the dream of going home. In the same breath that he mourns his broken promise to Patroclus' father, he says the thing he has tried not to know: for both of us are fated to redden the same earth. Peleus will never welcome him back; Thetis will never see him in the old house. Later he will ask that their bones be laid in a single golden urn, mixed together, as they were raised together.

This card arrives when your life is bound up with someone or something more deeply than you have admitted. A partner, a friend, a family, a cause, a town. Part of you may still be keeping a ship ready, telling yourself that whatever happens to them, you could always leave. The line says the ground beneath you both is the same ground.

There is sorrow here, but also a strange freedom. Once Achilles accepts that his fate and his friend's are one, he stops hesitating and acts with his whole heart. You can do the same. Name the bond for what it is. Throw in your lot fully. What you share, you will not face alone.
entries.context: In Iliad 18, Achilles laments over Patroclus to the Myrmidons. He says that he promised Menoetius to bring Patroclus home, but that both of them are fated to redden the same earth at Troy, since he too will never return to his father Peleus or his mother Thetis.

aspects.love: You are more deeply joined to this person than your caution has let you say. Stop holding back part of your heart as insurance. Whatever comes, you will meet it together; say so, and live as though you mean it.
aspects.work: Your fortunes are tied to your colleagues or your company more closely than you think. Stop acting as a visitor. Invest in the shared outcome, because if the field falls, it will fall under all your feet alike.
aspects.home: You belong to your family's story, its gifts and its wounds alike, and the same soil holds all of you. Rather than standing apart in judgement, take your place within it. Shared burdens weigh less when no one pretends to be outside them.
aspects.health: What you carry in body or mind may be shared with others in your family or circle, a common inheritance of the same earth. Let that become companionship rather than dread. Talk with those who understand, and face it shoulder to shoulder.
aspects.journeys: You may have imagined leaving as a way of escaping a common fate. Ask whether you are truly drawn elsewhere, or only afraid. If your place is here, commit to it and stop living half packed.

entries.message: Some bonds go all the way down to the ground. Stop planning to walk away untouched, and stand where your people stand.
entries.reflect: Where are you still keeping one foot on the ship, and what would it mean to bring it ashore?

entries.greek: βάλλʼ οὕτως, αἴ κέν τι φόως Δαναοῖσι γένηαι
entries.english: Keep shooting like this, and you may become a light to the Greeks.
entries.reading:
Teucer kneels behind the great shield of his brother Ajax. Ajax lifts it aside; Teucer looks out, looses an arrow, and a Trojan falls; then he ducks back like a child running to its mother. Eight men go down this way. Agamemnon, watching, is delighted: keep shooting like this, and you may become a light to the Greeks, and a glory to your father Telamon, who raised you in his house though you were not his wife's son.

Drawn for you, this is an encouraging card. You have found a way of working that suits you, not the loudest or the most heroic, but steady, protected and effective. Others are noticing. You may also have spent years feeling you had to prove your place, as Teucer did, the son brought in from outside. The line says you have earned it.

But Homer adds a warning. Teucer next aims again and again at Hector, the one man he cannot bring down. He misses, Hector strikes him with a jagged stone, and Ajax must carry him from the field. So keep shooting, as you are, from behind the shield that serves you. Leave the impossible target for another day.
entries.context: In Iliad 8, the archer Teucer, sheltering behind the shield of his half-brother Ajax, shoots down Trojan after Trojan. Agamemnon, delighted, encourages him with this line to keep shooting, so that he may become a light to the Greeks and bring glory to his father Telamon, who brought him up in his house though he was not his wife's son.

aspects.love: Your quiet, faithful way of loving is doing more good than you realise; keep loosing those small arrows of care. Recognise too the person who gives you shelter to be yourself, the Ajax at your side, and tell them how much their protection means.
aspects.work: Your method is producing results; do not abandon it for a bolder style because someone else shines. Watch out, though, for the single prize you keep aiming at and missing. Pursuing it may expose you more than it rewards you.
aspects.home: If you joined a family by marriage, adoption or circumstance, know that your place is real and your contribution seen. Keep giving in your own way, and let the person who first made room for you share the credit.
aspects.health: A routine that protects you is serving you well; keep to it. Do not suddenly push for one dramatic goal beyond your present strength. Steady effort behind the shield will carry you further than one exposed leap.
aspects.journeys: Continue the course you have set; it is sound. Travel with the companion who covers your blind side. If you feel drawn toward one risky detour to prove yourself, consider whether it is worth stepping out from cover.

entries.message: What you are doing is working. Keep on from where you stand, honour the shield that covers you, and do not fix on the one target too big for you.
entries.reflect: Who has been holding the shield for you, and have you thanked them?

entries.greek: ὡς οὐκ ἔσθʼ ὃς σῆς γε κύνας κεφαλῆς ἀπαλάλκοι,
entries.english: So there is no one who could keep the dogs from your head,
entries.reading:
Hector lies in the dust with the bronze in his throat, and with his last breath he begs: take ransom, return my body to my parents. Achilles answers with the most savage words in the Iliad. There is no one who could keep the dogs from your head, not for ten times the ransom, not for your weight in gold. It is a terrible vow. And it does not hold. Aphrodite keeps the dogs away day and night, Apollo covers the body with a cloud, and in the end Achilles himself takes Priam's hand and gives his son back.

This card does not soften the line; it shows you its limit. If you are the one swearing never, never to forgive, never to return what you hold, never to let go of a wrong, know that rage makes promises it cannot keep. The hardness feels like strength now. It will not last, and you will be glad of that.

If instead you are on the other side, refused, scorned, told there is no ransom high enough, take heart. A cruel no spoken in the heat of grief is not the final word. The gods keep watch over what matters. Wait, keep faith, and the door may open after all.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Hector lies mortally wounded and begs Achilles to accept ransom from his parents and return his body to Troy for burial. Achilles refuses with savage contempt, saying that no one will keep the dogs from Hector's head, not even if ten or twenty times the ransom were brought, or his weight in gold.

aspects.love: Words spoken in a rage between lovers or friends may sound like an ending. They may not be. If you said them, prepare to unsay them. If you heard them, do not answer in kind; leave room for the slow return of tenderness.
aspects.work: A business rival or former partner may have refused every offer with contempt, swearing no price would ever be enough. Do not keep raising the ransom. Let time and circumstance work; positions taken in anger are often softened by events, as Achilles' was by an old man's visit.
aspects.home: Someone in your family may have declared a breach unforgivable, with words as hard as Achilles' over the body. Keep your own heart unhardened, and keep a lamp lit for reconciliation. Grief and fury pass; the bond underneath can still be tended.
aspects.health: Anger carried too long hardens the body as well as the heart. Notice where you clench, at night, in the jaw, in the shoulders. Letting go of a vow of vengeance may be the kindest thing you do for your own health.
aspects.journeys: You may have sworn never to return to a place or a person. Hold that vow loosely. There may come a night, as there came for Achilles and Priam, when going back is the brave and healing thing.

entries.message: Rage swears it will never relent, never forgive, never give back. The end of the poem says otherwise.
entries.reflect: What have you sworn never to do that a calmer part of you already knows you will?

entries.greek: οὐ μέν με κτενέεις, ἐπεὶ οὔ τοι μόρσιμός εἰμι.
entries.english: You will not kill me, for I am not fated to die by you.
entries.theme: Chasing a God Across the Plain
entries.reading:
All afternoon Achilles has pursued a Trojan across the wheat fields, faster and faster, sure that he is about to make the kill. Then the runner turns and laughs. It is Apollo, who has drawn him away from the city so the broken Trojans could pour in through the gates. You will not kill me, says the god, for I am not fated to die by you. And all the while you have forgotten the men you came to fight.

This card asks where your best effort has been going. There may be a pursuit in your life that keeps leading you on: a goal that recedes as you near it, an argument you can never win, a person you can never satisfy, a perfection you can never reach. It feels urgent and close. But it may be leading you away from the real work, which is now safely beyond reach because you looked elsewhere.

Achilles, furious, turns and runs back toward Troy. You can turn too. It is not too late. Recognise the immortal you have been chasing, let it go with a curse or a laugh, and put your swiftness to the task that is truly yours.
entries.context: At the start of Iliad 22, Apollo, who in the guise of the Trojan Agenor has lured Achilles away from Troy so that the routed Trojans can escape into the city, reveals himself and mocks Achilles, telling him with this line that he cannot kill him, for he is not fated to die. Achilles, furious at the deception, races back toward the walls.

aspects.love: You may have been chasing approval from someone who will never give it, while those who already love you wait to be seen. Stop running after the unreachable one. Turn back to the people within the walls of your life.
aspects.work: Much effort is going into a prize or a perfection that keeps receding. Meanwhile the ordinary, essential tasks have slipped past you. Recover them first. The chase will look very different once the real work is in hand.
aspects.home: A long-running household argument may be a decoy, drawing everyone across the fields while the real needs slip inside the gates. Leave the endless debate. Attend instead to the repairs, the meals and the conversations that keep the home alive.
aspects.health: If you have been chasing an ideal body or a flawless routine, notice how it draws you away from simple care. You cannot catch a god. You can rest, move and eat well today, which is what actually heals.
aspects.journeys: A change you keep pursuing may be leading you further from where you should be. Ask whether it serves your real aims or only feeds the thrill of the chase. Turning back is not defeat; it can be wisdom.

entries.message: You have been pouring your strength into something that cannot be caught, while what truly mattered slipped behind the walls.
entries.reflect: What have you been chasing that, if you are honest, can never be caught?

entries.greek: ἐνθάδε κʼ αὖθι μένων σὺν ἐμοὶ τόδε δῶμα φυλάσσοις
entries.english: Stay here with me instead, and guard this house,
entries.reading:
In the scented cave, over a last meal, the goddess makes her final offer. Calypso has been ordered by the gods to let Odysseus go, and she does not fight it. But she warns him: if you knew the sorrows still waiting before you reach home, you would stay here with me and guard this house, and be immortal. He will not. He answers with courtesy, admits she is more beautiful than his wife, and still chooses the raft and the grey sea.

This card comes to someone who has found shelter. Perhaps it is a safe position, a comfortable relationship, a place that asks little, a life that is pleasant but not quite yours. There is nothing wicked in it; Calypso loved him and fed him well. Yet you feel the pull of the shore you have not reached, and the voice that says it will be hard is not lying.

The oracle does not choose for you, but it names the choice honestly. Staying is comfort without return. Leaving will cost you dearly, and it will be your own life. If you go, go with gratitude to those who sheltered you, as Odysseus did, and build your raft well.
entries.context: In Odyssey 5, the nymph Calypso, ordered by the gods to let Odysseus go, shares a last meal with him. She warns that if he knew the sorrows awaiting him before he reached home, he would stay with her, keep her house and become immortal, however much he yearned for his wife; Odysseus still chooses to leave.

aspects.love: Someone may be offering you a safe, kind love that asks you to give up a deeper longing. Be honest with them and with yourself. Kindness is not the same as belonging, and both of you deserve the truth.
aspects.work: A secure, well-paid position may be keeping you from the work you are truly meant for. The way out will be hard and uncertain. Weigh it carefully, and if you go, part from your employer with grace and gratitude.
aspects.home: You may be living comfortably somewhere that has never felt like home. Ask what home actually means to you: people, place or purpose. Then decide whether to stay and make it so, or set out to find it.
aspects.health: Comfort can become a kind of stillness that slowly weakens us. If your easy routine has stopped serving your body or spirit, choose a harder, healthier rhythm, even though it will ask more of you at first.
aspects.journeys: A big decision lies before you between a pleasant present and a costly return. Do not pretend the road will be easy. Choose with your eyes open, prepare carefully, and accept whatever help is offered for the voyage.

entries.message: You may be offered comfort without end and still know it is not your life. Choose the harder road home with open eyes and a grateful heart.
entries.reflect: What is the island in your life, and what is the shore you still long for?

entries.greek: εἶκε, γέρον, προθύρου, μὴ δὴ τάχα καὶ ποδὸς ἕλκῃ.
entries.english: Get away from the doorway, old man, before you are dragged off by the foot.
entries.reading:
A big man shoulders his way into the palace doorway. He is Irus, the well-known beggar of the town, huge to look at and feeble in strength, and he wants the place by the door for himself. Get away from the doorway, old man, he snarls, before you are dragged off by the foot. The suitors laugh and set the two beggars to fight for a goat's paunch stuffed with fat. Irus, seeing the muscles under Odysseus' rags, starts to tremble. One blow ends it.

This card meets you at a threshold. Someone is blocking your way with bluster: a rival, a gatekeeper, a person who has made a small kingdom of a doorway and defends it with threats. Their size may be impressive. Their substance is not. The line asks you to look past the voice to the strength, or lack of it, behind it.

Notice how Odysseus fights. He weighs whether to kill and chooses a lighter blow, so that he will not give himself away too soon. Answer the bully, then, but with no more force than is needed. Then calmly take your place by the door and wait for what you really came for.
entries.context: In Odyssey 18, a burly but feeble beggar of Ithaca named Arnaeus, nicknamed Irus, arrives at the palace and tries to chase the disguised Odysseus away from the doorway with this threat. The suitors set them to fight for sport, and Odysseus fells Irus with a single blow.

aspects.love: Someone may be loudly guarding access to a person you care about, a parent, a former partner, a jealous friend. Do not be frightened off by bluster. Stand your ground with calm dignity, and use no more force than kindness allows.
aspects.work: A gatekeeper who controls access to the opportunity you want may be more bark than bite. Do not grovel or retreat. Present yourself firmly and politely; you may find they fold at the first sign of quiet strength.
aspects.home: A family member may be laying claim to a room, a role or an inheritance with threats. Answer once, clearly and fairly, and do not humiliate them. Shamed bullies become lasting enemies; checked ones often subside.
aspects.health: A loud fear may be standing in the doorway of a healthier life, telling you to stay away. Look at it closely. It may be weaker than it sounds, and one steady step may send it tottering out of the hall.
aspects.journeys: Officials, rules or naysayers may seem to bar a change you wish to make, standing in the doorway with loud warnings. Test whether the obstacle is real or merely noisy. Often a single calm, determined effort is enough to clear the threshold.

entries.message: The loudest guard at the door is often the weakest man in the house. Do not let a threat decide where you stand.
entries.reflect: What threat at your threshold has looked larger than it really is?

entries.greek: βέλτερον ὃς φεύγων προφύγῃ κακὸν ἠὲ ἁλώῃ.
entries.english: Better to run and escape from trouble than to be caught.
entries.reading:
The wall is breached, and Agamemnon has lost heart. Let us drag the ships down to the sea, he proposes, anchor them out in the dark, and sail at night if the gods allow; there is no shame in running from ruin. Better to run and escape from trouble than to be caught. It sounds like a proverb, and in many places it would be one. But Odysseus turns on him in fury: if the army sees the ships launched in the middle of battle, they will lose all heart, and the retreat itself will destroy them.

This card arrives when you are thinking of getting out. Perhaps you should; there are fires no one should stay in, and a clean escape can be the bravest choice. But the line comes to you with Odysseus' question attached. Are you leaving a danger, or leaving a duty? Who will see you go, and what will your going do to them?

In the end Diomedes, wounded himself, says they will go back to the battle line, not to fight but to hearten the others. Weigh your situation honestly. If you must leave, leave in daylight, with a plan, and not in panic.
entries.context: In Iliad 14, as the Trojans press the Greeks back to their ships, Agamemnon proposes launching the ships by night and sailing away, concluding with this line that it is better to flee and escape disaster than to be caught. Odysseus rebukes him angrily, and Diomedes rallies the leaders to return to the battle.

aspects.love: When a relationship becomes difficult you may feel the urge to slip away quietly. Sometimes that is right, especially if you are in danger. But if this is only a hard season, ask whether leaving would be escape or abandonment.
aspects.work: You may be thinking of withdrawing from a project or a role when the going is worst. Consider who depends on your presence. If you go, plan the handover openly; a sudden flight can sink the whole crew.
aspects.home: Family troubles may make you long to move away or cut contact. Distance can be healthy, and genuine harm is a reason to go. If it is ordinary strife, though, your steady presence may be what holds the house together.
aspects.health: Rest and retreat can be good medicine, and there is no shame in stepping back from a fire. Just be sure you are withdrawing to recover, not launching the ships to avoid what must be faced. A planned pause heals; a panicked flight usually postpones the trouble.
aspects.journeys: A sudden plan to leave may feel like rescue. Sleep on it, talk it over with someone as blunt as Odysseus, and see whether the urge survives the morning. If it does, depart with care and clear sight.

entries.message: Sometimes running is wisdom. First be sure you are escaping danger, and not only the fight that is yours to stand in.
entries.reflect: If no one were watching, would you still choose to go, and if everyone were watching, would you still choose to stay?

entries.greek: μηδέ τῳ ἐκφάσθαι μήτʼ ἀνδρῶν μήτε γυναικῶν,
entries.english: and tell no one, neither man nor woman,
entries.reading:
Odysseus wakes on a beach he does not recognise, beside a heap of treasure, and curses the Phaeacians for abandoning him somewhere strange. Then a young shepherd approaches, and turns into a tall, beautiful woman: Athena. This is Ithaca, she tells him. You are home. But you must endure many sorrows in your own house, and tell no one, neither man nor woman, that you have come, but suffer in silence the insolence of men.

This card arrives for someone who has reached a turning point that others do not yet know about. A decision made, a recovery begun, a plan formed, a love found, a goal very nearly achieved. You long to announce it. The oracle counsels silence, not out of shame, but because the ground is not yet prepared. Speaking too early would put the whole homecoming at risk.

Silence is not passivity. Odysseus spends these days watching, testing who is loyal, gathering allies one by one. Do the same. Hold your knowledge like a hidden blade under a beggar's cloak. Bear the slights of those who do not see you yet. When the time comes, you will know it, and your revelation will carry all the more weight.
entries.context: In Odyssey 13, Odysseus wakes on Ithaca, and Athena reveals herself to him. She promises to help him hide the Phaeacians' gifts and to plan the suitors' downfall, and warns him that he must endure many sorrows in his own house, telling no one, man or woman, that he has come home, but suffering in silence the insolence of men.

aspects.love: A new feeling or a decision about a relationship may still need time before it is shared. Let it ripen in private. Speak first to the one person it most concerns, and only when you are sure.
aspects.work: Plans for a change of role, a new venture or a negotiation are best kept close for now. Gather your information quietly and see who can be trusted. Announced too early, a good plan can be blocked.
aspects.home: Family news you are carrying may need careful timing. Choose the hour and the hearer wisely, as Odysseus chose Telemachus first. In the meantime you may have to endure assumptions and remarks you know to be wrong; let them pass like the suitors' jeers.
aspects.health: Your progress may not yet be visible to others, and their comments may wound. You need not explain yourself, any more than the beggar in the hall did. Keep doing what helps, quietly; your strength will speak for itself when it is ready.
aspects.journeys: A big change you have settled on can be prepared in silence, as Athena helped Odysseus hide his treasure in the cave. Arrange the practical things first. When you finally tell others, you will be able to answer their questions from firm ground.

entries.message: You have arrived, but it is not yet the hour to say so. Carry it quietly; the time to reveal yourself will come.
entries.reflect: What do you know about yourself that is not yet ready to be spoken aloud?

entries.greek: πυρῶν ἢ κριθῶν· τὰ δὲ δράγματα ταρφέα πίπτει·
entries.english: of wheat or barley, and the cut handfuls fall thick and fast.
entries.reading:
Homer stops the fighting for a moment and shows us a farm. Two lines of reapers are working toward each other across a rich man's field of wheat or barley, and the cut handfuls fall thick and fast. It is a picture of plenty and of labour. It is also the Greeks and Trojans, rushing together, and the sheaves are men. Neither side thinks of flight.

You may be in such a season now. Two forces in your life are moving toward each other with full determination: two parties in a dispute, two duties competing for the same hours, two people who will not give ground. Everything is happening quickly. There is a terrible efficiency to it, and an odd exhilaration, the rhythm of the sickles, no time to stop and think.

The line asks you to look up from the row. Whose field is this? Reapers in Homer cut for the wealthy owner, not for themselves. If you are spending yourself in a hard contest, be sure the harvest will feed you and yours, and not only someone standing at the edge of the field. And if the cutting cannot be avoided, work steadily, side by side with your own, and do not lose heart.
entries.context: In Iliad 11, as Agamemnon's great day of fighting begins, the Trojans and Greeks charge into each other. The poet compares them to two lines of reapers moving towards each other across a wealthy man's field of wheat or barley, with the cut handfuls falling thick, so that neither side thinks of flight.

aspects.love: Two people locked in steady opposition can wear each other down without either noticing. Pause the rhythm of reply and counter-reply. Ask together what you are each giving up, and whether the quarrel is really serving your life together.
aspects.work: This is a season of heavy, fast work, perhaps against a strong competitor. Commit to it, but check who profits from your exhaustion. Make sure your share of the harvest is agreed before the last row is cut.
aspects.home: Two family members may be advancing on each other over an inheritance, a house or a decision. Before more is lost, ask who actually benefits. Sometimes the field belongs to neither, and the cutting harms them both.
aspects.health: You may be driving yourself through a long, demanding stretch without pause. The work may be necessary, but reapers rest at noon. Build short breaks into the rhythm, or the harvest will be taken from your own strength.
aspects.journeys: A change may bring you face to face with rivals for the same place or prize. If you decide to go forward, go wholeheartedly. Yet know what you hope to reap, and whether it will truly be yours.

entries.message: When both sides advance like reapers and neither thinks of turning, the cutting is fast and heavy. Ask whose harvest it is.
entries.reflect: If this contest ends with every sheaf cut, who will carry home the grain?

entries.greek: ὁπποῖόν κʼ εἴπῃσθα ἔπος, τοῖόν κʼ ἐπακούσαις.
entries.english: Whatever word you speak, that word will you hear in return.
entries.reading:
Two warriors face each other across the dust, and instead of fighting they are trading boasts. Achilles has mocked Aeneas; Aeneas has answered with the whole long story of his descent from Zeus. Then he stops himself. Enough, he says; we are standing here insulting each other like children. Men's tongues are supple and full of words, and the pasture of speech runs wide in every direction. Whatever word you speak, that word will you hear in return.

This card puts your speech in your hands. You may be in an exchange that keeps escalating, or one that keeps going cold, and you have been waiting for the other person to change their tone. The line reminds you that conversation is an echo. Sharpness comes back sharp. Contempt returns as contempt. And, more quietly, courtesy tends to return as courtesy, honesty as honesty.

Aeneas' wisdom has a second edge: he knows when the talking is done. After his speech he hurls his spear. So weigh your words; choose the ones you would be glad to receive. And when words have nothing more to give, stop speaking and act.
entries.context: In Iliad 20, Aeneas faces Achilles in battle. After Achilles taunts him, Aeneas recites his lineage and says they should stop exchanging insults like children, for the human tongue is supple and full of words, and the kind of word one speaks is the kind one hears in return; he then hurls his spear.

aspects.love: Listen to the tone you have been using with someone close to you. Their replies may simply be your own words returning. Change the first word, warmth for coldness, a question for an accusation, and notice what comes back.
aspects.work: In a tense negotiation, the voice you set will be mirrored back across the table. Begin with respect and clarity, even if you feel little of either. When the talk goes in circles like boasting warriors, put it in writing and move forward.
aspects.home: The way you speak at the family table becomes the way your household speaks. Children especially echo what they hear, word for word and tone for tone. Let the words you send out be ones you would gladly hear repeated back to you.
aspects.health: Your inner voice also echoes. If you speak harshly to yourself, body and mind answer with tension and fatigue, as surely as insult answers insult. Practise saying to yourself what you would say to a friend you love, and listen for the reply.
aspects.journeys: As you approach a big change, the way you describe it shapes how others respond; speak of it fearfully and you will hear fear back. Speak of it plainly and hopefully. When the discussion has run its course, stop debating and throw your spear.

entries.message: The word you send out is the word you will be answered with. Speak the reply you would want to hear.
entries.reflect: If someone said back to you exactly what you have been saying, how would it land?

entries.greek: οὐκ εἴασχʼ Ἑλένην δόμεναι ξανθῷ Μενελάῳ,
entries.english: would not let Helen be given back to fair-haired Menelaus.
entries.reading:
In the thick of his great day, Agamemnon comes upon two brothers in a chariot. Their horses have bolted, and they kneel and beg: our father Antimachus is rich, he will ransom us with bronze and gold. But Agamemnon knows their father. Antimachus was the Trojan who took Paris' gold and splendid gifts and so would not let Helen be given back to fair-haired Menelaus; he even urged the Trojans to kill Menelaus when he came as an envoy. The sons are cut down.

This is a grim card, and it speaks plainly. Somewhere in your situation, counsel is being bought. Perhaps someone's advice to you has been shaped by what they stand to gain. Perhaps you yourself have accepted a favour, a payment, a flattering promise, that has made it harder to say what you know is right. Antimachus did not think his gold had a price.

The line asks you to trace the consequence forward. Who will bear the cost of the choice that gift is buying? Often it is not the taker but those near them: the family, the colleagues, the people who trusted the counsel. If you hold such a gift, it is not too late to give it back and speak honestly.
entries.context: In Iliad 11, during Agamemnon's onslaught, the narrator describes how he kills Peisander and Hippolochus, sons of Antimachus. Antimachus was the Trojan who, having taken Paris' gold and splendid gifts, most strongly opposed giving Helen back to Menelaus; his sons now beg for their lives and are refused.

aspects.love: Be careful of a friend whose advice about your relationship benefits them more than it benefits you. And look honestly at whether favours you have received have bought your silence about something that needs saying. Gold given quietly can keep a Helen from going home.
aspects.work: An incentive, commission or perk may be colouring your judgement or someone else's. Consider who would suffer if the advice proved wrong. Declare your interests openly, and refuse a gift that asks you to change your counsel.
aspects.home: Family decisions about money, property or care can be quietly bent by who has been generous to whom. Make sure everyone's voice is heard, and that the children, the elders or the absent are not the ones left to pay.
aspects.health: A habit or pleasure may be offering you a short-term reward at a cost your future self, or those who love you, will carry. It is a gift with a hidden price, like Paris' gold. Look at the true cost, not only the immediate sweetness.
aspects.journeys: Before you accept a generous offer that would set you on a new path, ask what it obliges you to do and to whom. A road bought with someone else's gold may lead where you never meant to go.

entries.message: The price of a bribe is rarely paid by the one who took it. Ask who will carry the cost of what you accept.
entries.reflect: Whose gift is quietly shaping what you say, and who would pay if you kept it?

entries.greek: ἦ τι μεταστρέψεις; στρεπταὶ μέν τε φρένες ἐσθλῶν.
entries.english: Will you change your mind a little? The hearts of good men can be turned.
entries.reading:
Poseidon is in the thick of the battle when Iris arrives with a message from Zeus: leave the field. The god of the sea bristles. We are three brothers, he says, and the world was divided among us by lot; I am Zeus' equal in honour. Iris does not argue. She asks gently whether she must really carry so hard a reply back to Olympus. Will you change your mind a little? The hearts of good men can be turned. And Poseidon, to his credit, yields, even praising her for speaking so fitly.

This card may come to you in either role. If you are holding a hard position, a refusal, a grievance, a stand on your dignity, it asks whether it is truly worth keeping. You may be right on the principle and still wise to bend. Turning does not make you less; Homer says it is a mark of the noble.

If you are the messenger, carrying an unwelcome word to someone proud, the line shows you how. Do not attack their pride. Offer them a graceful way to move, and honour them for taking it. Either way, a flexible heart will spare you a war.
entries.context: In Iliad 15, Zeus sends Iris to order Poseidon to withdraw from the battle. Poseidon angrily insists that he is Zeus' equal in honour. Iris asks whether she must carry this harsh reply back, or whether he will relent a little, since the hearts of the noble can be turned and the Furies always side with the elder; Poseidon yields.

aspects.love: You may be refusing to give way in an argument because you are technically right. Ask what the relationship needs more: your victory or your warmth. A small turning now can save a great deal of grief later.
aspects.work: If you must deliver an unpopular decision to a proud colleague, frame it so they can accept it with dignity. If you are the proud one, consider bending; reputations are made by those who can change course.
aspects.home: A family standoff may need only one person to soften first, as Poseidon finally did. It need not be a surrender of what you hold dear. Let it be you, and do it with grace, and you may find others turning too.
aspects.health: A fixed idea about how you should be treated, or how your recovery should go, may be making things harder. Allow yourself to change your mind about a habit or a plan; flexibility is part of strength.
aspects.journeys: You may have committed publicly to a decision that no longer feels right, and pride now keeps you on course. Revisiting it is no shame; even the earth-shaker turned. Better to change now, with good reasons, than to sail on stubbornly into the wrong waters.

entries.message: Changing your mind is not defeat. The hearts of the good are the ones that can still be turned.
entries.reflect: What position are you holding mainly because it would feel like losing to let it go?

entries.greek: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ τὸ μὲν οὔ ποτʼ ἀπίστεον, ἀλλʼ ἐνὶ θυμῷ
entries.english: But I never doubted it; in my heart I knew
entries.reading:
On the shore of Ithaca, the goddess drops her disguise and laughs at Odysseus' endless caution, because it is exactly why she loves him. Then she answers the question he has carried for ten years: where were you? I never doubted it, she says; in my heart I knew you would come home, though you would lose all your companions. But I did not wish to fight my father's brother Poseidon, who was angry with you for blinding his son.

You may have felt abandoned in a long trial. Help you hoped for did not come; someone you counted on seemed silent or far away. This line offers you a different reading of that silence. The faith was there. The support was held back, not from indifference, but because of forces you could not see: obligations, fears, a quarrel not your own.

This does not erase the loneliness of the voyage, and you need not pretend it did not hurt. But let it change the story you tell yourself. You were not forgotten. Someone knew all along you would make it. Now that you are home, accept their help, and let the hard years become wisdom rather than grievance.
entries.context: In Odyssey 13, on Ithaca, Athena reveals herself and praises Odysseus' caution. She says that she never doubted but knew in her heart that he would return home after losing all his companions, but that she did not wish to fight her father's brother Poseidon, who was angry with him for blinding his son.

aspects.love: A partner or friend may have seemed distant during your hardest time. Ask them gently why, and listen without accusation. You may find they never stopped believing in you, but were held back by something they could not explain, a Poseidon of their own.
aspects.work: A mentor or senior figure may have quietly backed you while being unable to help openly, perhaps because of rivalries above them. Now that you have proven yourself, their support may become visible. Accept it without bitterness about the years before.
aspects.home: A parent or relative who seemed absent may have carried silent faith in you all along. Before deciding they did not care, let them tell their side, as Athena told hers on the shore. The reconciliation may be warmer than you expect.
aspects.health: After a long struggle you may feel no one understood. Some did, even if they could not show it. Let your recovery include the healing of that loneliness, by speaking of it with those who stood quietly by.
aspects.journeys: As you return from a long venture or a hard season, know that you were expected. Those who waited may not say much, and may never have shown their hope openly. Their quiet welcome is their way of saying they always knew you would come.

entries.message: Someone believed in your homecoming all along, even when they could not stand openly at your side.
entries.reflect: Whose silence have you read as abandonment that might have been something else?

entries.greek: Εὐρύμαχʼ, οὐχ οὕτως ἔσται· νοέεις δὲ καὶ αὐτός.
entries.english: Eurymachus, it will not be so; and you know it yourself.
entries.reading:
Eurymachus has warmed the bow by the fire, greased it with tallow, and still cannot bend it. He groans: we are shamed, all of us, weaker than Odysseus. Antinous, the ringleader, answers at once: Eurymachus, it will not be so, and you know it yourself. Today is Apollo's feast, he says; no one should be bending bows. Let us set it aside and try again tomorrow. It is a smooth speech. It is also the last plan he will ever make, for there will be no tomorrow for the suitors.

This card carries a warning in its shape. Someone, perhaps a friend, perhaps your own clever mind, is reassuring you that the failure you have just felt is not real. There is a reason, a festival, a bad day, an excuse that sounds pious and plausible. Put it off. Try again tomorrow. But the line itself says the deeper thing: you know it yourself.

What do you know? Not the comforting story, but the plain fact under it, the one that made Eurymachus groan. The oracle asks you to listen to that knowing now, while there is time to act on it, rather than postponing the reckoning to a dawn that may not come as you expect.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, after Eurymachus fails to string the bow and laments the shame of the suitors' weakness, Antinous answers with this line, insisting it will not be so. He says that it is a holy festival of Apollo, so no one should be bending bows; they should set it aside and try again the next day.

aspects.love: If you keep telling each other that a difficulty is just stress or a bad season, ask what you both already know. Naming the real issue is frightening, but it is the beginning of putting it right.
aspects.work: A failed attempt is being explained away with good-sounding reasons, a festival, bad timing, the wrong day. Look at the plain result. If the bow will not bend, the method needs to change, and postponing the trial until tomorrow will not change it.
aspects.home: Families are skilled at soothing stories that let everyone avoid a hard truth, and at putting the bow aside for another day. You know what is really happening at home. Say it gently, once, to the person who most needs to hear it.
aspects.health: You may be reassuring yourself that a symptom or a strain means nothing. Perhaps it does mean little. But if part of you knows otherwise, listen to that part and seek proper advice rather than waiting for tomorrow.
aspects.journeys: You keep deferring a decision with reasons that sound sensible and even pious. Set them aside for a moment and ask what you already know about where you need to go. Once you stop pretending, the next step usually becomes clear.

entries.message: Comfort that asks you to forget what you already know is no comfort. Listen to your own knowing.
entries.reflect: What explanation have you accepted that, in your heart, you know is not the whole truth?

entries.greek: ἆ δειλὲ ξείνων, ἔνι τοι φρένες οὐδʼ ἠβαιαί·
entries.english: Wretched stranger, you have not a scrap of sense in you.
entries.reading:
The beggar asks humbly for a turn at the bow, and the hall erupts. Antinous rises to put him in his place: wretched stranger, you have not a scrap of sense in you. Is it not enough that you dine with your betters and hear our talk? The insult is meant to shrink him. But listen to what lies under it. The suitors are afraid. They have all failed, and they suspect, without wanting to, that this ragged man might not.

This card arrives when someone has belittled you, perhaps in public, perhaps in the steady small ways that wear a person down. You have been told you lack sense, standing, the right to try. Part of you may have started to believe it. The line asks you to look at the faces of those who scorn you, and see how much fear is hiding in their mockery.

Odysseus does not answer Antinous with anger. He has borne worse insults on his own floor, and he holds his peace because he knows who he is and what the bow will soon prove. You need not shout back. Hold your dignity, stay at the table, and let your quiet certainty outlast their noise.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, the disguised Odysseus asks to try the bow to test his old strength. The suitors are indignant, fearing he will succeed, and Antinous berates him with this line, calling him a wretched stranger without a scrap of sense who ought to be content to dine among his betters.

aspects.love: If someone close to you speaks with contempt about your intelligence or your hopes, notice whether they fear losing you or being outshone. You do not need their permission to grow. Speak calmly, and do not accept scorn as the price of love.
aspects.work: Colleagues may sneer when you put yourself forward, especially if they have already tried and failed. That reaction often shows that they fear what you might do. Keep your composure, prepare thoroughly, and let your work, not a retort, answer them.
aspects.home: In some families one member is always cast as the fool. If that is you, recognise the role for what it is. You can step out of it, gently but firmly, without starting a war at the table.
aspects.health: Repeated belittling can lodge in the body as shame and tiredness. Treat your mind as you would a wound: keep it clean of the insults, and seek company that reminds you of your true measure, as the swineherd and the nurse reminded Odysseus of his.
aspects.journeys: When you share a bold plan, some will mock it as senseless. Weigh their objections for any truth, and then set aside the scorn. Fear in others is not a reason for you to stay put.

entries.message: Contempt is often fear in fine clothes. Do not let the scorn of a frightened room teach you your worth.
entries.reflect: What would you attempt if you stopped believing the people who belittle you?

entries.greek: τῷ δʼ ἕτερον μὲν ἔδωκε πατήρ, ἕτερον δʼ ἀνένευσε·
entries.english: The father granted him one thing, and refused him the other.
entries.reading:
Achilles takes a special cup from the chest his mother packed, a cup from which no one else drinks, purifies it with sulphur, pours wine, and prays. Let Patroclus drive the Trojans from the ships, he asks, and then let him come back to me unharmed, with his armour and his men. Zeus hears. The father granted him one thing, and refused him the other. The ships are saved. Patroclus does not return.

This card comes to someone who has asked for two things at once. Perhaps you want success and safety, victory and peace, the breakthrough and no cost. The line warns, honestly, that you may receive one without the other. It does not tell you which half will be refused; it tells you not to assume the whole prayer is answered just because the first part comes true.

Notice what Achilles had told his friend before the prayer: drive them from the ships, then turn back; do not chase them to the walls. Patroclus, carried away by success, forgot. The refused half of a prayer is often the one that depended on restraint. So when your first wish is granted, stop, remember the second, and come home.
entries.context: In Iliad 16, as Patroclus leads the Myrmidons into battle, Achilles pours a libation and prays to Zeus that Patroclus will drive the Trojans from the ships and return safely. Zeus hears him and grants the first request but refuses the second: Patroclus saves the ships but is killed by Hector.

aspects.love: You may be hoping for both passion and stability, or for reconciliation without any hard conversation. One may come more easily than the other. Do not let the first success make you careless about the second, as Patroclus was careless at the walls.
aspects.work: A project may succeed in its main aim while costing you something you hoped to keep. Decide now where you will stop, as Achilles told Patroclus to stop at the ships. When the target is reached, resist the urge to push further into risk.
aspects.home: Your wish for a family member may be partly granted: they get the chance, but not the ease you hoped for. Be ready to support them through the part of the prayer that was not answered.
aspects.health: Treatment or effort may mend one thing while another remains. Celebrate the gain without assuming you are done. Keep up the care that protects what is still vulnerable, especially once you feel stronger and are tempted, like Patroclus, to chase too far.
aspects.journeys: A venture may get you where you aimed but not back as easily. Plan your return as carefully as your departure. When you reach the first goal, remember that coming home safely was always part of the purpose.

entries.message: Some prayers are answered in part. Do not mistake the half that is granted for the whole, and guard the other half yourself.
entries.reflect: When the first thing you asked for arrives, what will you need to remember to do?

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ εἰς οἶκον ἰοῦσα τὰ σʼ αὐτῆς ἔργα κόμιζε
entries.english: But go to your room, and see to your own work,
entries.reading:
At the Scaean Gate, beside the tower, Andromache has wept and begged Hector to stay on the wall. He has taken off his gleaming helmet to hold their son, who was frightened by its horsehair crest. Now he hands the child back and speaks tenderly, and with finality: no man will send me down to death before my time, and no one escapes their fate. But go to your room, and see to your own work, the loom and the distaff. It is the last time they will see each other alive.

This is a heavy line. Hector's words come from an old world with its own divisions, and the card does not ask you to take them as a rule for who should do what. It hears something else in them: the plea of a person who has accepted their path, asking the one who loves them not to wear themselves out trying to change it.

You may be anxiously holding someone else's fate, rehearsing their risks, trying to talk them out of a road they have chosen. Or you may be Hector, sending away those who plead. If so, be gentle, as he was. Either way, there is your own work waiting. Return to it, and let it steady you.
entries.context: In Iliad 6, Hector speaks to his wife Andromache at the Scaean Gate, after she has begged him not to return to battle. He tells her that no one escapes their fate, and sends her home to her loom and her maids, saying war is the concern of men; it is the last time they meet alive.

aspects.love: You cannot fight your partner's battles for them, however much you love them. Say your piece once, from the heart, and then return to your own life. Your steadiness at home may be the greatest help you can give.
aspects.work: Worrying about a colleague's decisions or a project outside your control is draining you. Turn back to your own loom: the tasks that are truly yours. Doing them well is your best contribution to the larger effort.
aspects.home: A family member is set on a course you fear. You have pleaded; now tend the house and the people within it. If you are the one leaving, part with tenderness and do not dismiss the fear of those who love you.
aspects.health: Absorbing others' worries can exhaust body and mind. Give yourself a simple, absorbing task for the hands, mending, cooking, walking, the humble loom of your own day, and let it bring you back to yourself. Your own wellbeing is the work at hand.
aspects.journeys: Someone close to you may be making a big change you cannot control, walking back out through the gate. Instead of trying to steer it, attend to your own plans and your own house. Letting them go with your blessing may free both of you.

entries.message: Not every fate is yours to carry. Go back to the work in your own hands, and let those who face the battle face it.
entries.reflect: What part of someone else's struggle have you been carrying that is not yours to bear?

entries.greek: τῷ νῦν μηδὲ σὺ ταῦτα τεῇ εἴπῃσθα γυναικί.
entries.note: The papyrus has its own wording here, blending Odyssey 8.548 and 11.224.
entries.english: So now, do not you tell these things to your wife either.
entries.reading:
The papyrus that keeps this oracle gives a line of its own, stitched from two places in the Odyssey. In one, King Alcinous presses the weeping stranger to stop hiding who he is. In the other, Odysseus' mother speaks to him from among the dead and tells him to remember all she has said, so that one day he may tell it to his wife. The oracle's line turns that charge around: so now, do not you tell these things to your wife either.

Whatever its source, the line drawn for you is about discretion close to home. You may be carrying something, news, a confidence, a frightening experience, a hard truth about yourself, and wondering whether to bring it to the person you share your life with. The oracle counsels restraint, for now.

That is not the same as permanent secrecy. Homer's whole poem bends toward the moment when husband and wife sit up through the night and tell each other everything. Silence that protects, while the time ripens, is wise. Silence that hides, so as to avoid accountability, is not. Ask which yours is. If it is the first, keep it a little longer. If it is the second, begin to find the words.
entries.context: The papyrus line differs from the standard text, blending Odyssey 8.548 and 11.224, so its exact source is uncertain. At 8.548 King Alcinous urges the weeping Odysseus not to hide his identity from his Phaeacian hosts; at 11.224 the ghost of his mother Anticleia tells Odysseus to learn all she has said so that he may later tell it to his wife.

aspects.love: You may be holding something back from a partner or close friend. Ask whether you are sparing them a burden or sparing yourself a difficult conversation. Wait if the timing truly is wrong, but do not let waiting become hiding.
aspects.work: Some confidences from work should not travel home, and some home matters should not travel to work. Keep what you have been trusted with. If it is weighing on you, find a proper and discreet place to set it down.
aspects.home: Not every family member needs to know everything at once. Consider who should hear first, and how, and at which hearth. Careful timing can spare pain, but secrets kept too long tend to hurt more when they finally surface.
aspects.health: You may be keeping a worry about your health from those who love you. Some privacy is your right, and you may choose your moment. Yet carrying fear alone is heavy; choose at least one trusted person to share it with.
aspects.journeys: A plan to change your life may not be ready to share with everyone. Let it take shape quietly. Before you act, though, tell those who will be most affected; they deserve to hear it from you first.

entries.message: Not every story belongs at every hearth, not yet. Choose with care what you carry home, and when you tell it.
entries.reflect: Is your silence protecting someone you love, or protecting you from them?

entries.greek: λάϊνον ἕσσο χιτῶνα κακῶν ἕνεχʼ ὅσσα ἔοργας.
entries.english: you would be wearing a tunic of stone, for all the harm you have done.
entries.reading:
The armies are drawn up, and Paris strides out in front in his leopard skin, challenging the best of the Greeks. Then he sees Menelaus, the husband he wronged, leap down from his chariot, and he shrinks back into the ranks like a man who has trodden on a snake. Hector is disgusted. Paris, fair to look at, woman-mad: if the Trojans were not so timid, you would be wearing a tunic of stone, for all the harm you have done. In other words, they would have stoned you long ago.

The line is harsh, and it is meant to be. It may be for someone who has caused harm and slipped back into the crowd each time the consequences came near. Or it may be for someone who has watched another escape accountability, again and again, while everyone else paid.

What happens next matters. Paris does not argue. He says, you rebuke me rightly, and he agrees to meet Menelaus in single combat. That is the way out of the stone tunic: not more hiding, but stepping forward to face the one you wronged. If this is your situation, do it now. If it is another's, say plainly what Hector said, and let them answer.
entries.context: In Iliad 3, Hector rebukes his brother Paris, who has shrunk back from facing Menelaus, the husband of Helen. He says that if the Trojans were not so timid, Paris would long ago have been stoned to death ('wearing a tunic of stone') for all the harm he has brought on the city; stung, Paris agrees to fight Menelaus in single combat.

aspects.love: If you have hurt someone and avoided the conversation, the silence is setting hard around you both. Go to them, name what you did, and accept their response. If you were the one harmed, you have the right to say so plainly.
aspects.work: Mistakes left unacknowledged weigh on a whole team like stones. Own yours openly; it often costs less than you fear, and Paris' honest answer won him more respect than his leopard skin. If a colleague keeps evading responsibility, raise it directly and fairly.
aspects.home: A family member may have caused real damage and never faced it. Others may be quietly carrying the cost. Speak honestly, without cruelty, and give them the chance Paris was given: to step forward and make amends.
aspects.health: Guilt that is never faced can feel like wearing stone. If something you did still weighs on you, find a way to acknowledge it, to the person concerned, to someone you trust, or before the gods in your own heart.
aspects.journeys: Before a fresh start, settle old debts of harm, or they will travel with you in the baggage. Moving away does not remove the tunic of stone. Facing the wrong first, honestly and in person, will let you set out lighter.

entries.message: Harm left unanswered hardens around a person like a garment of stone. The only way out of it is to step forward and face what you did.
entries.reflect: Where have you, or someone close to you, been stepping back into the ranks to avoid a reckoning?

entries.greek: ἠρῶ ἀθανάτοισι γενειήσαντα ἰδέσθαι.
entries.english: I prayed to the immortals to see him grown, with a beard on his chin.
entries.reading:
Penelope has been weeping again, and she wants to go down to the hall to warn her son about the suitors. Her housekeeper Eurynome stops her. Do not go down with your face all stained with tears, she says; it does no good to grieve forever. Your son is now grown, and that was what you always prayed to the immortals for: to see him grown, with a beard on his chin.

This card is a gentle shake of the shoulder. Somewhere in your life a long prayer has quietly been answered, and you have not noticed, because you are still praying it. A child is grown; a debt is paid; a skill is learned; a hard year is over; a fear has passed. You are still treating the situation as if it were what it was, still worrying, still guarding, while the thing you longed for stands in the hall with a beard on its chin.

See what happens when Penelope listens. She washes, sleeps, and Athena makes her radiant; she goes down to the suitors and holds the whole hall spellbound. Your fulfilled prayer asks the same of you. Stop mourning the old need. Let the answer change your face, and walk into the room as someone whose prayer was heard.
entries.context: In Odyssey 18, the housekeeper Eurynome speaks to Penelope, who wishes to go down and warn her son about the suitors. Eurynome urges her to wash away her tears, since Telemachus is now grown, as she always prayed to the gods she might see him; Athena then makes Penelope beautiful before she appears to the suitors.

aspects.love: A relationship you worried over may have grown into the steadiness you once prayed for. Notice it, as Eurynome made Penelope notice her son. Stop guarding against old dangers, and enjoy the bond as it is now, ripened and strong.
aspects.work: You may have already reached a level of skill or security you once only dreamed of. Look at the evidence, not the old fear. Allow yourself to work from confidence rather than anxiety, and let others see the change in your face.
aspects.home: A child or younger relative has grown up more than you have let yourself see; the beard is already on the chin. Treat them as the adult they are becoming. Your trust will help them step into the full measure of themselves.
aspects.health: A recovery or improvement you prayed for may have quietly come while you were still bracing for the worst. Acknowledge it, wash away the old tears, and adjust your habits to the strength you now have, rather than living as though you were still unwell.
aspects.journeys: The conditions you were waiting for before making a change may already be in place. Check honestly, without the old worry colouring the view. If they are, wipe your face, as Penelope did, and step into the new chapter clear-eyed.

entries.message: What you prayed for has already come. Wash your face, lift your eyes, and let it change how you live.
entries.reflect: Which of your prayers has already been answered while you were still praying it?

entries.greek: εὔχεο δʼ Ἀπόλλωνι Λυκηγενέϊ κλυτοτόξῳ
entries.english: And pray to Apollo, the wolf-born, famed for his bow,
entries.reading:
A friendly voice speaks in the archer's ear. The truce is sworn, the two armies are sitting quietly in the field, and a Trojan comrade, who is really Athena in disguise, comes to Pandarus. Think of the gifts Paris would give you, she whispers, if you shot Menelaus now. And pray to Apollo, the wolf-born, famed for his bow, and vow him a glorious sacrifice of firstborn lambs. Pandarus is persuaded. He strings his horn bow, the arrow flies, Menelaus is wounded, and the war begins again.

This card is a warning, and an important one. You may be tempted to break a promise, an agreement, an understanding, for a gain someone has dangled before you. And you may be dressing the act in good intentions: a vow to make things right later, a noble reason, a prayer. The line asks you to notice how easily a betrayal can be made to sound pious.

Notice also who is speaking. Pandarus never asks why this comrade is so eager for him to shoot. Before you act, look closely at the voice urging you on and what it stands to gain. Then keep the truce. The gods, in Homer, remember broken oaths.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, Athena, disguised as the Trojan Laodocus, persuades the archer Pandarus to shoot at Menelaus during a sworn truce, telling him to vow a hecatomb of firstborn lambs to Apollo the wolf-born. Pandarus is persuaded, wounds Menelaus, and the broken truce sets the war going again.

aspects.love: If you are tempted to break faith with someone, notice the stories you are telling yourself to justify it. Good intentions afterwards will not undo the wound. Keep your word, or end things honestly before you act.
aspects.work: Someone may be encouraging you to undercut a partner or quietly bend an agreement, promising rewards like Paris' gifts. Ask who really benefits, and why they are so eager. Integrity held in a single tempting moment can protect your name for many years.
aspects.home: A family truce, after a quarrel or over an inheritance, may be fragile. Resist anyone who urges you to strike first while others are at rest. Peace kept carefully is worth more than any gain won by breaking it.
aspects.health: You may be making a pact with yourself to indulge now and repair the damage later, a vow of lambs to excuse the arrow. Notice that bargain for what it is. Choose the course that does not need a promise of future amends.
aspects.journeys: A tempting opportunity may require you to break a commitment already made. Look hard at who is offering it and why, and whether they wear a borrowed face. If you must change course, do so openly, not by a shot from cover.

entries.message: No prayer can make a betrayal holy. If you find yourself vowing gifts to the gods for a wrong, put down the bow.
entries.reflect: What reasoning are you using to make a broken promise feel acceptable?

entries.greek: οὐδὲ λύκοι τε καὶ ἄρνες ὁμόφρονα θυμὸν ἔχουσιν,
entries.english: Wolves and lambs are never of one mind,
entries.reading:
Hector has stopped running. He turns to face Achilles beneath the walls of Troy and offers a fair bargain: let the winner strip the armour, but return the body to the other's people for burial. It is a decent, human request. Achilles refuses it with an image as old as the hills. There are no oaths between lions and men; wolves and lambs are never of one mind, but plot evil against each other always. So there can be no pact between you and me.

You may be trying to make an agreement with someone who has no intention of keeping one. You draft fair terms, appeal to reason, offer the courtesy you would want, and each time it is thrown back. The line asks you to see the situation as it truly is. Some people, some forces, are not looking for common ground. Hoping otherwise only keeps you exposed.

This is not a counsel to become a wolf yourself. Hector's decency is the noblest thing in that scene, and Achilles' refusal is the darker part. But decency need not be naive. Stop waiting for the oath that will never be sworn. Prepare, protect what you love, and meet what comes with open eyes.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Hector, at last standing to face Achilles outside the walls of Troy, proposes that the victor return the other's body. Achilles refuses: as there are no oaths between lions and men, and wolves and lambs are never of one mind, so there can be no pact between the two of them.

aspects.love: If someone repeatedly shows that they do not share your values or your care, believe them. You can remain kind without continuing to bargain for a closeness they will not give. Protect your heart and stop negotiating.
aspects.work: A rival or counterpart may simply not want a fair deal, however reasonable your terms. Recognise it, keep your records clear, and plan for competition rather than cooperation. Courtesy is still yours to give, as Hector's was; illusions need not be.
aspects.home: Within families, some divides cannot be closed by goodwill alone. Keep your own conduct decent, as Hector did beneath the walls, but stop expecting a pact with someone set against you. Look after those who are most exposed to the conflict.
aspects.health: Some habits or pressures will never compromise with you; like the wolf, they take whatever ground you give. Do not bargain with them or hope for a truce. Make clear, firm arrangements in your life that keep them at a distance.
aspects.journeys: A decision may depend on someone who will never be of one mind with you. Stop waiting for their consent or for an oath they will not swear. Weigh the risks honestly, gather your allies, and make your move on your own terms.

entries.message: Some parties will never be of one mind with you. Stop seeking terms with the wolf, and plan for what is.
entries.reflect: Where are you still hoping for an agreement that the other side has already refused?

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ ἤτοι μὲν ταῦθʼ ὑποείξομεν ἀλλήλοισι,
entries.english: But in this, let us give way to one another,
entries.reading:
High on Olympus, two powers who could each wreck the world sit down and bargain. Hera wants Troy destroyed; Zeus loves the city. Neither can simply overrule the other, so Hera makes an offer: let us give way to one another, you to me and I to you. It ends a quarrel between gods. It also costs the lives of cities that had no voice in the room.

This line comes to you when you are locked with someone whose strength matches yours: a partner, a colleague, a sibling, an old rival. You have each been holding ground, and the holding has become the whole relationship. The oracle says the way out is mutual. Not one of you surrendering, but both stepping back a pace at the same moment, so that neither has to lose face.

Yet Homer does not let the bargain look innocent, and neither should you. Before you agree, look at what is being traded and who pays for it. A good compromise costs the two of you something. A bad one quietly hands the bill to someone else: a child, a friend, a value you used to hold. Yield generously, but keep your eyes open while you do.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, during a council on Olympus, Hera bargains with Zeus over the fate of Troy. She allows him to destroy her own favourite cities if he wishes, and asks in return that they give way to one another, he to her and she to him; Zeus agrees and sends Athena to break the truce.

aspects.love: The quarrel you keep having is two people guarding the same doorway. Agree on one thing each of you will let go of this week, and say it aloud together. Yielding feels smaller when it is shared, and it is far easier to step back when you see the other stepping back too.
aspects.work: A stalemate with an equal is costing more than either side is winning. Propose a trade: their point here, yours there. Write it down plainly, and check that the terms do not quietly fall on a team, a supplier or a client who was never asked.
aspects.home: Families often settle arguments between the adults by giving away the ground of someone smaller. If you and another grown-up in the house are striking a truce, make sure the children, or the quietest member of the household, are not the price of it.
aspects.health: Two parts of you are bargaining: the one that wants to push and the one that wants to rest. Let each give way a little. A gentler pace that you actually keep will serve your body better than winning one argument with yourself and losing the next.
aspects.journeys: A decision about where to go or what to change is shared with someone whose wishes pull against yours. Neither of you will get the whole of what you want. Meet in the middle, but name honestly what each of you is giving up, so it does not sour later.

entries.message: Peace between equals is not won; it is traded. Give way where you can, and know exactly what you are giving.
entries.reflect: Where could you give way first, and what are you unwilling to let the peace cost?

entries.greek: ἐν δʼ Ἔρις ἐν δὲ Κυδοιμὸς ὁμίλεον, ἐν δʼ ὀλοὴ Κήρ,
entries.english: Strife and Uproar were in the thick of it, and deadly Doom,
entries.reading:
On the shield of Achilles, Hephaestus hammered out the whole world: weddings, harvests, dancing floors, and a fight at a river where herdsmen were ambushed with their cattle. Into that skirmish the smith set three figures who belong to no side: Strife, Uproar and deadly Doom. They move among the fighters, seizing one man still living, another freshly wounded, dragging a third by the feet. They do not care who was right.

This card arrives when a conflict near you has started to take on a life of its own. Perhaps it began with a real grievance over something real, like the cattle at the river. But now there is noise where there was argument, and people are being hurt who were never part of the quarrel. You may feel the pull to join in, to be heard above the din.

Notice the figures before you notice the enemy. Strife and Uproar are not on your side, however righteous your cause; they feed on any fight that lasts long enough. Your task now is to shrink the field: fewer voices, quieter words, the original question set back on the table. The same shield holds the dance and the harvest too. Those are also yours to choose.
entries.context: In Iliad 18, Hephaestus forges new armour for Achilles and works scenes of the whole world onto his shield. In one, a besieged city's warriors ambush herdsmen at a river; as the two sides fight, the figures of Strife, Uproar and deadly Doom move among them, dragging the wounded and the dead.

aspects.love: A disagreement between you and someone dear has drawn in friends, relatives and opinions from every side. The crowd is making it louder, not clearer. Take the matter back between the two of you, somewhere quiet, and speak only about the thing itself.
aspects.work: Quarrels in an office or a market have a way of spreading until no one remembers the first cause. If a dispute is now about pride and alliances, step outside the din. Ask what the actual loss or claim was, and deal with that alone.
aspects.home: Raised voices in a household land on everyone, especially those too young or too tired to answer back. When an argument starts, notice who else is in the room. Some fights should wait for a closed door and a calmer hour.
aspects.health: Your mind may be a crowded field just now, with worries jostling and every small thing feeling urgent. Uproar is exhausting by nature. Lower the noise where you can: fewer sources of alarm, longer silences, and sleep guarded like a city gate.
aspects.journeys: A change you are weighing has become tangled in other people's conflicts. Before you decide, separate your own reasons from the clamour around you. Choose for the harvest and the dance you want, not to win a fight that was never yours.

entries.message: Conflict is never only between the two who started it. Once Strife enters the field, she chooses her own victims.
entries.reflect: What did this conflict begin as, and what has the noise turned it into?

entries.greek: ψεύδεά τʼ ἀρτύνοντας ὅθεν κέ τις οὐδὲ ἴδοιτο·
entries.english: making up lies about things no one could ever see.
entries.theme: The Story No One Can Check
entries.reading:
Odysseus has been telling the Phaeacians about the dead, about ghostly queens and his own mother's shade, and he pauses. King Alcinous answers him generously: we do not take you for a cheat, like the many men the dark earth breeds, making up lies about things no one could ever see. Your words have shape and good sense, like a bard's. There is an irony here that Homer surely enjoyed. Odysseus is the most gifted liar in Greek story, and this time he happens to be telling the truth.

Drawn for your question, the line asks you to weigh a story you have been told, or one you are telling. Someone may be offering you an account that is beautifully made and impossible to test: a past you cannot visit, a promise about places you will never see. Charm alone does not settle it. Nor does suspicion; Alcinous was right to trust.

So look for the parts that can be checked, and let those carry the weight. Then turn the lens on yourself. If there is a tale you tell about your own life that no one could ever verify, ask whether it still serves you, or only flatters you. Truth told with grace is a rare gift. Offer it.
entries.context: In Odyssey 11, Odysseus pauses in telling the Phaeacians of his wanderings. King Alcinous replies that they do not take him for a cheat, like the many men the earth breeds who make up lies no one could verify; his words have grace and good sense, like a bard's, and Alcinous asks him to continue.

aspects.love: A new person tells their history beautifully, or an old love explains the past in a way you cannot test. Do not interrogate, but notice whether their present actions match the tale. What someone does on ordinary days is the part of the story you can see.
aspects.work: A proposal, a pitch or a reference sounds polished and leans on claims no one can verify. Ask for the piece you can hold in your hand: the sample, the figures, the person who was there. Honest people are glad to show it.
aspects.home: Families keep legends about themselves: who was to blame, who was the good one. Some of these were never witnessed by anyone living. Gently question a family story that is still shaping how you treat a parent, a sibling or a child.
aspects.health: The mind tells stories about the body that no one has confirmed, some dark and some falsely hopeful. Bring them into the light by asking someone qualified, and let what can actually be seen replace what you have only imagined in the small hours.
aspects.journeys: A place or opportunity far away is being described to you in glowing terms. Before you decide, find someone who has actually walked there and can tell you the ordinary truth of it. Then you will choose with your eyes open.

entries.message: Grace in the telling is not proof of truth. Listen for what can be seen, and be that kind of speaker yourself.
entries.reflect: Which story in your life rests most on things no one could ever see?

entries.greek: εἴ τι νόος ῥέξει· πόλεμον δʼ οὐκ ἄμμε κελεύω
entries.english: if thinking can achieve anything; but I do not urge us to fight.
entries.reading:
The wall has been breached, the Trojans are at the ships, and three of the greatest Greek captains are limping from the field with spear wounds. Old Nestor meets them and says what no one wants to hear: let us consider whether thinking can achieve anything; but I do not urge us to fight. Wounded men cannot fight. The temptation, in such an hour, is to charge back in anyway, to prove you still can.

This line finds you hurt and under pressure at the same time. Something has gone badly, the danger is close, and every instinct says act now, act harder. But you are not at full strength. You may be tired in body, bruised in spirit, short of money or support. Throwing yourself into the fray in that state is not courage; it only adds to the losses.

Nestor's counsel is not to give up. It is to change the kind of help you give. Sit with the people you trust and think it through. What can be done by planning, by persuasion, by sending fresher hands? There is a time to fight, and it will come again. Today, the oracle asks you to be the one who thinks.
entries.context: In Iliad 14, the Greek wall has been breached and the fighting has reached the ships. Old Nestor meets the wounded leaders Agamemnon, Diomedes and Odysseus and urges them to consider whether any plan might help, but advises that they should not enter the battle themselves, since wounded men cannot fight.

aspects.love: After a painful exchange, both of you are wounded and quick to strike. This is not the night to settle it. Agree to talk when you have rested, and in the meantime think honestly about what each of you actually needs from the other.
aspects.work: A crisis has landed while you are already depleted. Resist the urge to work through the night by sheer force. Gather a few clear heads, map the problem, and decide who is best placed to act. A good plan from a tired captain can still save the ships.
aspects.home: The household is in some difficulty and you have been holding the line alone. You cannot also be the one doing all the lifting. Sit down with the others and work out a plan together, sharing the tasks according to who still has strength.
aspects.health: If you are injured or worn down, the line is plain: do not rush back into the battle. Recovery is a time for thinking, planning and gentle steps, not for proving you were never hurt. Listen to those who know your body well.
aspects.journeys: You are tempted to make a dramatic move to escape a bad situation. First ask whether you are choosing from strength or from pain. Plan the change carefully now, and act on it when your wounds have closed.

entries.message: When your strength is spent, your best weapon is thought. Plan from the shelter before you walk back into the fire.
entries.reflect: If you could not use force or effort to fix this, what would you think of instead?

entries.greek: οὐδέ τις ἔστʼ ἀλκή· φυγέειν κάρτιστον ἀπʼ αὐτῆς.
entries.english: There is no defence against it: the best thing is to flee from it.
entries.reading:
Odysseus has heard about Scylla: six heads on long necks, rows of teeth, a cave high above the strait. And his first question, being Odysseus, is how he might fight her. Circe is almost scornful.
