aspects.love: If you have been proved right in an argument, or a former partner's choices have caught up with them, resist the urge to say so. Quiet grace now will be remembered far longer than any moment of triumph.
aspects.work: A competitor has stumbled or a difficult colleague has left. Do not celebrate publicly. Speak respectfully, keep to the work, and let your conduct show that you were never in it for anyone's downfall, only for the work.
aspects.home: When a family conflict resolves in your favour, avoid reminding anyone that you were right. Help to restore peace in the house instead. Gloating would only reopen wounds that need to close, and the children are always listening.
aspects.health: If you have come through a hard battle with illness or habit, be glad, but do not look down on those still struggling. Gratitude and humility will serve your recovery far better than pride, and keep you kind to yourself on harder days.
aspects.journeys: You have left behind a situation that treated you badly. Do not look back to mock it. Walk into your new circumstances with a clean heart, and let the old matter rest where it fell.

entries.message: When the fight is won, keep silence over the fallen. Victory needs no boast, only the next right thing.
entries.reflect: How would you carry this victory if no one were watching?

entries.greek: νύκτα διʼ ἀμβροσίην, ὅτε θʼ εὕδουσι βροτοὶ ἄλλοι;
entries.english: through the immortal night, when all other mortals are asleep?
entries.reading:
Old King Priam is driving his mule cart across the plain toward the camp of the man who killed his son. It is night, and he has only an old herald with him. Near the river a young man appears out of the darkness, and Priam's hair stands on end. But the stranger takes his hand gently and asks where he is going, father, with these horses and mules, through the immortal night, when all other mortals are asleep. He is Hermes in disguise, sent by Zeus to guide him safely through the enemy lines.

The line finds you on a lonely errand. You may be doing something no one else understands, at an hour when others are resting: caring for someone through the night, attempting a reconciliation that seems impossible, carrying a grief that will not let you sleep. You may feel exposed and foolish, an old man on the open plain.

The oracle asks you to notice the question. It is not an accusation; it is the opening of help. Someone is ready to walk beside you, if you will let them see where you are going and why. Answer them honestly. The night is long, but you will not cross it alone, and your errand matters more than sleep.
entries.context: In Iliad 24, the aged King Priam is driving by night to Achilles' camp to ransom Hector's body. The god Hermes, disguised as a young Myrmidon, meets him on the plain and asks where he is going through the night when other mortals sleep; he then offers to guide him safely.

aspects.love: You may be reaching out to someone at a time and in a way others would think unwise. Your errand comes from love. Let a trusted friend know where you are going, and accept their support along the way.
aspects.work: Long hours and lonely effort have marked this season. Someone may soon ask what you are working toward. Tell them plainly; they may be the guide who helps you through the hardest stretch of the plain.
aspects.home: Night-time vigils are part of family life: a sick child, an ageing parent, a worried teenager. You are not foolish to keep watch. Accept help from those who offer it, so that you can also rest.
aspects.health: Sleeplessness may be troubling you. Notice what your mind is travelling toward in the dark. Speak about it with someone who can help, and give your body the chance to rest when the errand allows.
aspects.journeys: You are setting out on an unusual or difficult road, at a time when others would stay home. Expect help to appear in an unexpected form. Be open to the stranger's question; it may lead you safely through.

entries.message: You are out in the dark on an errand of the heart. You are not as alone as you think; a guide is walking toward you.
entries.reflect: If someone asked what you are travelling toward through this night, what would you answer?

entries.greek: πῶς ἂν ἔπειτʼ Ὀδυσῆος ἐγὼ θείοιο λαθοίμην,
entries.english: How could I ever forget godlike Odysseus,
entries.reading:
It is a night of fear in the Greek camp, and someone must spy on the Trojans. Diomedes volunteers at once, and Agamemnon tells him to pick any companion he likes, the best man, not the highest-born. Diomedes hardly pauses. How could I ever forget godlike Odysseus, whose heart is eager in every hardship, and whom Athena loves? With him beside me, the two of us could come back even from blazing fire.

This card asks you to look at your companions. You may be facing something dangerous or demanding, and you have more choice than you think about whom you take with you. The temptation is to choose by rank, by habit, by who would be offended if passed over. Diomedes chooses by one test: who will be truly useful, quick-minded and steady, when the night grows dark.

Perhaps someone like that is already in your life, overlooked because they are familiar. Or perhaps you are being asked to become such a companion for another. Either way, the line honours a kind of friendship that is proved in action. Choose well. Then go together, and come home through the fire.
entries.context: In Iliad 10, Diomedes volunteers to spy on the Trojan camp and is told to choose any companion he wishes. He answers that he could not overlook godlike Odysseus, whose heart is eager in every toil and whom Athena loves; with him, they could return even from blazing fire.

aspects.love: In love and friendship, notice who shows up eagerly when things are hard. That is the person to hold close. Tell them plainly that you would choose them again, and be that same companion for them in return.
aspects.work: When forming a team or picking a partner for a difficult task, do not choose by seniority or politics. Choose the person who is resourceful, steady and willing. The right companion matters more than the most impressive one.
aspects.home: In your household, someone may be quietly carrying more than their share with good heart. Recognise them. And when the family faces a challenge, plan it with the one who brings both wit and willingness.
aspects.health: Choose your companions for this season with care: a friend who encourages good habits, a practitioner you trust, a walking partner who actually turns up. The right company makes hard things possible, and makes the long middle stretch bearable.
aspects.journeys: Before a big move or venture, ask who you would most want beside you. If they are willing, invite them. Even a dangerous crossing can be made, and returned from, with the right companion at your side.

entries.message: When you may choose anyone, choose the one whose heart is eager in every toil. With such a friend, you can come back even through fire.
entries.reflect: Who would you choose to walk with you through fire, and have you told them?

entries.greek: ἔλλαβε πορφύρεος θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα κραταιή.
entries.english: dark death and mighty fate seized him.
entries.reading:
The Greek word is porphyreos: dark and surging, the colour of a wave as it rises and of blood as it falls. In Iliad 5 it comes down over the eyes of Hypsenor, a priest of the river Scamander, honoured among the Trojans like a god. He was running when Eurypylus caught him. Neither his holiness nor his speed could keep the sword from his shoulder, and dark death and mighty fate took hold.

This is a hard card, and it would be false to soften it. It does not foretell your death; it speaks about the things in your life that are already ending. A role, a season, a hope that has run its course: somewhere you have been fleeing something that has, in truth, already seized you. You are spending your strength on the run, looking back over your shoulder, when the matter was settled some time ago.

Homer never lets a death pass unnamed, and that is the counsel here. Name what is ending. Grieve it properly instead of trying to outrun it. Whatever is mighty enough to take hold of you cannot be argued with, but it can be faced, and the facing gives back to you the part of the story that is still yours to write.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, the narrator describes a series of killings in battle. The Greek Eurypylus cuts off the arm of the Trojan Hypsenor, priest of the river Scamander, as he flees, and dark death and mighty fate seize him.

aspects.love: If a bond has ended in all but name, the pretending is costing you more than the loss would. Speak the truth of it, gently, to yourself first and then to the other person. Mourning a love honestly is the only way to keep what was good in it.
aspects.work: A project, a post or a way of trading may have reached its natural close while you keep paying to hold it open. Look at the figures and the hours with clear eyes. What is finished should be finished well, not dragged across the field.
aspects.home: Families often flee the hard conversation: an ageing parent, a house that must be sold, a child who has already grown. The longer it is avoided, the harder it grips. Sit at the table together and say plainly what everyone already knows.
aspects.health: This is not a card of illness, but of honesty with the body. If something has changed and will not change back, stop measuring yourself against who you were. Ask what strength remains, and build on that ground rather than on the old.
aspects.journeys: You may be fleeing a decision as Hypsenor fled across the plain, hoping speed alone will save you. It will not. Turn and face the choice; the moment you stop running is the moment you can begin to steer.

entries.message: Some things are already decided. Stop running from them and turn, and you will find you can still choose how you meet them.
entries.reflect: What have you been running from that has, in truth, already caught up with you?

entries.greek: ὣς οὐκ αἰνότερον καὶ κύντερον ἄλλο γυναικός,
entries.english: So nothing is more terrible or shameless than a woman
entries.reading:
Agamemnon speaks from the land of the dead, and his anger has not cooled. He came home from Troy to a feast, and at that feast his wife and her lover cut him down like an ox at the manger. Clytemnestra would not even close his eyes. So when he meets Odysseus among the shades, the wound does the talking, and it talks in sweeping terms: nothing, he says, is more terrible or shameless than a woman.

The line is drawn here as a mirror, not as wisdom. Agamemnon's grief is real, but his verdict is the voice of injury, and in almost the same breath he admits that Penelope is wise and true. That contradiction is the heart of the card. Someone has hurt you badly, perhaps someone close enough to share your table, and part of you has begun to turn one person's deed into a rule about a whole kind of people: all partners, all colleagues, all of a certain family or temperament.

Let the betrayal be what it was, and mourn it fully. But keep your judgement for the one who did it. A heart that condemns everyone will find no Penelope, even when she is waiting at the loom.
entries.context: In Odyssey 11, the ghost of Agamemnon tells Odysseus how he was murdered at his homecoming feast by Aegisthus and his own wife Clytemnestra, who also killed Cassandra and would not close his eyes as he died. In his bitterness he declares nothing is more terrible or shameless than a woman who plots such deeds, though he goes on to praise Penelope.

aspects.love: If you have been hurt before, a new love may be paying for an old crime. Notice when you brace against someone for things they have never done. Tell them where the scar is, so that they can be judged by their own deeds.
aspects.work: One partner who cheated you, one manager who lied, and suddenly every offer looks like a trap. Prudence is wise; contempt is not. Check the terms carefully, then give the person in front of you the fair hearing you were once denied.
aspects.home: Old family betrayals harden into sayings: 'the men in this family', 'women like your aunt'. Such sayings outlive their cause and teach children to fear. Name the real hurt, and refuse to hand down the sweeping verdict.
aspects.health: Bitterness carried long enough settles into the shoulders and into sleep. Agamemnon is still raging among the dead. If an old grievance replays itself at night, it may be time to seek help in setting it down, so that it does not haunt you as it haunted him.
aspects.journeys: Do not let one bad crossing keep you from every sea. If a past move, partnership or place went wrong, learn its particular lesson, and then judge the next harbour by its own shore, not by the wreck you remember.

entries.message: A deep wound tempts you to condemn everyone who resembles the one who hurt you. Grieve the betrayal; do not let it write the law.
entries.reflect: Whose face have you begun to see in people who have done you no wrong?

entries.greek: μὴ ἴομεν Δαναοῖσι μαχησόμενοι περὶ νηῶν.
entries.english: Let us not go and fight the Greeks beside the ships.
entries.reading:
An eagle flies across the Trojan left, carrying a blood-red snake still alive in its talons. The snake twists back and bites the bird, and the eagle lets it fall among the soldiers and flies off crying on the wind. Polydamas reads the omen: like the eagle, Troy will seize its advantage and fail to carry the prize home. Let us not go and fight the Greeks beside the ships. Hector, hot with success, scorns him, and the cost of that scorn runs through the rest of the Iliad.

This card comes when you are on the edge of pressing forward and something has already flickered at the corner of your eye. A delay, an odd remark, a figure that does not add up, a friend who goes quiet when you describe your plan. You may be tempted, as Hector was, to treat every warning as faint-heartedness, because momentum feels like proof.

Momentum is not proof. The line does not ask you to give up your aim, only to stop at the trench and look again. Find your Polydamas, the person who has nothing to gain by flattering you, and hear them all the way through before you cross.
entries.context: In Iliad 12, as the Trojans prepare to cross the Greek trench, an eagle drops a wounded snake among them. Polydamas tells Hector the omen means they should not go on to fight the Greeks by the ships; Hector scornfully rejects the advice.

aspects.love: If you are about to press a relationship forward, with a proposal, a move together or a confrontation, notice whether there are signs you have been explaining away. Pausing is not the same as retreating. Ask the question you are afraid to ask before you cross the trench.
aspects.work: A deal that is going well can blind you to the snake in its talons. Before you commit more money or people, have someone with no stake in your pride read the omens: the terms, the cash flow, the client's hesitations.
aspects.home: Someone in your family may be trying to tell you something you keep brushing off as fussing. Hector called Polydamas a coward and lived to regret it. Sit down with the one who keeps raising the concern and let them finish.
aspects.health: When the body sends a small sign, do not argue with it because you are in the middle of something important. A twinge, a tiredness that will not lift, a change in sleep: these are birds crossing on the left. Have them looked at by someone qualified.
aspects.journeys: The plan may be bold and the wind behind you, but the line counsels a halt at the edge. If several small things have gone wrong while you prepare to leave or change, read them together. Waiting a season may be the bravest choice.

entries.message: When the sign is plain and the voice that reads it is honest, do not mistake caution for cowardice.
entries.reflect: Which warning have you dismissed because hearing it would slow you down?

entries.greek: ἄνδρʼ ἀπαμύνασθαι, ὅτε τις πρότερος χαλεπήνῃ.
entries.english: to defend yourself, when someone else starts the quarrel.
entries.theme: The Stranger Who Takes the Reins
entries.reading:
It is night on the plain of Troy. An old king and an old herald are driving a wagon heaped with treasure towards the camp of the man who killed Hector. Out of the dark comes a young stranger, and the herald's first thought is to run. The stranger names what both men know: you are old, and so is your companion, too old to defend yourselves if someone picks a quarrel. Then he says the unexpected thing. He will do them no harm. He will protect them, because the old man reminds him of his own father. The stranger is Hermes, and he takes the reins.

This card speaks to someone who has been bracing for a fight they cannot win alone. You have measured your strength against what lies ahead and found it wanting, and you are right; pretending otherwise would be foolish. But the line does not end in helplessness. It turns into an offer.

Help may come from a direction you did not expect: from someone younger, or a stranger, or a person you assumed was on the other side. Do not be so proud of your solitude that you send them away. Admit your limits honestly, and let a guide drive for a while.
entries.context: In Iliad 24, Hermes, disguised as a young Myrmidon, meets King Priam on his night journey to Achilles. He points out that Priam is old, and his attendant too, unable to defend themselves if anyone picked a quarrel; but he says he will do him no harm and will protect him, for Priam reminds him of his own father.

aspects.love: Perhaps you feel too worn to defend yourself in another quarrel, and you have been avoiding closeness for fear of it. A gentle friend may be ready to go with you through the hard conversation. Let someone sit beside you rather than across from you.
aspects.work: If a dispute is brewing, with a client, a landlord or a rival, you may lack the means to fight it on your own. Seek out the one who knows the road: a mentor, an adviser, a colleague who has crossed this ground before. Accepting guidance is not weakness.
aspects.home: Older members of a family often carry fears they never voice, of being unable to cope if trouble comes. Like Hermes, offer your protection without making them ask. A visit, a call, a hand on the reins can lift the dread of the dark road.
aspects.health: Acknowledge where your strength has limits, whether from age, illness or exhaustion. That honesty is the beginning of being helped. Let those who are able carry part of the load, and do not mistake every kindness for pity.
aspects.journeys: You are being asked to set out on a road you fear, carrying something precious. You need not travel unescorted. Ask for directions, for company, for the advice of those who have gone before, and watch for the unexpected friend who appears by the river.

entries.message: You do not have to be strong enough for every danger. Accept the help that meets you on the road.
entries.reflect: Where are you insisting on facing alone something that was never meant to be faced alone?

entries.greek: οὐδέ τί μιν παῖδες ποτὶ γούνασι παππάζουσιν
entries.english: No children will climb on his knees and call him 'Papa'.
entries.reading:
Aphrodite has been wounded by a mortal spear and flees weeping to Olympus. Her mother Dione takes her in her arms, tells her of other gods who have suffered at human hands, and then speaks of Diomedes, who struck her. The fool does not know that a man who fights the immortals does not last long. No children climb on his knees and call him 'Papa' when he comes home from the war.

Of all the punishments Dione could name, she chooses this one: not a thunderbolt, but an empty lap. The cost of striving against what is greater than us is often paid at home, in the small, warm, ordinary things we never meant to give up.

Ask yourself what you are fighting at present. It may be a limit that will not move, another person's nature, the passing of time, your own body, the shape of a life that was given and not chosen. You may be winning skirmishes. But look at who is waiting for you at the door, and how long it has been since you sat still long enough for anyone to climb into your lap. Some wars are not worth their victories. Lay down the spear, and go home while the hearth is still warm.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, Aphrodite has been wounded by Diomedes and flees to Olympus. Her mother Dione comforts her and says that Diomedes is a fool not to know that whoever fights the immortals does not last long, and no children climb on his knees calling him father when he comes home from war.

aspects.love: If you are locked in a struggle to change someone at their core, ask what it is costing the tenderness between you. Some natures are as fixed as the gods. Love the person who is actually present, not the one you are fighting to create.
aspects.work: Ambition can become a war on Olympus: against the market, the hours in a day, the limits of one person. Count what the campaign has cost you at home. A smaller success with time for those you love may be the greater prize.
aspects.home: This card is not about who has children and who does not; it is about presence. Whoever waits for you at home, a child, a partner, a friend, an old dog, needs you to come back from your battles with something left to give.
aspects.health: Pushing against the body's limits as if they were an enemy rarely ends well. Rest is not surrender. Lay down the effort for a while and notice what your body is asking of you, before it has to insist more loudly.
aspects.journeys: Before a bold move, ask whether you are striving with the gods, chasing something that would require the world to bend to your will. Choose the change you can actually live with, the one that brings you home, not one that keeps you forever at war.

entries.message: Fight what is greater than you and you may win the battle, but lose the welcome home.
entries.reflect: What ordinary joy are you sacrificing to a battle you cannot truly win?

entries.greek: ἔνδον μὲν δὴ ὅδʼ αὐτὸς ἐγώ, κακὰ πολλὰ μογήσας
entries.english: Here I am, I myself, home at last after many hardships,
entries.reading:
For days Odysseus has sat in his own hall dressed in rags, insulted by the men who are eating his cattle. Now, out in the courtyard, he has tested two herdsmen and found them loyal. The disguise drops. Here I am, he tells them, I myself, home after many hardships, in the twentieth year. And he pulls back his rags to show the scar on his leg, the old boar-wound they would know anywhere. The two men weep, and kiss his head and his hands.

Notice that he does not reveal himself to everyone, only to those who have proved true. This card comes when you have been hidden for a long time: holding back your real opinions, your gifts, your hurt or your history, playing a lesser part to survive among people who had not earned the truth. It may have been wise. But the twentieth year has come.

There are people, perhaps only two or three, who have kept faith with you. Let them see you. Show the scar, the thing that proves it is you, the thing you have been hiding. Being known is its own homecoming, and it is the first step to setting your house in order.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, Odysseus, still disguised as a beggar, tests the herdsmen Eumaeus and Philoetius and finds them loyal. He then reveals himself, saying he has come home in the twentieth year after many hardships, and shows them the scar on his leg as proof.

aspects.love: You may have shown a partner or friend only the safe version of yourself. If they have stood by you through hardship, they have earned the rest. Show them the scar: the old story, the true feeling. Love grows deeper once it is no longer loving a disguise.
aspects.work: You have been working beneath your real capacities, waiting to be noticed. Choose the colleagues or clients who have treated you fairly and let them see what you can do. Step out of the beggar's cloak and claim the work that is yours.
aspects.home: After a long absence, whether of body or of spirit, coming home needs a plain word: here I am. Do not slip back in as if nothing had happened. Sit with your family, tell them what the hard years were like, and let them welcome you.
aspects.health: After long illness or strain, there comes a day when you recognise yourself again. Mark it. Tell those who cared for you that you are back, while still honouring the scars, which are the proof of what you have come through.
aspects.journeys: A long wandering is ending, and you are allowed to arrive. Stop thinking of yourself as a traveller in someone else's story. Unpack, announce yourself, and take up the life you came back to claim.

entries.message: After the disguises and the long years, there comes a moment to say plainly who you are, and to be known.
entries.reflect: Who has earned the right to see you as you really are?

entries.greek: μὴ δʼ οὕτως ἀγόρευε· πάρος δʼ οὐκ ἔσσεται ἄλλως,
entries.english: Do not talk like that. Things will not change before
entries.reading:
Pandarus is the finest archer among Troy's allies, and he is sulking. Twice today he has shot true, at Menelaus and at Diomedes, and twice the man has not fallen. He left his horses at home to spare them fodder, he complains, and trusted this bow instead, and when he gets home he will break it with his own hands and throw it on the fire. Aeneas cuts him off. Do not talk like that. Nothing will change until we two go out together and face the man.

Here is a voice you may recognise from inside your own head. Something has failed twice, and you have begun narrating the failure: the wrong choice, the wrong tools, the bad luck that follows you, the vow to throw it all away. The talk feels like action. It is not. It is the bow still in your hand while you rail at it.

The card asks you to stop the speech mid-sentence. Lament will not move the matter a hand's breadth. What will move it is a different approach: closer, braver, shared with someone else. Homer does not hide that the next attempt was dangerous. But it was at least an attempt, and not a complaint.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, the archer Pandarus complains that his arrows have failed to kill Diomedes and swears to burn his bow. Aeneas tells him not to talk that way: things will not change until the two of them face Diomedes together in Aeneas' chariot; Diomedes kills Pandarus in the attempt.

aspects.love: If you keep rehearsing what went wrong, 'I always choose badly', 'it never works for me', notice how the talk has become a wall. Stop the speech. Ask a friend you trust to look at the matter with you, and try a different way of meeting people.
aspects.work: Cursing the tools, the market or the boss is satisfying and changes nothing. Name the one thing you have not tried: a direct conversation, a partner, a fresh method. Then try it, instead of explaining once more why the old one failed.
aspects.home: A household can fall into a chorus of complaint, everyone explaining why nothing can improve. Be the Aeneas who says, kindly but firmly, 'Don't talk like that.' Then propose one practical thing to do together this week.
aspects.health: Words shape the body's courage. If you hear yourself saying 'I'll never be well' or 'what's the use', take it as the cue to stop and seek one new kind of help, rather than abandoning everything you were already doing.
aspects.journeys: You have tried this move before and it fell short, and you have half-vowed to give up. Do not burn the bow yet. Ask what a different vehicle would look like: another route, a companion, a better-timed departure.

entries.message: Complaining about your tools changes nothing. Things shift only when you change the way you face the problem.
entries.reflect: What story about your failure have you been telling that keeps you from trying again in a new way?

entries.greek: μιμνέτω αὐτόθι τεῖος ἐπειγόμενός περ Ἄρηος·
entries.english: Let him wait here for now, however eager he is for war.
entries.theme: Let the Oath Be Sworn First
entries.reading:
Achilles has come to the assembly burning to fight. Patroclus is dead, and every moment spent talking feels like a betrayal of him. But Agamemnon, ready at last to make his peace, asks for something maddening: let him wait here for now, however eager he is for war, until the gifts are brought from my hut and the oath is sworn before the gods. The quarrel that tore the Greek army apart must be closed properly, in daylight, before witnesses, or it will not be closed at all.

This card comes to the eager. You are ready to go, and the delay feels like an insult to your purpose. Perhaps you are about to throw yourself into a new venture, a reconciliation or a cause, and others are asking for papers, ceremonies, a pause to set things straight.

Wait. Not forever, only until the oath is sworn. Unfinished business has a way of following us into the fight, and a broken trust that is never formally mended will crack again at the worst moment. Let the gifts be carried out, the words be said, the hands be clasped. Then go, with nothing behind you but solid ground.
entries.context: In Iliad 19, at the assembly of reconciliation, Agamemnon agrees to swear the oath and bring out his gifts. He asks that Achilles, however eager for battle, should wait there for now, with the rest of the army, until the gifts are brought and the oaths sworn.

aspects.love: After a rift, rushing back to normal can leave the wound half-closed. Let there be an actual reconciliation: the apology spoken aloud, the promise made, perhaps a small gift that means something. Then go forward together, without the old quarrel waiting in the shadows.
aspects.work: You want to start now, but the agreement is not yet signed and the terms are vague. Wait for the oath. A handshake on the doorstep is no foundation. Get the understanding clear and written down before you put your whole strength into it.
aspects.home: A family decision made in heat, about care, money or a move, may need a slower hour. Gather everyone, let each say their piece, and settle it together. Agreement reached properly saves years of muttering.
aspects.health: Eagerness to get back to full activity can outrun recovery. Let healing finish its work before you charge back in. A short wait now is better than a setback that keeps you from the field for far longer.
aspects.journeys: The departure date calls to you, but loose ends remain: a debt, a farewell, a promise to keep. Tie them first, one by one, before the ship is loaded. You will travel lighter for leaving nothing unspoken behind you.

entries.message: Your eagerness is real, but some things must be settled before you charge: the agreement, the amends, the word given.
entries.reflect: What needs to be properly settled before you can give yourself fully to what comes next?

entries.greek: μὴ δʼ ἐπαγαλλόμενος πολέμῳ καὶ δηϊοτῆτι
entries.english: And do not, glorying in war and battle,
entries.theme: Turn Back When the Ships Are Saved
entries.reading:
Achilles lends Patroclus his armour, his chariot, his immortal horses, and one clear set of instructions. Drive the Trojans from the ships. Then come back. Do not, glorying in war and battle, lead the charge on to the walls of Troy, for a god may come against you; Apollo loves the Trojans. Patroclus does everything he was asked, splendidly, and then the one thing he was told not to do. Three times he climbs the angle of the wall, three times Apollo throws him back, and soon he is dead.

This card is a gift wrapped as a warning. It arrives when things are going well, perhaps better than you dared hope. You have done what you set out to do, and the success has a thrill to it, a sense that you are unstoppable today and should press on. That is the moment of greatest danger.

Remember the task as it was first given. Was it to save the ships, or to take the city? Finish what was asked, enjoy it, and return. There will be other days for larger aims, chosen with a cool head rather than a hot one. Stop while the victory is still a victory.
entries.context: In Iliad 16, Achilles sends Patroclus into battle in his armour, instructing him to drive the Trojans from the ships and then return. He warns him not to be carried away by the glory of war and lead the attack on Troy, lest a god, especially Apollo, should intervene; Patroclus goes too far and is killed.

aspects.love: A happy reconciliation or a promising new love can tempt you to rush: to move in, to make vows, to pour out everything at once. Let the good thing be good at its present size for a while. Pressing too far too fast can undo what you have won.
aspects.work: You have hit your target, and there is talk of expansion. Before you stretch, return to the original plan and ask what it truly required. Bank the gain, rest your people, and make the next push a decision rather than a matter of momentum.
aspects.home: After a good season in the household, resist the urge to fix everything at once. The renovation, the new rules, the grand family plan can wait. Let everyone enjoy the peace you have built before you ask more of it.
aspects.health: When you feel strong again, it is tempting to train harder, work longer, do it all. That is when injuries happen. Keep within the plan you made when you were thinking clearly, and let your strength settle before you test it.
aspects.journeys: A first step has gone well, and the horizon is calling. Before you add another country, another venture or another risk, come back to your base. The traveller who knows when to turn for home is the one who gets to travel again.

entries.message: Do what you were sent to do, then come back. The danger of a good day is believing it can go on forever.
entries.reflect: What would 'enough' look like, if you decided it before the excitement decided for you?

entries.greek: μή ποτε τῆς εὐνῆς ἐπιβήμεναι ἠδὲ μιγῆναι,
entries.english: that I never went up to her bed or lay with her,
entries.theme: The Oath Over the Untouched Bed
entries.reading:
Agamemnon has finally admitted he was wrong. Before the council he lists the gifts he will give Achilles to win him back: tripods, gold, horses, cities, his own daughter in marriage. And he will return Briseis, the woman he took, and swear a great oath that he never went up to her bed or lay with her. It is a solemn promise, and very likely true. When Odysseus carries it all to Achilles' hut, Achilles turns it down.

The card sits where two things meet: the need to give a pledge, and the limits of any pledge. If you have done harm, you may be gathering your amends now, wondering whether they will be enough. If you are the one who was wronged, you may be holding someone's oath in your hands, wondering whether to believe it.

Agamemnon's failure lay not in his gifts but in his pride. He sent others to speak for him, and he ended his offer by insisting that Achilles yield to him as the greater king. Make your pledge plainly, face to face, and keep it. And if you are receiving one, weigh the word as well as the gifts. A true oath, sworn and honoured, is worth more than a heap of tripods. But it cannot be forced on anyone.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, Agamemnon tells the Greek council the gifts he will give to win back Achilles, including the return of Briseis, and says he will swear a great oath that he has never gone to her bed or lain with her. Odysseus later repeats the offer to Achilles, who refuses it.

aspects.love: Where faithfulness has been doubted, a promise is needed, but it must be spoken face to face and lived out day by day. If you are offering it, offer it without conditions. If you are receiving it, give yourself time to see whether deeds match words.
aspects.work: In a damaged business relationship, compensation alone rarely restores trust. Alongside the refund or the better terms, give a clear, honest account of what went wrong and a promise you can keep. Then keep it, visibly, for longer than seems necessary.
aspects.home: A family member may be trying to make up for an old wrong with presents or favours. Accept what is good in it, and gently ask for the conversation the gifts are standing in for. Houses are mended by truth, not by tripods.
aspects.health: Promises to yourself count too. If you have broken faith with your own body, sworn to rest and then not rested, make a smaller pledge, one you can keep, and keep it daily. Trust within yourself is rebuilt the same way as trust between people.
aspects.journeys: Before you leave a place, a post or a partnership, be sure your word is clean. If something needs to be sworn or settled, do it in person. A departure that carries an unspoken grievance will follow you down the road.

entries.message: When trust has been broken, gifts alone cannot rebuild it. Offer the word you can truly swear to, and say it in your own voice.
entries.reflect: If you are making amends, what are you offering in place of the words you have not yet said?

entries.greek: χείλεα μέν τʼ ἐδίηνʼ, ὑπερῴην δʼ οὐκ ἐδίηνε.
entries.english: He wets his lips, but never wets the roof of his mouth.
entries.theme: A Cup That Only Wets the Lips
entries.reading:
Andromache has just seen Hector dragged behind Achilles' chariot, and her grief runs ahead to her son. She sees him orphaned, tugging at the cloaks of his father's old friends at their feasts. One, out of pity, holds out a small cup for a moment. It wets the boy's lips, but never the roof of his mouth. Another drives him away: your father does not dine with us.

It is one of the most exact images of half-help ever made. The cup is real, the pity is real, and the child stays thirsty. This card may be speaking to you from either side of it. Perhaps you are living on scraps of what you need: the occasional warm word from someone who cannot truly be there, a little encouragement at work that never becomes real support, a love that tastes like enough for a moment and leaves you drier than before.

The line is not cruel, but it is honest. Stop calling the wetted lip a drink. Look for those who will set a place for you and fill the cup to the brim. And if you are the one holding out the small cup, ask whether pity is all you can give, or whether there is room at your table.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Andromache, lamenting Hector's death, imagines the life of their son Astyanax as an orphan. He goes begging among his father's friends, and one, out of pity, holds out a small cup, wetting his lips but not his palate, while another drives him from the feast.

aspects.love: A relationship that offers only rare moments of warmth can keep you returning out of thirst rather than joy. Notice whether you leave each meeting fed or wanting. You deserve more than a cup held out briefly and then withdrawn.
aspects.work: Praise without pay, promises of advancement that never arrive, a token bonus: these wet the lips. Ask clearly for what would actually sustain you, and be willing to look elsewhere if this table will not provide it.
aspects.home: Someone in your family may be getting only the edges of your attention, a quick word between other things. Children and elders especially notice when the cup is pulled away. Give them a full measure of your time, even if it is short.
aspects.health: Snatched rest, half-meals at the desk, a few minutes of quiet that never become real recovery: the body notices. Give yourself a proper meal, a full night, an honest pause. A little is not the same as enough.
aspects.journeys: If a move or a change offers only a taste of what you want, a slight improvement or a token gesture, think twice before crossing seas for it. Hold out for the change that truly feeds you, or reshape the one on offer.

entries.message: A kindness that wets the lips but leaves the throat dry is not enough. Seek a table where you are truly fed, and be that table for others.
entries.reflect: Where are you accepting a taste in place of what you actually need?

entries.greek: θάρσει· μή τοι ταῦτα μετὰ φρεσὶ σῇσι μελόντων.
entries.english: Take heart: do not let these things trouble your mind.
entries.reading:
Thetis climbs to the bronze house of Hephaestus with a mother's request. Her son has lost his armour and will soon go out to die. The lame smith rises from his anvil, wipes his face and hands with a sponge, and hears her out. Long ago, when he was thrown from heaven, she took him in and hid him in the sea. Now he says: take heart, do not let these things trouble your mind. I will make him armour that men will marvel at. Then he adds, with rare honesty, that he wishes he could hide Achilles from death as surely.

This card brings comfort, and the comfort is the more trustworthy because it does not promise everything. You have been carrying a worry around and around, perhaps for someone you love, perhaps for yourself. You may have been trying to solve it alone, by fretting, as if worry were a kind of work.

The line asks you to take your trouble to the forge: to the person with the skill, the friend who owes you a kindness, the expert who can do what you cannot. Let them take it in hand. Some things no craft can change, but much can be changed, and you need not hold all of it in your mind tonight.
entries.context: In Iliad 18, Thetis comes to the smith-god Hephaestus to beg new armour for Achilles. Hephaestus tells her to take heart and not let it trouble her: he will make armour to amaze all who see it, though he wishes he could also hide Achilles from death.

aspects.love: Sometimes the most loving thing is to let another person help you carry your fear for someone you both love. Say it aloud to your partner or a close friend. Hearing 'take heart' from someone who means it can loosen a knot you have tied for weeks.
aspects.work: You have been lying awake over a problem that a skilled colleague could solve in an afternoon. Bring it to them. There is no shame in commissioning the armour rather than forging it yourself; that is what crafts and trades are for.
aspects.home: A parent's worry for a grown child can become a heavy, silent thing. Do what can be done, offer the practical help, and then set the rest down. Your anxiety will not shield them; your love and your practical aid might.
aspects.health: Bring your concern to someone qualified instead of turning it over endlessly alone. Much that frightens us at night looks smaller in a good practitioner's hands. Let the expert do their craft, and let your mind rest.
aspects.journeys: Before a big change, write down what is troubling you and see which items others can take on: the paperwork, the arrangements, the advice. Hand over what can be handed over. Arrive at the threshold with a clearer head, not a heavier one.

entries.message: Bring your trouble to someone who knows the craft, and let them take it in hand. Not every burden is yours to beat out at the forge.
entries.reflect: Which worry are you holding that someone else is better placed to work on?

entries.greek: τοῦτον δʼ οὐ δύναμαι βαλέειν κύνα λυσσητῆρα.
entries.english: But this mad dog I cannot hit.
entries.theme: Eight Arrows and One Mad Dog
entries.reading:
Teucer crouches behind his brother Ajax's great shield, rising to shoot and ducking back like a child behind its mother. He is doing magnificently. Eight long-barbed arrows, he tells Agamemnon, and every one lodged in Trojan flesh. But this mad dog I cannot hit. He means Hector. He shoots again, and the arrow flies past and kills another man. He shoots again: another man. And while Teucer is fixed on his one target, Hector leaps from his chariot and strikes him down with a jagged stone.

You have a Hector. It may be a person you cannot win over, a habit you cannot break, a goal that slips away while lesser successes pile up. What the line shows is not only the frustration of missing, but the danger of the fixation. Teucer stopped watching for the stone.

Count your eight arrows; they matter, and you have been dismissing them. Then ask whether this one target has to be struck by you, from here, in this way. Some opponents are met on other fields, at other hours, by other hands. Step back behind the shield. Your aim is good. Your choice of target may need rethinking.
entries.context: In Iliad 8, the Greek archer Teucer, shooting from behind Ajax's shield, tells Agamemnon that he has lodged eight arrows in Trojan warriors but cannot hit Hector, that 'mad dog'. He shoots again and misses, killing another Trojan instead; soon after, Hector strikes Teucer down with a stone.

aspects.love: Perhaps there is one person whose approval you can never win, however many others love you. Count the arrows that landed: the friends, the family, the partner who cherishes you. Stop staking your worth on the one who keeps slipping out of reach.
aspects.work: One client, one rival, one examination keeps defeating you while the rest of your work goes well. Do not let it consume your judgement. Change your approach, seek another route, or accept that this target is not yours, before the fixation leaves you exposed.
aspects.home: In families there is often one argument that never resolves, and you keep aiming at it from the same position. Lower the bow for a while. Strengthen what does work, and come back to the hard matter with fresh eyes or a fair-minded go-between.
aspects.health: If one stubborn habit or symptom will not shift, do not let frustration undo the good you are doing elsewhere. Acknowledge your progress, and bring this particular problem to someone who can approach it differently.
aspects.journeys: If one door in your plans stays shut, a permit, a sale, a permission, do not wear yourself out hammering on it. Look at the routes already open. The way forward may lie beside the target, not through it.

entries.message: You have succeeded everywhere but at the one target that matters most to you. Stop spending your arrows on it from the same place.
entries.reflect: What has your fixation on one unreachable thing caused you to stop noticing?

entries.greek: τέττα, σιωπῇ ἧσο, ἐμῷ δʼ ἐπιπείθεο μύθῳ·
entries.english: Sit quietly, friend, and do as I say.
entries.reading:
Agamemnon is going through the ranks before battle, and when he reaches Diomedes he is unfair: your father Tydeus was a better fighter than you will ever be. Diomedes says nothing. It is his friend Sthenelus who flares up in defence of them both. Diomedes turns to him with a rare, affectionate word, tetta, something like 'old friend', and says: sit quietly, and do as I say. I do not blame the king for driving the army on. If we take Troy, the glory is his; if we fail, so is the grief. Then he leaps from his chariot, his bronze ringing, and goes to fight.

This card comes when you have been criticised, perhaps unjustly, and your instinct, or the instinct of those who love you, is to hit back. The line offers another way: a deep, deliberate quiet that comes not from fear but from understanding.

Diomedes saw the weight on the man who spoke. He chose to answer with deeds. Calm the loyal voices who want to fight on your behalf, and your own voice too. Let the unfair word fall unanswered, and let your work be the reply.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, Agamemnon reproaches Diomedes for holding back from battle. Diomedes' companion Sthenelus angrily answers back, but Diomedes tells him to sit quietly and do as he says, explaining that he does not blame Agamemnon for urging the Greeks to fight, since the glory or the grief of the war will be his.

aspects.love: When a partner speaks sharply under strain, you need not meet it blow for blow. Ask what weight they are carrying. A quiet answer and a patient day can do more for the bond than winning the argument tonight.
aspects.work: A superior's criticism may have been unfair, and colleagues may be urging you to protest. Weigh it calmly. If the person speaking carries the burden of the outcome, their impatience may not really be about you. Let your results answer.
aspects.home: In family quarrels, loyal allies can make things worse by rushing to your defence. Gently ask them to sit quietly. You can handle this yourself, more calmly, without turning a hard word into a feud.
aspects.health: The urge to retort keeps the body on a war footing long after the moment has passed. Practise the pause: breathe, sit, let the sting fade. Calm chosen deliberately is a strength, not a defeat.
aspects.journeys: Others may be loudly urging you to take offence and leave. Before you act, sit quietly with the decision. If you go, go because you have chosen to, not because a single harsh word stung you into motion.

entries.message: When someone's harsh word stings, you do not always have to answer it. Sometimes strength is a silence that understands why they spoke.
entries.reflect: What would you gain by letting the unfair word go unanswered, and answering with your deeds instead?

entries.greek: οὐκ ἀρετᾷ κακὰ ἔργα· κιχάνει τοι βραδὺς ὠκύν,
entries.english: Wicked deeds do not prosper: the slow catch up with the swift,
entries.theme: The Lame Smith Catches the Swift
entries.reading:
In the hall of the Phaeacians the bard Demodocus sings a comic and pointed song. Aphrodite, wife of the lame smith Hephaestus, has been meeting Ares in secret. Hephaestus does not storm or shout. He goes to his forge and makes a net of chains as fine as spider's thread, drapes it about the bed, and pretends to leave. When the lovers lie down, the net falls. The gods crowd to the doorway, laughing, and one says to his neighbour: bad deeds do not prosper. The slow catches the swift.

You may feel slow in a race against someone faster, louder, more charming. Perhaps you have been wronged by someone who seems to glide past every consequence, while you limp along doing honest work. This card tells you that the race is not run on the track you think. And if you are the one gliding, the song is a warning: the net is already being forged.

Hephaestus won through craft, patience and a plain refusal to be fooled. Keep to your forge. Do your work carefully and quietly, without hurry and without dreams of revenge. Truth has its own net. Your part is not to chase the swift, but to be ready, clear-eyed and steady, when the moment comes.
entries.context: In Odyssey 8 the bard Demodocus sings of Ares and Aphrodite caught in the net forged by Hephaestus. The gods gather to look, and one says to another that the slow, lame smith has caught Ares, the swiftest of the gods, by his craft.

aspects.love: If you suspect deceit, do not race into accusations. Watch, wait, and let the truth show itself. And if you are the one keeping a secret, remember the net: what is hidden in love has a way of coming to light before many witnesses.
aspects.work: A rival may be quicker to market, quicker to talk, quicker to take credit. Keep building. Good work, careful records and patience have a way of catching up with flash. The steady trader is still at the forge when the swift are explaining themselves.
aspects.home: In family life the quieter, slower person is often underestimated. If that is you, take heart: steadiness is noticed in the end. If someone at home is slower, honour their pace; they may see what the quick ones miss.
aspects.health: Recovery and fitness are rarely won in sprints. Slow, regular care catches up with what quick fixes promise and fail to deliver. Be the smith at his patient work, not the swift god caught in the net of his own haste.
aspects.journeys: There is no need to rush this decision because others are moving fast. Let them run. Prepare carefully, and you may well arrive, slow and sound, ahead of those who set out in a hurry.

entries.message: Patience and craft outlast speed and cunning. What is done in the dark is caught in the end, and steady hands do the catching.
entries.reflect: Where are you trying to outrun someone when your real advantage is patience?

entries.greek: κληῗσαι μεγάροιο θύρας πυκινῶς ἀραρυίας,
entries.english: to lock the tight-fitting doors of the hall,
entries.theme: Bar the Doors Before the Bow
entries.reading:
The moment is close. Odysseus has made himself known to two loyal herdsmen, and now, before the great bow is in his hands, he gives orders that sound almost domestic. Bring me the bow. Tell the women to lock the tight-fitting doors of the hall and to stay at their work whatever they hear, groans or the clash of men. You, bar the courtyard gate and lash it fast. The battle will be won by arrows, but it is made possible by doors.

This card falls when something important is coming and you are thinking about the dramatic part: the speech, the launch, the confrontation, the leap. The line draws your eye to the hinges. What needs closing before you begin? Which distractions, leaks, open accounts or wandering commitments could let the decisive moment drain away?

There is a second meaning too. The women are told to keep to their looms, whatever noise they hear. Not everyone needs to be in the hall. Protect those who should not be caught up in your struggle, and protect yourself from the clamour of everything else. Lock the doors, quietly and firmly. Then take up the bow.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, Odysseus, having just revealed himself to the swineherd Eumaeus and the cowherd Philoetius, gives his orders before the slaying of the suitors. He tells Eumaeus to bring him the bow and to tell the women to lock the tight-fitting doors of the hall and stay at their work whatever they hear.

aspects.love: Before a serious conversation with someone you love, close the doors: put the world aside, set apart an evening, make sure you will not be interrupted. A crucial word deserves a room where it can be heard in full.
aspects.work: Before a deadline or a big negotiation, shut what leaks: the side tasks, the open invitations, the unfiled accounts. Brief your allies, shield your team from the noise, and give the main work your undivided attention.
aspects.home: A household going through a crisis needs some doors kept closed. Not every child or relative needs to hear every detail. Keep the house running, let others stay at their work, and handle the hard part where it belongs.
aspects.health: Rest and recovery need closed doors too: a bedroom the outside world does not reach, hours when no one can call on you. Fit the doors tight. Healing comes more easily when it is not constantly interrupted.
aspects.journeys: Before you set out, secure what you leave behind: the house, your affairs, the people who rely on you. A departure is stronger, and the mind on the road freer, when nothing at home is left swinging open in the wind.

entries.message: Before the decisive hour, close the ways by which trouble can come in or the moment slip out. Quiet preparation wins more battles than it is given credit for.
entries.reflect: What open door could let your most important hour drain away?

entries.greek: ἆ δείλʼ οὐδέ τί τοι θάνατος καταθύμιός ἐστιν
entries.english: Poor wretch, you give no thought to death,
entries.reading:
Hector has stripped the armour of Achilles from the body of Patroclus, and, apart from the fighting, he puts it on. It is the work of the gods, a gift to Achilles' father, and Hector stands taller in it. Far above, Zeus watches, shakes his head, and speaks to his own heart: poor wretch, you give no thought to death, though it is already close beside you. The god even grants him a great surge of strength, and Hector, shining, never notices the shadow that comes with it.

This card does not prophesy disaster. It names a blindness. You may be wearing something that was not made for you: a position you gained through someone else's fall, a success won in a way that leaves debts, a standing borrowed from your title or your company. It feels splendid. People are impressed. And you have stopped asking what it will cost.

Do the thinking Hector would not do. Ask whose armour this is, and what claim others have on it. Ask where the danger lies, not to frighten yourself, but so that you can choose freely. Then wear only what you can bear to answer for.
entries.context: In Iliad 17, Zeus watches from afar as Hector puts on the immortal armour of Achilles, stripped from the dead Patroclus. Shaking his head, Zeus speaks to his own heart, pitying Hector, who gives no thought to the death that is already close to him.

aspects.love: A new relationship can bring status, comfort or excitement that dazzles. Make sure you are seeing the person and not the armour. Ask what you are entering into, what history comes with it, and whether you can truly carry it.
aspects.work: A promotion or windfall may have come on the back of someone else's misfortune. Take it graciously, but do not swagger. Learn what is owed, to whom and when, and prepare for the reckoning that often follows sudden gains.
aspects.home: Inheritance, of property, of a family role, of a parent's expectations, can feel like wearing borrowed armour. Talk openly with others who have a claim on it. Pride in what you have taken up should not drown out their grief.
aspects.health: When you feel unbeatable, it is easy to ignore warnings. Running bright on adrenaline, little sleep or sheer will can hide a bill that is coming due. Look honestly at what your present pace is costing, and adjust before the body has to insist.
aspects.journeys: A bold change may make you feel newly powerful. Before you commit, ask whose resources or goodwill you are relying on, and what happens if they are withdrawn. Go forward with open eyes, not borrowed confidence.

entries.message: Borrowed glory fits for a day. Before you put on what belonged to someone else, count what it may cost you.
entries.reflect: What are you enjoying now whose cost you have not yet counted?

entries.greek: ἦλθʼ Ὀδυσεὺς καὶ οἶκον ἱκάνεται, ὀψέ περ ἐλθών.
entries.english: Odysseus has come, he is home, though he has come late.
entries.reading:
Old Eurycleia climbs the stairs so fast that her knees stumble and her feet trip over each other. Penelope is asleep, the deep sleep that comes after long grief. The nurse bends over her: wake up, dear child, and see with your own eyes what you have longed for every day. Odysseus has come, he is home, though he has come late. The suitors lie dead in the hall. Twenty years of waiting are over.

There is an old ache in the words 'though late'. Late is real. Years have been lost, youth has gone, the house has been plundered. Eurycleia does not pretend otherwise. But she will not let the lateness swallow the news.

This card comes to someone who has waited a long time: for recognition, for healing, for a person, for a door to open. Perhaps it is opening now, and you are tempted to meet it with bitterness: what good is it to me now? The line asks you to wake up and look. Grieve the lost years if you must, but do not sleep through the arrival. What comes late can still be loved, and what is home is home.
entries.context: In Odyssey 23, the old nurse Eurycleia hurries upstairs to wake Penelope after the suitors have been killed. She tells her to come and see with her own eyes what she has longed for every day: Odysseus has come home, though he came late.

aspects.love: A love, a reconciliation or a friendship that seemed lost may come back after many years. Do not refuse it because of the time that was wasted. Two older, wiser people can begin again, and the late harvest is often the sweetest.
aspects.work: Recognition you deserved long ago may finally arrive. Accept it with grace rather than resentment. The delay was not just, but the reward is real, and there is still time to make good use of it.
aspects.home: A family member long estranged or far away may be coming back. Let the household make room, even though the years have changed everyone. Welcome is a choice, and late is still better than never.
aspects.health: Recovery may have taken far longer than you hoped, and you may hardly believe you are better. Wake up to it. Let yourself notice the strength that has returned, even if there is time you cannot get back.
aspects.journeys: A long-postponed homecoming, move or dream may at last be possible. Do not let the voice that says 'it is too late now' make the decision for you. Go and see with your own eyes.

entries.message: What you waited for so long has come. That it came late does not make it any less real, or any less yours.
entries.reflect: If what you waited for arrived late, would you let yourself rejoice in it anyway?

entries.greek: ἔκ τε καὶ ὀψὲ τελεῖ, σύν τε μεγάλῳ ἀπέτισαν
entries.english: he fulfils it in the end, even if late, and they pay a heavy price,
entries.reading:
The truce was sworn over lambs and poured wine, and the armies sat down in peace to watch Paris and Menelaus settle the war in single combat. Then Pandarus, egged on by Athena in disguise, drew his bow and shot Menelaus. The wound proves shallow, but Agamemnon, holding his brother, speaks in grief and fury: an oath is not made void. Even if Zeus does not fulfil it at once, he fulfils it in the end, even if late, and the oath-breakers pay a heavy price.

This is a card for someone wronged by a broken word. A promise was made to you and not kept, and the person who broke it seems to be doing well enough. You may be torn between rage and resignation. Either one is a kind of exile from your own peace.

The line holds a harder and steadier truth. Broken faith carries its own consequences, in time, often in ways no one could have arranged. Your task is not to be the hand of Zeus. It is to keep your own oaths clean, remember clearly what was promised, and hold your ground. Justice moves slowly, but it is not blind, and it is not asleep.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, the Trojan Pandarus has broken the sworn truce by wounding Menelaus with an arrow. Agamemnon, grieving over his brother, declares that oaths are never in vain: even if Zeus does not fulfil them at once, he fulfils them in the end, and the oath-breakers pay a great price.

aspects.love: If someone broke faith with you, the hurt is real and so is the injustice. You do not need to arrange their reckoning. Turn your strength towards your own healing and towards people whose promises hold. And if you broke a vow, mend it before the price grows.
aspects.work: A broken agreement or an unpaid debt galls you. Keep the records, follow the proper channels, and seek qualified advice rather than plotting revenge. Proper process is slow, but it is the shape justice takes among people.
aspects.home: Old family promises, about care, inheritance or support, sometimes go unkept, and bitterness can poison the whole house. Name what was promised, ask for it clearly once, without threats, and then let time and conscience do their slow work.
aspects.health: Long resentment wears on the body like a wound left open. You are allowed to want justice and still set down the weight of waiting for it. Rest from the vigil, and let your sleep belong to you again.
aspects.journeys: Before you commit to a new venture or place, look closely at the promises being made to you. Ask for them clearly and in writing. And make sure every oath you swear in the new place is one you will keep.

entries.message: Broken promises are not forgotten just because they go unpunished for a while. Keep your own word, and let justice keep its own time.
entries.reflect: What would it free in you to stop waiting to see them pay?

entries.greek: ἐν δʼ Ἔρις, ἐν δʼ Ἀλκή, ἐν δὲ κρυόεσσα Ἰωκή,
entries.english: In it were Strife, and Courage, and chilling Pursuit,
entries.reading:
Athena lets her soft embroidered robe slip to her father's floor and arms herself for war. Over her shoulders she throws the aegis, the dreadful tasselled shield-cloak, ringed all round with Rout. On it are Strife, and Courage, and chilling Pursuit, and the Gorgon's head, grim and terrible. She steps into the blazing chariot, and the gates of heaven open for her of their own accord.

Look at the company on that shield. Courage is there, but it does not travel alone: it sits between Strife and the cold rush of the chase. Homer sees what we would rather not see, that any real fight calls all of them out together.

This card falls when you are arming yourself for something: a confrontation, a stand, a campaign for what you believe. Your cause may be good; Athena's was. But when you take up the shield, you take up its whole face. You will feel the courage, and you will also feel strife spreading beyond what you intended, and the chill of pursuit that can turn a defence into a hunt. Go armed, if you must. But know what you carry, and keep Pursuit on a short rein, so that it never becomes the master of your Courage.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, Athena arms herself for battle to go with Hera against Ares and help the Greeks. Over her shoulders she throws the terrible tasselled aegis, wreathed with Rout and bearing Strife, Courage, chilling Pursuit and the Gorgon's head.

aspects.love: Before a hard conversation with someone you love, look at what you are bringing. Courage to speak the truth, yes; but notice the strife, and the urge to chase down every point. Win what matters, and let the rest run free.
aspects.work: A dispute at work may demand a firm stand. Take it with courage, but watch for strife that turns colleagues into camps, and for the cold pursuit that wants the other side not just answered but routed. Fight cleanly, and stop when the point is won.
aspects.home: Family conflicts escalate when one person arms for battle. If you must stand firm, do it plainly and briefly. Lay the shield down as soon as you can, so that the house does not become a field of war.
aspects.health: Fighting an illness or a habit is a real battle, but the mind can turn the fight against itself. Bring courage, and leave self-blame and relentless self-pursuit at the door. Your body is your ally, not the enemy.
aspects.journeys: A bold move may need you to arm yourself with resolve. Make sure the impulse is courage, and not the thrill of the chase or a hunger for conflict. Choose the change for what it builds, not for the fight it lets you have.

entries.message: Courage never rides alone. Whatever shield you carry into the fight bears strife and the cold thrill of the chase as well; know them all before you go.
entries.reflect: When you take up this fight, which of its companions do you fear will take you over?

entries.greek: λιμῷ δʼ οἴκτιστον θανέειν καὶ πότμον ἐπισπεῖν.
entries.english: But to die of hunger is the most pitiful way to meet one's fate.
entries.theme: The Argument of the Empty Belly
entries.reading:
For a month the winds have pinned Odysseus' ship to the island of the Sun. The stores are gone; the men fish and snare birds, their bellies twisting. They have sworn not to touch the god's cattle grazing on the slopes. Then Odysseus goes inland to pray and falls asleep, and Eurylochus speaks. Every death is hateful, he says, but to die of hunger is the most pitiful way to meet one's fate. Let us take the best of the cattle. They do. The hides crawl, the meat lows on the spits, and when at last they put to sea, Zeus strikes the ship with lightning.

This line is drawn as a warning. Eurylochus is not a villain; he is frightened, and what he says is true as far as it goes. That is what makes him persuasive. Fear always argues from something real.

You may be in a lean season, and a voice, perhaps your own, is urging you to break something that should not be broken in order to find relief: a vow, a trust, a principle, a sacred limit. The need is genuine. But the shortcut has a cost that will come later, and larger. Hold out. Help is often nearer than the hungry hour believes.
entries.context: In Odyssey 12, Odysseus' men are stranded on Thrinacia, the island of the Sun, and their food has run out. While Odysseus sleeps, Eurylochus urges his companions to slaughter the sacred cattle of Helios, saying that of all deaths, dying of hunger is the most pitiful; the deed brings their destruction.

aspects.love: Loneliness can make a dangerous choice look reasonable: going back to someone who harmed you, breaking a promise for a moment's comfort. Do not let the hungry hour choose for you. Lean on true friends until the lean season passes.
aspects.work: When money is tight, the clever shortcut appears: cutting a corner, bending a rule, taking what is not quite yours. That is the Sun's cattle. Look for honest relief, however small, and refuse the bargain that costs more later.
aspects.home: When a household is under strain, someone will often propose the drastic remedy. Listen with compassion, but test it against what you have agreed together. A family that holds faith through scarcity is stronger than one that breaks faith to escape it.
aspects.health: Desperation for relief can lead to remedies that do more harm than the trouble itself. Do not take risks with your body in a frightened hour. Seek proper advice, and choose the slower help that will not turn on you.
aspects.journeys: Stuck and out of patience, you may be tempted to leave by any means. Do not burn the ship to escape the island. Wait for the true wind, or find an honest way out, even if it is slower.

entries.message: Fear argues very well. When it urges you to break what is sacred to save yourself, the wiser path is to endure a little longer.
entries.reflect: What line are you being tempted to cross because the need feels so urgent?

entries.greek: κείσομʼ ἐπεί κε θάνω· νῦν δὲ κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἀροίμην,
entries.english: I shall lie still when I die. But now let me win great glory.
entries.reading:
Thetis has risen from the sea to comfort her son, and she tells him the truth: after Hector, your own death is waiting. Achilles does not argue. Even Heracles, he says, dearest of men to Zeus, could not escape his fate. If the same lot is mine, I shall lie still when I die. But now let me win great glory. He knows exactly what he is choosing, and why.

This card is not about recklessness, and it does not foretell anything grave. It is about clarity. Achilles has stopped bargaining with the shortness of life and has let it show him what matters. You may have been putting off the thing you care about most, the work, the word, the voyage, the making, as if there were endless time to rest first and live afterwards.

The line reverses the order. There will be stillness enough, later. The present is for doing. What deed would you be glad to have done, looking back on this year? Name it. Begin it while your strength is in you and the light is still on the field. Glory, in the end, means only this: having been fully alive to the thing that was yours to do.
entries.context: In Iliad 18, Achilles, grieving for Patroclus, tells his mother Thetis that he will go out to kill Hector, though he knows his own death will follow. If the same fate awaits him as took even Heracles, he says, he will lie still when he dies, but now he will win great glory.

aspects.love: If you have been waiting for a perfect moment to say what you feel, to make a commitment or to mend a friendship, the line says: now. Rest and certainty can come afterwards. Do the brave, loving thing while the chance is in your hands.
aspects.work: The project you keep postponing until things are calmer may be the one that matters most. Calm will come later. Clear an hour this week and start the work you would be proud to be remembered for.
aspects.home: The family gathering, the visit to an elderly relative, the story you mean to write down: these things wait politely until suddenly they cannot. Choose one, and do it soon, while all of you are here to share it.
aspects.health: Rest is good, but do not make rest your whole life while strength is still in you. Spend that strength on what you love, at a pace you can keep up. Then rest deeply, knowing it was well spent.
aspects.journeys: A move, a pilgrimage or a long-dreamed voyage may never come at an ideal moment. If it truly matters, begin planning it now. Let the knowledge that life is not endless push you gently across the threshold.

entries.message: Rest will come in its own time. The hour you have is for the deed that matters most to you.
entries.reflect: What are you saving for later that is really meant for now?

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ ὄρσευ πόλεμον δʼ οἷος πάρος εὔχεαι εἶναι.
entries.english: Rise up and go to war, as brave as you always boast you are.
entries.reading:
Agamemnon walks the lines before battle and comes to Idomeneus, the grey-haired king of Crete, standing in the front rank like a wild boar. I honour you above all the Greeks, says Agamemnon; at the feast your cup is always kept full, while others drink their measure. So rise up and go to war, as brave as you always boast you are. Idomeneus does not bristle. He answers that he will be the faithful comrade he promised to be, and goes into the fight.

There is a sting and an honour in this line together. You have spoken about who you are: your values, your loyalty, your skill, your readiness. Others have believed you, and perhaps rewarded you for it with their trust, your cup filled to the brim. Now the battle is joined, and the words are being called in.

Do not take offence at being reminded. Take it as respect. The card asks you to close the gap between your speech and your deeds, quietly and fully. Be the person you said you were at the feast. It may be harder than talking. It is also far more satisfying, and once it is done it will never need saying again.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, Agamemnon goes through the ranks before battle, rousing his captains. To Idomeneus of Crete he recalls the honour he always shows him at feasts, and bids him rise to war as brave as he has always claimed to be.

aspects.love: You have told someone you would always be there. A moment may be coming, or may already be here, when that promise needs action rather than repetition. Show up fully, in the ordinary ways by which love is proved.
aspects.work: Your application, your pitch or your confident words in a meeting promised something. Now deliver it. If you promised too much, say so early and give your honest best. Credibility grows when talk is followed by work.
aspects.home: Parents and elders often speak of family values at the table. Children watch to see whether those words hold under pressure. Let your actions match the stories you tell about what this family stands for.
aspects.health: If you have announced a change, to eat better, to rest more, to move more, the line asks you to begin. Not perfectly, but genuinely. Let your body hear the promise you have been making to everyone else.
aspects.journeys: You have talked about this venture for years. The time for talking may be over. Take the first real step, and let your courage become something people can see rather than something they hear about.

entries.message: Words spoken at the feast are promises. The hour has come to be what you have said you are.
entries.reflect: Which of your own words is now asking you to live up to it?

entries.greek: οὔ τί σε λωβεύω, τέκνον φίλον, ἀλλʼ ἔτυμόν τοι
entries.english: I am not mocking you, dear child; it is true,
entries.reading:
Penelope is angry. The old nurse has woken her from the first sweet sleep she has had in years, with a tale that her husband is home and the suitors dead. The gods have driven you mad, says the queen; why mock me with such stories? Eurycleia stands her ground: I am not mocking you, dear child; it is true. He is here. He is the stranger everyone in the house insulted.

Penelope's anger is not foolish. She has been deceived before; wanderers have come to Ithaca with invented news to win a meal or a cloak. When hope has been burned that often, doubt becomes a kind of armour. That is likely where you stand. Something good is being offered, a reconciliation, a recovery, an opportunity, an honest word of praise, and part of you suspects a trick.

The card is gentle and firm at once. Your caution is understandable; keep it, and test the news, as Penelope will test Odysseus with the secret of their bed. But do not shut the door on it for fear of being fooled. Ask your questions. Look for the scar. And let yourself believe, when the proof comes, that something good may be exactly what it seems.
entries.context: In Odyssey 23, Penelope scolds the nurse Eurycleia for waking her with what she takes for a cruel joke. Eurycleia replies that she is not mocking her: Odysseus really has come home, and he is the stranger whom everyone mistreated. The papyrus line is identified here only probably, as Maltomini marks it uncertain.

aspects.love: Someone may be telling you sincerely that they love you, or that they have changed. If old hurts make you disbelieve, say so honestly and ask for the time and the signs you need. Testing is wise; refusing to listen is not.
aspects.work: An offer, a compliment or a success may seem too good to be true. Look into it calmly and make your checks. If it holds, accept it fully. You may have grown so used to disappointment that you no longer recognise good fortune when it knocks.
aspects.home: A family member brings news you can hardly believe: they are mended, or they are sorry, or they are coming back. Do not dismiss them as Penelope first dismissed her nurse. Listen. The loyal voice in your house may be telling the truth.
aspects.health: When you are told that a recovery is real or a fear unfounded, the mind may refuse to rest. Let qualified people reassure you, ask what you need to ask, and then allow the good news to settle into your body.
aspects.journeys: If an unexpected door opens, do not assume it is a trap. Look into it with care. Many have missed the right ship because they were sure, from bitter experience, that no ship would ever come for them.

entries.message: Good news can feel like a cruel joke when hope has hurt you before. Test it, by all means; but this one may be true.
entries.reflect: What good thing are you refusing to believe because hope has hurt you before?

entries.greek: Ἀλκμήνης δʼ ἀπέπαυσε τόκον, σχέθε δʼ Εἰλειθυίας.
entries.english: She held back Alcmene's labour, and stopped the birth-goddesses.
entries.reading:
Agamemnon is telling a story against himself. Even Zeus, he says, was once blinded by Folly. On the day Heracles was due to be born, Zeus boasted to the gods that a child of his blood born that day would rule all who lived around him. Hera made him swear to it. Then she sped down from Olympus, brought another child, Eurystheus, early into the world, and held back Alcmene's labour, keeping the birth-goddesses away. Heracles came late, and spent his life labouring at the orders of a lesser man.

It is a strange line for an oracle, and a precise one. Something you are ready to bring into the world, a plan, a piece of work, a new stage of life, is being held back. It may be someone else's interest, a rule, a rival who moved faster. The delay is real, and it may cost you something: credit, position, the order of things.

But notice what the story does not say. It does not say Heracles was diminished. The labours laid on him became the very deeds that made his name undying. Guard your word against those who would twist it. Then, if the birth is delayed, let the delay become your labours: the work that proves what you are.
entries.context: In Iliad 19, Agamemnon tells the story of how Zeus himself was led astray: Zeus swore that a child born that day would rule his neighbours, and Hera then held back Alcmene's labour and stopped the birth-goddesses, while bringing Eurystheus early to birth. Agamemnon tells this tale while making amends to Achilles.
