aspects.home: A family member keeps telling you not to worry about something you sense is serious. Love them, but ask direct questions and look at the facts yourself. Peace bought by not knowing rarely lasts long, and the bill tends to arrive later.
aspects.health: Do not let anyone talk you out of a genuine concern about your wellbeing with easy reassurance, least of all someone selling something. Seek a trusted, independent opinion, and keep asking until you are satisfied.
aspects.journeys: An offer seems generous, and the people making it say there is nothing to fear. Before you commit, find out what they want from you. Read the terms by daylight, not by the glow of comforting words.

entries.message: Be wary of comfort offered by someone who wants something from you. Reassurance is not the same as safety.
entries.reflect: Whose reassurance are you leaning on, and what do they gain from your believing it?

entries.greek: ἐξ ὕπνου γοόωσα φίλους οἰκῆας ἐγείρῃ
entries.english: wakes her household from sleep with her weeping,
entries.reading:
On Olympus, Aphrodite lies in her mother's lap, her wrist bleeding where a mortal spear has grazed it. Diomedes has wounded a goddess. Dione comforts her daughter, and then speaks a warning aimed at the man below: let him beware, lest someone stronger meet him, and his wife wake her household from sleep with her weeping, mourning the husband she has lost. For one line Homer turns from the battlefield to a dark house far away, a woman crying, servants stirring in their beds.

This card asks you to see the household behind the hero. If you are taking a great risk, pushing past limits, testing powers stronger than you, you may think of the danger as yours alone. It is not. Somewhere there are people who would be woken by your fall: a partner, children, parents, friends who would grieve.

This is not a call to timidity. Diomedes was brave, and courage has its place. It is a call to count the cost honestly, including the cost that others would pay. Let love for those at home temper your daring. Fight the fights that matter, and refuse the ones that only feed your pride. Come home to the house, rather than leaving it to wake in tears.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, the goddess Aphrodite, wounded by Diomedes, flees to Olympus and is comforted by her mother Dione. Dione warns that Diomedes should take care lest a stronger foe fight him, and his wife Aegialeia wake her household from sleep weeping for her husband.

aspects.love: Your partner lives with the results of your choices: the late nights, the risks, the battles you pick. Before you take on something dangerous, talk with them honestly. Give them a voice in what they might one day have to carry.
aspects.work: Ambition is pushing you toward a gamble that would hurt more than you if it failed. Think of the people who depend on your income and your steadiness. Bold moves are better when they are not reckless ones.
aspects.home: Someone in your household may be lying awake worrying over you, though they say nothing at breakfast. Reassure them with honesty, and with real changes if changes are needed. A home should not have to brace itself for your next battle.
aspects.health: Pushing your body or mind past sensible limits affects everyone who loves you, not just yourself. Take reasonable care of yourself, as much for their sake as for your own. Your wellbeing is woven into theirs, thread by thread.
aspects.journeys: A venture with real danger is calling. Weigh it with the faces of your family in mind. If you go, prepare well and stay in touch; if you stay, know that staying can also be a kind of courage.

entries.message: Your daring is never yours alone. Before you take on powers stronger than you, think of who would wake in tears.
entries.reflect: Whose sleep would be broken by your fall, and does that change what you are willing to risk?

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ ἴθι σιγῇ τοῖον, ἐγὼ δʼ ὁδὸν ἡγεμονεύσω,
entries.english: Come, go quietly, and I will lead the way.
entries.reading:
Odysseus has washed up on a strange coast with nothing but his wits. Now, at the edge of a city, a young girl with a water jar offers to show him the way to the king's palace. She is Athena in disguise. Her instruction is simple: go quietly, do not look at anyone or ask questions, and I will lead the way. The people here are wary of strangers. Wrapped in a mist the goddess has poured around him, he passes through the streets unseen.

This line arrives for someone who has been talking, planning and striving hard, perhaps too hard. You may be in unfamiliar territory, a new workplace, a new community, a delicate situation, and your instinct is to explain yourself to everyone and make your mark at once. The oracle advises the opposite. Not every moment calls for your voice.

There is help on the path, though it may look ordinary: a modest guide carrying water. Follow it. Watch, listen, and save your words for the hall where they will count. Silence here is not weakness; it is the cloak that lets you pass unharmed. When the time comes to speak, you will stand before the right people, and they will hear you.
entries.context: In Odyssey 7, Athena, disguised as a young Phaeacian girl, agrees to show Odysseus the way to the palace of Alcinous. She tells him to walk in silence while she leads, and not to look at or question anyone, since the people are wary of strangers.

aspects.love: A relationship is at a delicate stage, and too many words may unsettle it. Let actions and patience speak for a while. Follow the slow lead of trust rather than pressing for declarations before their time.
aspects.work: In a new role, observe before you assert. Find the person who knows the corridors and the history, and learn from them. Your ideas will land far better once you understand the customs of the place and the people who keep them.
aspects.home: A tense household needs fewer speeches and more quiet steadiness. Let someone wiser or calmer guide the next conversation, and support them by holding your tongue when you are tempted to interrupt. Your silence can be a gift to everyone there.
aspects.health: Quiet practices may help you more than striving: walking, stillness, earlier nights, less noise. Let a trusted guide set the pace of your recovery, and resist the urge to argue with every step or to hurry ahead of the one who leads.
aspects.journeys: In a strange place, be a modest guest. Follow local guidance, keep a low profile at first, and trust that you are being led toward the right door, even if you cannot yet see it.

entries.message: For now, say little and follow well. Guidance is with you, but it asks for quiet steps.
entries.reflect: Where would saying less and following more carefully serve you better right now?

entries.greek: οὔατʼ ἀκουέμεν ἐστί, νόος δʼ ἀπόλωλε καὶ αἰδώς.
entries.english: You have ears to hear, but your sense and your shame have gone.
entries.reading:
Ares has just learned that his son is dead. Wild with grief and fury, he calls for his horses, determined to go down and avenge the boy, though Zeus has forbidden the gods to fight. Athena reaches him before he reaches the battle. She pulls the helmet from his head, the shield from his shoulders, the spear from his hand, and tells him the truth to his face: you have ears to hear, but your sense and your shame have gone.

There is real pain in this scene. Ares is not merely reckless; he is bereaved. But pain has made him deaf. He has heard the command, and it means nothing to him; he has forgotten what he owes to others and what his act would bring down on them all.

This card asks whether some strong feeling, anger, hurt, jealousy, wounded pride, has taken your hearing. You may know the counsel; you may even be able to repeat it word for word. It simply is not reaching you. Let someone take the spear from your hand for an hour. Sit down. Feel the grief beneath the rage. Your sense and your shame are not lost forever; they are waiting for the noise to pass so they can speak again.
entries.context: In Iliad 15, Ares learns that his son Ascalaphus has been killed and arms himself to avenge him against Zeus' command. Athena stops him, taking his helmet, shield and spear, and rebukes him as a madman whose ears hear but whose sense and shame have perished.

aspects.love: In a quarrel you may be hearing every word your partner says and understanding none of it. Stop the argument before anything unforgivable is said. Return to it when you can listen as well as hear.
aspects.work: Anger at a decision is pushing you toward a move that breaks rules you agreed to keep. Let a trusted colleague talk you down. A night's pause costs little; a rash act could cost a great deal.
aspects.home: When family members are swept up in rage or grief, they may need someone to gently take away the weapon: the angry message, the slammed door, the drive in a temper. Be that person, kindly and firmly.
aspects.health: Strong emotions can override good sense about your own wellbeing. When you notice yourself refusing advice you know is right, pause and breathe. If the feeling will not settle, talk it through with someone who can help.
aspects.journeys: Do not make a sweeping decision in the heat of grief or fury. Let the feeling run its course before you choose the road. The right path will still be there when your hearing has returned.

entries.message: Hearing is not listening. When grief or rage drowns out sense, let someone take the spear from your hand.
entries.reflect: What have you heard clearly but refused to let in, because a strong feeling was louder?

entries.greek: γηράς· ἀλλʼ οὐχ υἱὸς ἐν ἔντεσι πατρὸς ἐγήρα.
entries.english: grew old; but the son did not grow old in his father's armour.
entries.reading:
Hector stands apart from the fighting and strips off his own armour, putting on the armour of Achilles, taken from the body of Patroclus. The poet pauses over it. These arms were a gift of the gods to Peleus, who wore them, grew old, and passed them to his son. But the son, Homer says, did not grow old in his father's armour. In one line we see Peleus aged and waiting at home, Achilles who will die young, and Hector, glittering in borrowed bronze, who will die in it sooner still.

This card asks you to look at what you have inherited or taken on: a family role, a trade, a name, a set of expectations, a position someone else held before you. Such armour can be magnificent, and it can protect you. It can also be heavy, ill-fitting, and carry a fate that was never meant for you.

The line does not tell you to throw your inheritance away. It asks you to wear it knowingly. Learn whose it was, and what it cost them. Honour it, but do not let it decide your whole life. The armour will pass on; you are the one who must live inside it, and live well, while you can.
entries.context: In Iliad 17, Hector puts on the armour of Achilles, which he has stripped from Patroclus. The poet recalls that the gods gave it to Peleus, who passed it on to his son when he grew old; but the son would not grow old in his father's armour.

aspects.love: You may be carrying patterns of love from your parents' marriage, good and bad. Notice which ones you are wearing without having chosen them. Keep what protects, and take off what was only ever theirs.
aspects.work: Stepping into a predecessor's role, or into a family business, brings honour and weight together. Respect what was built, but shape the work to your own strength rather than straining to fill someone else's shape.
aspects.home: An heirloom, a house or a family duty has come to you. Treasure it, but remember it is not the whole of who you are. The people around the hearth matter more than the bronze hanging on the wall.
aspects.health: Some families pass down physical tendencies as surely as they pass down furniture and faces. Knowing your inheritance can help you care for yourself wisely, without assuming that your parents' story must become yours. Their armour need not decide your fate.
aspects.journeys: Before you take up a path because it was your father's or your mother's, ask whether you would choose it freely. It is no betrayal to take a different road and carry their memory with you on it.

entries.message: What you inherit may outlast you. Wear it with honour, but do not mistake it for your own skin.
entries.reflect: What have you put on that once belonged to someone else, and does it truly fit you?

entries.greek: οἴκαδέ τʼ ἐλθέμεναι καὶ νόστιμον ἦμαρ ἰδέσθαι,
entries.english: to reach home and see the day of my return.
entries.reading:
In the palace at sandy Pylos, young Telemachus has lost heart. His father, he says, will never come home; the gods have settled his death. Beside him sits an old man who is really Athena in disguise, and she answers with a startling preference. She would rather suffer many hardships and then reach home and see the day of her return, than come home quickly and be cut down at her own hearth, as Agamemnon was on the very day he arrived.

This line is for anyone tired of the long way round. You have been struggling toward something, a recovery, a reconciliation, a return to a place or to yourself, and the road has been longer and rougher than you ever imagined. You may envy those who seemed to get there quickly.

The oracle invites another view. Speed is not the measure of a good homecoming; safety and wholeness are. Hard years can prepare you to arrive wiser and ready for what waits at the hearth, in a way an easy return could not. Agamemnon came home fast and unguarded. Odysseus came home late and ready. Keep going. The day of your return is worth every hardship that makes you fit to live it.
entries.context: In Odyssey 3, at Pylos, Telemachus despairs of his father's return. Athena, disguised as Mentor, answers that a god can easily save a man even from far away, and that she would rather suffer many hardships and then reach home and see the day of return than come home and be killed at her hearth, as Agamemnon was by Aegisthus and his wife.

aspects.love: A love that has been slow to settle may be stronger for the trials it has come through. Do not envy couples who seem to have had it easy. What you are building through difficulty can hold when the storms come.
aspects.work: Your progress has been slower than other people's, and that can gall. But a long apprenticeship in hardship is building judgement that a quick promotion never could. Better to arrive ready, with steady hands, than to arrive early and unprepared.
aspects.home: Returning home, or making a home, after hard years can feel long overdue. Let the delay make you careful with what you have come back to. Look at your hearth with fresh and grateful eyes.
aspects.health: Recovery is taking longer than you hoped. Hard as that is, a steady, patient return can last better than a quick one. Keep going, and mark each small sign that you are on the way home.
aspects.journeys: The long way round has its reasons. If your path to a goal keeps winding, use each detour to learn what you will need when you arrive. A rushed arrival could leave you unready for what is waiting.

entries.message: Better a hard road that ends at home than a quick arrival that ends in ruin. The length of the way is not your enemy.
entries.reflect: How might the length of your road be making you ready for what waits at the end of it?

entries.greek: τὸν μὲν ἄκουρον ἐόντα βάλʼ ἀργυρότοξος Ἀπόλλων
entries.english: Silver-bowed Apollo struck him down, still with no son,
entries.reading:
As Athena guides Odysseus toward the palace, she tells him the story of its queen. Arete's father, Rhexenor, was newly married when silver-bowed Apollo struck him down, still with no son. In a world that counted a house's future through its sons, his line seemed to end there. But he left a daughter. She grew up, married her uncle the king, and became Arete, honoured by her husband and her people beyond any woman on earth, the one who settles quarrels, the one Odysseus must win to get home.

This card speaks to a loss that seemed to cut something off: a plan that died early, a family line that ended, a hope that had no heir. You may feel that a story you cared about has simply stopped. The grief is real, and the line does not deny it. Apollo's arrow came, and nothing called it back.

Yet the line leads straight to Arete. What remains after a loss is not nothing. Sometimes it is the very thing that was overlooked, the daughter rather than the son, the small remnant rather than the grand design, and it grows into the centre of everything. Look carefully at what survived. Tend it. It may yet become what the whole house turns to.
entries.context: In Odyssey 7, Athena, disguised as a young girl, tells Odysseus about the family of Queen Arete. Her father Rhexenor was struck down by silver-bowed Apollo while still without a son, leaving only a daughter, Arete.

aspects.love: A relationship ended before it could become what you hoped. Grieve it honestly. Then notice what it left you, a friendship, a strength, a self you discovered, and let that remainder become something you value.
aspects.work: A project was cut short before it reached its goal. Look at what it produced along the way: the skills, the contacts, a smaller idea nobody noticed. That overlooked piece may be the real future of your work.
aspects.home: Families do not continue only through the expected lines. A daughter, a niece, an adopted child, a friend who became family over many years: honour whoever carries your household forward, whatever shape they take and however unlikely it once seemed.
aspects.health: A loss of some ability, or of a plan for your life, can feel like an ending. Grieve it, and then ask what strengths remain. Many people find that what survives can be built into a full and honoured life.
aspects.journeys: When one path is closed by forces beyond anyone's control, the option that remains may seem lesser. Give it a second look. What is left can turn out to be the road that leads you home.

entries.message: What looks like a line cut short may continue in a way no one expected. The one who remains can become the heart of the house.
entries.reflect: What remains after your loss that has not yet been given the honour it deserves?

entries.greek: ἐλπωρή τοι ἔπειτα φίλους τʼ ἰδέειν καὶ ἱκέσθαι
entries.english: then there is hope that you will see your friends and reach
entries.reading:
Odysseus is about to enter a palace where no one knows him. His guide, the disguised Athena, gives him one crucial piece of advice. Do not go first to the king. Go to the queen, Arete, honoured by all, wise enough to settle the quarrels even of men. If she looks on you with kindness, there is hope that you will see your friends again and reach your high-roofed house and your own country. Odysseus does exactly that, falling at her knees by the hearth.

Drawn for your question, this card points to the person whose goodwill really matters. In many situations the obvious authority, the title, the loudest voice, is not the one who decides. There is often an Arete: a quiet, respected figure whose judgement others trust. Your hope may run through them.

So look for the true centre of the house. Then approach with humility and honesty, not flattery. Arete was wise; she would have seen through a performance. Tell your story plainly, show who you are, and ask for what you need. Goodwill freely given by the right person can open roads that no amount of pushing would ever open. The way home often passes through a kind heart.
entries.context: In Odyssey 7, Athena, disguised as a young girl, tells Odysseus about Queen Arete, who is honoured by all and settles quarrels with her good sense. If Arete is kindly disposed to him, she says, there is hope that he will see his friends and reach his home and native land.

aspects.love: Being welcomed into a partner's family may depend less on its obvious head than on the quiet person everyone listens to. Show that person real respect and warmth. Their kindness can smooth your way to belonging.
aspects.work: The decision-maker on paper may not be the one whose opinion carries the day. Find the trusted adviser, the long-serving colleague, the person everyone quietly consults. Earn their goodwill through honest work and plain dealing, never through flattery.
aspects.home: In your own family someone is the Arete, the peacemaker whose word settles things. Seek their counsel in a dispute. If that person is you, recognise the trust others place in your judgement, and use it gently.
aspects.health: Finding the right helper can make all the difference to your wellbeing. Look for someone wise and kind, not merely impressive, and be honest with them. A good ally can help you find your way back.
aspects.journeys: In a new place, look for a respected local figure who can vouch for you: the elder of a congregation, the woman who runs the corner shop, the neighbour everyone greets. A single kind introduction may open more doors than months of effort alone.

entries.message: Your hope may run through one person's goodwill. Find who truly holds the heart of the house, and approach them with honest respect.
entries.reflect: Whose goodwill could open the way for you, and how might you approach them honestly?

entries.greek: σφῶϊν δʼ, ὡς ἔσεταί περ, ἀληθείην καταλέξω.
entries.english: To you two I will tell the truth, as it will be.
entries.theme: The Truth, As It Will Be
entries.reading:
Odysseus has shown his scar, and the two herdsmen are weeping in his arms. Now he does something kings rarely do with servants: he tells them the truth about the future, as it will be. If the god lets him overcome the suitors, he will give each of them a wife, goods and a house built near his own, and they will be to him as companions and brothers of his son. There is a condition in it, if the god allows, and a promise he means to keep.

This card comes to you when people have stood by you and deserve a straight word. You may be planning something, a change, a fight, a new venture, and there are loyal people whose lives will be shaped by it. They do not need flattery or vagueness. They need to know what you intend and what it will mean for them.

Speak honestly, including the conditions: what depends on things outside your control, and what you can surely give. Do not overpromise to soothe them, and do not underpromise to protect yourself. Then follow through. Odysseus kept faith with those who kept faith with him. Truth told before the battle is the foundation of trust after it.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, after revealing himself to the swineherd and cowherd, Odysseus tells them he will speak the truth about what will happen. If the god lets him overcome the suitors, he will give each of them a wife, possessions and a house near his own, and treat them as companions of Telemachus.

aspects.love: Someone who has waited for you deserves to know what you truly intend. Speak about the future honestly, with all its uncertainties, and promise only what you mean to give and can give. A plain truth will comfort them more than a bright vagueness.
aspects.work: The people who backed you need a clear account of what your plans mean for their roles and their rewards. Tell them directly, set out the conditions honestly, and keep every promise you make to them, even the small ones.
aspects.home: Family members affected by a coming change, a move, a new partner, a will, deserve the truth from you directly and not secondhand through rumour. Gather them and speak plainly about what will happen, and what you cannot yet know.
aspects.health: Be truthful with those who care for you about how you really are and what may lie ahead. Honest words let them help you well, and spare everyone the strain of pretending all is fine.
aspects.journeys: Before you set out, tell those coming with you what the road will really ask of them. Promise what you can give, admit what depends on fortune, and then keep faith with them all the way.

entries.message: To those who stood by you, speak plainly about what you mean to do, and then keep your word.
entries.reflect: Who has stood by you and is still waiting to hear plainly what your plans will mean for them?

entries.greek: ὧδε γὰρ ἐξερέω, τὸ δὲ καὶ τετελεσμένον ἔσται·
entries.english: For I will tell you this, and it will surely come to pass.
entries.reading:
Achilles' hand is on the hilt, the sword already half drawn, his rage fixed on Agamemnon. Then he feels a grip on his golden hair. Athena, seen by him alone, has come down from the sky. Stop, she tells him. Use words if you must, but not the blade. And she adds a promise: I will tell you this, and it will surely come to pass, a day when you are offered gifts three times as great for this insult. Achilles slides the sword home.

This line arrives at the edge of a rash act. You have been wronged, perhaps truly, and some part of you is ready to strike: to send the furious message, quit in a blaze, cut someone off, take what you feel is owed. The oracle does not tell you your anger is wrong. It tells you the sword is not the way.

Speak your grievance, clearly and even sharply if you must. But keep your hand off the hilt. What is just has a way of finding its owner when we stop trying to seize it by force; it rarely comes to those who burn everything to get it. Hold back. Give the matter time. The restraint you show today is the ground on which a fair outcome can stand.
entries.context: In Iliad 1, Achilles is drawing his sword against Agamemnon when Athena, sent by Hera, holds him back. She tells him to stop, to reproach Agamemnon with words only, and promises that one day he will be given gifts three times as great because of this insult.

aspects.love: You have been hurt and want to wound in return. Say what hurt you, honestly and firmly, but do not reach for the cruellest words you know. What is broken can be mended only if you leave something to mend.
aspects.work: Being passed over or insulted at work makes a dramatic exit tempting, and the speech is already written in your head. Voice your objection through proper channels instead. Restraint keeps your good name intact, and a fair outcome remains possible.
aspects.home: A family quarrel is close to breaking point. Step back before the blow that cannot be taken back, the word that would be remembered at every gathering for years. Speak your truth, then let time and calmer hearts do their slow work.
aspects.health: Anger held tightly can sour the body and spoil your sleep. Give it voice in safe ways, in words, in movement, in conversation with someone you trust, rather than in actions that harm you or others.
aspects.journeys: Do not make a sudden, angry decision about your future. Let the heat cool first. A choice made in rage often leads away from what you want; a patient one keeps the better road open.

entries.message: Hold back the blow you are about to strike. Say your piece, but leave the blade in its sheath.
entries.reflect: What would change if you said your piece but left the sword in its sheath?

entries.greek: πέμψω δʼ ὅππη μιν κραδίη θυμός τε κελεύει.
entries.english: and I will send him wherever his heart and spirit tell him to go.
entries.reading:
Telemachus is making promises about a stranger: clothes, a sword, sandals, and then the most generous gift of all, passage wherever the man's heart and spirit tell him to go. He does not mean to keep him, use him or bind him with obligations. He means to equip him and set him free. The irony, which only the gods and we can see, is that the beggar's heart already knows exactly where it wants to go. It wants to go home, into the very palace the young man is speaking of.

This card gives you a permission and asks a question. The permission: you are free to follow your own heart in this matter, not the expectations of others, not the safest course, not the road that would please the crowd. The question: do you know what your heart and spirit are telling you? Many of us have been obedient for so long that our own inner voice has gone quiet.

Take time to listen for it: in stillness, in walking, in honest talk with someone who knows you well. Beneath the noise there is usually a direction that has been calling for a long while, perhaps toward somewhere familiar. When you hear it, go. You have been given sandals for the road.
entries.context: In Odyssey 16, Telemachus speaks of the beggar in Eumaeus' hut, who is in truth his disguised father. He says he will give the stranger clothes, a sword and sandals, and send him wherever his heart and spirit tell him to go.

aspects.love: Love that sets the other free is the deepest kind. If you are holding someone close out of fear, consider letting them choose their own way. If you are the one being held, ask your heart honestly where it wants to be.
aspects.work: You have options, and the means to pursue one of them. Do not choose by default or out of fear. Ask which work your heart truly turns toward, and give it a serious and patient chance.
aspects.home: Children leaving home, or an adult child choosing an unexpected life, need equipping more than steering. Give them what they need for the road, a cloak, a blessing, a door left open, and let their own heart direct the rest.
aspects.health: Your body and spirit have their own sense of what restores them. Listen to that quiet guidance, whether it calls you to rest, to movement, to the sea, or to a place where you feel whole again, and follow it without apology.
aspects.journeys: You are free to go where you choose, and the means are in your hands. The harder work is listening: where does your spirit truly want to go? Answer that honestly, and the departure will follow.

entries.message: You are given leave to go where your own heart sends you. The question is whether you can hear what it is saying.
entries.reflect: If no one else's wishes counted for a moment, where would your heart send you?

entries.greek: πλαγκτέ; τάχʼ αὖ σʼ ἐφʼ ὕεσσι κύνες ταχέες κατέδονται
entries.english: you wanderer? Soon the swift dogs will eat you among the pigs,
entries.reading:
Eumaeus, the old swineherd, is carrying his master's bow across the crowded hall. One of the suitors, young and arrogant and full of wine, shouts after him: where are you taking that, you wretched wanderer? Soon your own swift dogs will eat you out among the pigs, if the gods are kind to us. It is a cruel, vivid insult, meant to remind the old man of his low place and frighten him into stopping.

Hear this line for what it is: the voice of people who are about to be proved wrong. The suitors mocked the faithful precisely because faithfulness threatened them. Within the hour, the bow they sneered at would be strung.

If you are being ridiculed for staying loyal, for doing humble work honestly, for carrying something to the one it belongs to, this card is for you. The sneer is not a verdict. It is a sign that you have touched something that matters. Do not answer in kind, and do not drop what you carry. Let the mockery fall behind you like noise in a hall. And if you notice yourself, in some corner of life, sneering at someone else's loyalty, stop and ask what in you feels threatened by it.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, the swineherd Eumaeus carries Odysseus' bow towards the disguised Odysseus. One of the arrogant young suitors shouts at him, calling him a wretched wanderer and saying his own dogs will soon eat him among the pigs, if Apollo and the other gods favour the suitors.

aspects.love: Friends may tease or scorn you for staying devoted to someone, or for waiting. Their laughter is no measure of what love is worth. Keep faith quietly, and let your steadiness be your only answer.
aspects.work: You are mocked for doing modest work with integrity while others cut corners and laugh about it. The sneer says more about them than about you. Keep your standards and carry on across the floor; the hall may soon look very different.
aspects.home: A family member's loyalty is being belittled by others in the house, perhaps as a running joke. Stand beside them openly. And if you are the one making cutting remarks about someone's devotion, notice it honestly, and choose kinder words.
aspects.health: Ridicule can sit in the body long after the words are spoken, tightening the jaw and stealing sleep. Shake off the insult deliberately: with good company, with movement, with a reminder of who you are and what you are faithful to.
aspects.journeys: Those who prefer you to stay small may jeer at your plans and predict your failure. Do not let their scorn turn you back. Finish carrying what you set out to carry, and let the result, in time, be your only answer to them.

entries.message: Scorn is often aimed at those doing the right thing. Let the sneer pass, and keep carrying what you were trusted with.
entries.reflect: Whose mockery has made you hesitate, and what does it tell you about the worth of what you carry?

entries.greek: γνοίης χʼ οἵη ἐμὴ δύναμις καὶ χεῖρες ἕπονται.
entries.english: you would learn how great my strength is, and how my hands obey me.
entries.reading:
In the courtyard, the disguised Odysseus swears an oath to the cowherd Philoetius: Odysseus will come home while you are still here, and you will see the suitors fall. The cowherd's answer is fierce and simple. If only Zeus would bring it about, then you would learn how great my strength is, and how my hands obey me. He is a herdsman, not a warrior. Yet he has been storing up his loyalty and his strength through years of insult, waiting for a cause worth spending them on.

This card is for the quiet strong. You may be someone whose capacities are mostly unseen, tending cattle, so to speak, while louder people hold the floor. You may even have begun to doubt that you have the force to act if it came to it. The line says otherwise. Strength that has been held in check, faithful and patient, is still strength. Your hands will obey you when the time comes.

Do not waste that strength on small quarrels or empty boasts. Keep it ready, and keep your heart pointed toward what you truly serve. When the right moment arrives, and it may come from a direction you do not expect, you may be surprised by how fully you rise to it.
entries.context: In Odyssey 20, the disguised Odysseus swears to the loyal cowherd Philoetius that Odysseus will come home while he is there and he will see the suitors killed. Philoetius replies that he wishes Zeus would fulfil this, for then the stranger would see how great his strength is and how his hands would follow.

aspects.love: You may not be showy in love, but your devotion runs deep and strong. When someone you love truly needs you, you will find your hands ready. Trust that, and stop measuring yourself against the loud.
aspects.work: Your abilities are underused where you are now. Keep them sharp anyway. When a real opportunity or crisis comes, you will be able to show what you can do, and others will learn what they overlooked.
aspects.home: In the family you may be the steady one in the background, rarely thanked and rarely noticed. When a real need arises, your strength will matter more than anyone expected. Keep yourself rested and ready for that day, and do not doubt it will find you.
aspects.health: Your body holds more resilience than you give it credit for. Build on it gently and patiently, so that when you call on it, it answers. Quiet, regular strengthening, like a herdsman's daily labour, is never wasted effort.
aspects.journeys: You have doubted whether you could manage a big change, and others may have doubted it too. Your capacity is greater than your fear suggests. When the moment comes to act, you will find that your hands follow your will.

entries.message: You have more strength than anyone has yet seen. Keep it ready for the cause that deserves it.
entries.reflect: What strength in you is waiting for a cause worthy of it?

entries.greek: οὔ τί σε τόνδʼ ἄξεσθαι ὀϊόμεθʼ· οὐδὲ ἔοικεν·
entries.english: We do not think he will marry you; that would not be right.
entries.reading:
Penelope has asked that the ragged stranger be allowed to try the bow. Eurymachus answers with mock reasonableness: no one imagines the beggar will marry you, my lady; that would hardly be fitting. What really troubles the suitors, he admits a moment later, is the talk. People would say that noble men could not string the bow, but some wandering beggar did it with ease. It is not propriety they are defending. It is their pride.

This line is a mirror, and a sharp one. Watch for the moments when you, or those around you, say that would not be right when what is meant is that would embarrass me. Fear of what people might say is one of the commonest reasons good things are kept from happening: the outsider is not given a chance, the unexpected candidate is turned away, the humble idea is never tried.

If you are the stranger at the door, shut out by someone else's pride, take heart. Penelope saw through it, and so did her son, and the bow came to the right hands. If you are the one guarding the door, ask yourself honestly what you fear. Being outdone is no disgrace. Refusing someone their fair turn is.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, Penelope asks that the beggar be allowed to try the bow. Eurymachus replies that the suitors do not think the stranger will marry her, which would not be fitting; rather, they are ashamed of what people would say if a beggar strung the bow that they could not.

aspects.love: You may be holding back from a person because of what others would think: a difference in background, age or standing. Ask whether the objection is truly about right and wrong, or only about appearances.
aspects.work: An outsider, a junior or an unconventional applicant deserves a fair turn at the bow. Do not dismiss them to protect the pride of the established, or your own. Let the results speak for themselves, and be gracious if they outshine you.
aspects.home: Families sometimes block a choice because of what the neighbours or relatives might say. Weigh whether the shame you fear is real or imagined, and whether it is worth the cost to the person you are holding back.
aspects.health: Worry about how you will look can stop you seeking help or trying something new for your wellbeing. The opinion of onlookers matters far less than your own good, and most of them are thinking about themselves. Step forward and try.
aspects.journeys: Do not let fear of gossip decide a major change. People talk about every bold choice. What matters is whether the choice is right for you, and whether you can bear a little talk for its sake.

entries.message: When pride hides behind propriety, it keeps the right person from the test. Ask what you are really afraid of.
entries.reflect: Where are you calling something improper when you are really afraid of how it would make you look?

entries.greek: ἐνθάδʼ ὁμιλέομεν, ποτιδέγμενοι ἤματα πάντα.
entries.english: We gather here, waiting day after day.
entries.reading:
Leodes was the gentlest of the suitors, the one who sat by the mixing bowl and disliked his companions' violence. Now he has tried the bow and failed, his soft hands worn by the string, and he says something close to despair: better to die than to live on and miss the prize for which we gather here, waiting day after day. He means the years of feasting in another man's house, eating his cattle, courting his wife, all in hope of a reward that was never theirs to win.

This card asks a searching question about your own waiting. Waiting can be a form of faithfulness. Penelope waited too, in the same house, through the same years. But the suitors waited in a different spirit: hanging on, consuming, hoping that time alone would hand them what they had not earned and did not rightly own.

Look honestly at what you are waiting for, and where. Is it truly yours? Is the waiting shaping you into someone better, or only keeping you from leaving? Some vigils should be kept. Others should be ended, with dignity, before they take more of your life. If this hall is not your home, you are free to rise from the feast and walk out into the daylight.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, the suitor Leodes fails to string the bow and declares that it will rob many champions of life and spirit. Better to die, he says, than to live and fail of the prize for which they gather in the house, waiting day after day.

aspects.love: You may be waiting for someone to choose you who has made it clear, in many quiet ways, that they will not. Waiting can be love, but it can also be a way of not living. Ask which this is.
aspects.work: You keep showing up for a promotion or reward that always seems about to arrive, next quarter, next year. Look at the evidence honestly. If it is not coming, consider taking your talents somewhere they will be valued and used.
aspects.home: A household can settle into a long, unspoken wait: for an apology, an inheritance, a change in someone's behaviour. Name the waiting aloud together. Decide what is worth waiting for, and what must be let go so the house can breathe.
aspects.health: Waiting for the perfect moment to make a change can stretch on for years. If you have been postponing care of yourself, begin in small ways now, rather than waiting for a day that keeps receding.
aspects.journeys: You have been lingering in a place because leaving feels like admitting defeat. It is not defeat. Walking out of a hall that is not yours, with your head up, is the beginning of finding one that is.

entries.message: Waiting is noble only when it is for what is truly yours. Ask whether you are keeping vigil or simply staying.
entries.reflect: Is your waiting a faithful vigil, or a habit of staying where nothing is truly yours?

entries.greek: κρυπτάδια φρονέοντα δικαζέμεν· οὐδέ τί πώ μοι
entries.english: to make your judgements in secret; and never yet
entries.reading:
On Olympus the feast has barely begun when Hera turns on her husband. She saw Thetis clasping his knees and knows that something has been decided. You always like it this way, she says, to make your judgements in secret, apart from me; never yet have you willingly told me what you are thinking. Zeus replies, coldly, that she should not hope to know all his counsels. The quarrel ripples through the hall until the gods are uneasy and their laughter strained.

This card speaks to secrecy in shared lives. Perhaps you are the one making decisions privately, believing it simpler, kinder or your right. Perhaps you are the one left guessing, piecing together what has been decided without you from glances and absences. Either way, the line names a hurt that goes beyond any single choice: the feeling of being shut out of the counsel of someone close.

Not everything needs to be shared, and some confidences are rightly kept. But if two people share a household, a work or a cause, decisions that shape both lives belong in the open. If you have been deciding in secret, invite the other in. If you have been shut out, say plainly what you need to know, without contempt. Trust grows where reasoning is shared.
entries.context: In Iliad 1, Hera sees that Thetis has been plotting with Zeus and taunts him, saying he always likes to make his judgements in secret, apart from her, and has never willingly told her his thoughts. Zeus answers that she should not hope to know all his words.

aspects.love: Decisions about money, time or the future are being made by one partner without the other. Bring them into the open, gently but without delay. Shared reasoning heals the quiet resentment that secret choices leave behind, even when the choices were sound.
aspects.work: A leader deciding behind closed doors breeds suspicion, even when the decisions themselves are good. If you lead, explain your reasoning before rumours explain it for you. If you are shut out, ask clearly and calmly to be included.
aspects.home: Parents, siblings or housemates are making plans that affect everyone without consulting them. Call a gathering around the table. A household runs better, and more kindly, when people know why things are decided and not merely what.
aspects.health: If you are keeping a worry about your wellbeing secret from those closest to you, consider sharing it. Hidden concerns grow heavier in the dark, and those who love you would rather know and help.
aspects.journeys: A big decision should not be sprung on the people it affects, however sure of it you are. Talk it through before it is final. Others may accept the change far better when they have been part of the counsel from the start.

entries.message: Decisions made behind closed doors breed suspicion. If you share a life, share the reasoning too.
entries.reflect: What decision affecting someone close to you are you making, or being kept from, behind closed doors?

entries.greek: μὴ δή μοι φύξίν γε Δόλων ἐμβάλλεο θυμῷ·
entries.english: Do not think of escape, Dolon, at all.
entries.reading:
Dolon has told them everything. He has given up the positions of the Trojan allies, the newly arrived Thracian king, the white horses, all in the hope of buying his life. Now he reaches up to touch Diomedes' chin in supplication. Diomedes looks at him grimly and speaks: do not think of escape, Dolon, at all. If we let you go, you would only come back to spy again. The bargain Dolon thought he was making was never on offer.

This is the final throw of the oracle, six upon six upon six, and it is one of the sternest. It speaks of the moment when the exits close. Perhaps you have been trying to talk your way out of a consequence, offering more and more in the hope that the reckoning will go away. Perhaps you made a reckless bid, as Dolon did when he volunteered for the night mission dreaming of Achilles' horses, and now the cost has come due.

The line offers no false comfort, and neither will this card. But there is dignity in ceasing to bargain. Stop running in circles in the dark. Face what has come, own your part in it plainly, and do not betray what you value in a panic to save yourself. How you meet the moment is still yours to choose.
entries.context: In Iliad 10, the Trojan spy Dolon, captured at night, has told Odysseus and Diomedes everything and begs to be spared. Diomedes, glaring at him, tells him not to think of escape, since if they let him go he would come again to spy; then he kills him.

aspects.love: If you have hurt someone and are trying to escape the consequences with promises and explanations, stop. Accept what your actions have cost. Honesty now will not undo the harm, but it keeps your integrity whole.
aspects.work: A mistake has caught up with you, and no clever explanation will make it vanish. Own it directly and early. People respect the one who faces a reckoning more than the one who keeps looking for a way out.
aspects.home: A family situation has reached the point where avoidance no longer works, and everyone can feel it. The conversation must be had. Go into it honestly, owning your part, without trading away anyone's trust in an attempt to protect yourself.
aspects.health: Some realities about your health or habits cannot be bargained with or put off any longer. Face them calmly and seek good, qualified help. Facing the truth is the first step toward whatever can still be done.
aspects.journeys: A risky venture you took on has not gone as you hoped, and there is no easy way back. Accept where you stand. From that honest ground you can still choose, with dignity, what to do next.

entries.message: Some consequences cannot be talked away. Stop bargaining with what has come, and meet it with your eyes open.
entries.reflect: What are you still trying to bargain your way out of, and what would it mean to face it instead?

translation: English translations made for this app from the Greek (Monro and Allen's Iliad, Murray's 1919 Odyssey Greek text); free to use with the app.
readings: Theme, message, reading, reflection, the scene in Homer and the five areas of life (love, work, home, health, journeys) are our own modern interpretation, written for this app; they are not part of the ancient papyrus.
